Introduction to Commodity Markets.overview: This chapter introduces commodities as an asset class: how physical (spot) markets work, the difference between forward and futures contracts, the evolution of commodity derivatives trading in India and the roles of exchanges, hedgers, speculators and arbitrageurs. It also covers the ecosystem that supports physical delivery, such as warehouses, assayers and electronic warehouse receipts. When revising, focus on why commodity derivatives exist (price discovery and price-risk management), how forwards differ from exchange-traded futures, and the classification of commodities into agricultural, bullion, base metals and energy.
questions: Compared with an over-the-counter forward contract, an exchange-traded commodity futures contract mainly removes which risk for the two parties?
Price risk, because futures prices cannot move against either party
Basis risk, because futures always converge to the local mandi price at expiry
Liquidity risk in the underlying physical commodity market
Counterparty default risk, as the clearing corporation guarantees settlement

The clearing corporation becomes the counterparty to every trade and collects margins, so default risk is largely removed. Price risk remains with the position holder, and basis risk still exists between futures and local spot prices.
A trader buys silver futures purely because he expects prices to rise over the next week and has no exposure to physical silver. He is best described as a:
Hedger
Speculator
Arbitrageur
Market maker

A speculator takes a position to profit from expected price moves without an underlying physical exposure. A hedger offsets an existing risk, while an arbitrageur exploits price differences between markets.
Which of the following is a key economic function of commodity futures markets?
Fixing minimum support prices for agricultural crops for each crop season
Providing working-capital loans to farmers against stored crops
Setting import duties on bullion and edible oils
Price discovery, giving producers and users a forward reference price
Futures markets aggregate the views of many participants and so discover expected future prices. MSP is fixed by the government, loans come from banks and duties are a fiscal decision.
Copper, zinc, aluminium and nickel are grouped in commodity markets as:
Bullion
Energy commodities
Base metals
Soft commodities

Industrial non-ferrous metals such as copper, zinc, aluminium and nickel are called base metals. Bullion refers to precious metals like gold and silver, and soft commodities are agricultural products.
An electronic negotiable warehouse receipt (e-NWR) is useful to a farmer mainly because it:
Guarantees that the produce will be sold at the minimum support price announced by government
Can be pledged for finance or transferred without moving the produce
Exempts the stored produce from quality testing by the warehouse
Converts the produce automatically into an open futures position
An e-NWR is a transferable electronic title to goods stored in a registered warehouse, so it can be used as collateral or traded. It does not guarantee any price and stored goods are still graded.
Why are commodity markets typically more exposed to seasonality than equity markets?
Commodity exchanges are open only during the harvest months
Commodity prices are fixed by the government outside the harvest season
Supply of many agricultural commodities depends on sowing and harvest cycles
Equity prices are set annually while commodity prices change monthly
Agricultural output arrives in harvest seasons, so supply, stocks and prices follow seasonal patterns. Exchanges trade all year and prices are market-determined, not fixed by government.
A jeweller in Jaipur buys gold in the spot market and simultaneously sells gold futures when futures trade well above the full cost of carry. The jeweller is acting as a/an:
Speculator, betting that gold prices will rise sharply over the coming months
Arbitrageur, locking in the gap over carrying cost
Hedger of a future purchase requirement
Market maker earning only the bid-ask spread
Buying spot and selling overpriced futures (cash-and-carry) locks in a near riskless gain if futures exceed spot plus carrying costs. It is an arbitrage, not a directional bet or a purchase hedge.
Which statement about participants in Indian commodity derivatives markets is correct as per the current framework?
Eligible FPIs may trade non-agricultural commodity derivatives, subject to SEBI conditions
Only farmers and farmer producer organisations may trade agricultural futures on exchanges
Mutual funds are prohibited from taking any exposure at all to commodity derivatives
Retail individuals may trade only options and not futures

SEBI has opened commodity derivatives to institutional participants such as eligible FPIs (in non-agricultural contracts), mutual funds and PMS within limits. Retail investors may trade both futures and options.

Commodity Indices.overview: This chapter explains how commodity indices are built and used. It covers spot-based versus futures-based indices, the choice of constituents and weights (for example production- or liquidity-based weighting), the roll mechanism for futures indices, and the sources of return in a futures index: spot return, roll yield and collateral return. It also introduces Indian commodity indices and index futures. Revise the purpose of an index, how contango and backwardation affect roll yield, and why rebalancing and weighting rules matter for an index that is used as a tradeable benchmark.
questions: In a commodity futures index, the return earned from replacing an expiring contract with a cheaper later contract when the market is in backwardation is called:
Collateral yield
Spot return
Positive roll yield
Convenience premium

In backwardation, later contracts trade below the expiring one, so rolling means selling high and buying lower, producing a positive roll yield. Spot return comes from changes in spot prices and collateral yield from interest on margin money.
A commodity futures index has consistently underperformed the spot price of its main constituent over several years. The most likely reason is that the futures curve has been in:
Backwardation, causing positive roll yield
Perfect convergence with zero basis
Inverted spread with a high convenience yield
Contango, causing negative roll yield
When futures are in contango, each roll buys a dearer contract, so index returns lag the spot price. Backwardation would have the opposite effect and add to returns.
The three components of the total return of a fully collateralised commodity futures index are:
Dividend yield, roll yield and currency return
Spot return, storage cost and insurance cost
Coupon return, roll yield and inflation return
Spot return, roll yield and interest on collateral
A fully collateralised index earns from spot price changes, from rolling contracts along the curve, and from interest on the cash backing the futures. Commodities pay no dividends or coupons.
Why might an index provider cap the weight of a single commodity in a diversified commodity index?
To ensure that the index always rises when inflation rises
Because exchanges prohibit indices containing more than one energy product
To eliminate the need for rolling futures contracts
To prevent one commodity's price moves from dominating index behaviour
Weight caps keep the index diversified so that a single commodity, such as crude oil, does not drive most of the index's risk. They do not remove rolling or guarantee any inflation link.
An index that weights constituents in proportion to the value of their world production is said to use:
Equal weighting
Liquidity-based weighting
Price-weighting by contract size
Production-based weighting
Production-value weighting reflects each commodity's economic importance. Liquidity-based weighting uses trading volumes instead, and equal weighting gives each constituent the same share.
A spot-price commodity index differs from a futures-based index in that a spot index:
Includes roll yield and interest on collateral in its reported returns
Is the only type of index permitted to have index futures in India
Is always calculated only once at the end of each month
Tracks physical prices and is hard for an investor to replicate

A spot index tracks current physical prices, which an investor cannot easily hold because of storage and delivery issues. Futures-based indices are designed to be investable and include roll and collateral returns.
An Indian exchange launches futures on a bullion index. Compared with buying separate gold and silver futures, a trader using the index future mainly gains:
Physical delivery of gold and silver in fixed proportions
Protection from all price falls in gold and silver
Exemption from margin requirements
A single position giving diversified exposure to the bullion basket
Index futures offer exposure to a basket through one contract. They are cash-settled, so no physical delivery takes place, and they carry normal price risk and margin requirements.
A commodity index is rebalanced annually to its target weights. After a year in which crude oil rose sharply and grains fell, rebalancing will typically:
Add further to crude oil and reduce grains
Leave weights unchanged, as rebalancing affects only roll dates
Reduce the weight of crude oil and add to grains
Remove grains from the index permanently

Rebalancing restores target weights, so outperformers like crude, now overweight, are trimmed and underperformers, now underweight, are topped up. Constituents are not removed merely because of one year's fall.

Commodity Futures.overview: This chapter covers the pricing and features of commodity futures. Key topics are the cost-of-carry model (spot price plus interest, storage and insurance, less convenience yield), contango and backwardation, basis and convergence, contract specifications (lot size, tick size, quotation unit, delivery centre, quality grade) and the different settlement types: compulsory delivery, both-option delivery and cash settlement against a reference price. Practise numerical questions on fair value, basis and profit or loss per lot, and understand how delivery logistics and grade differentials affect the price at which a contract finally settles.
questions: A commodity trades at ₹4,800 per quintal in the spot market. With a 9% annual (simple) financing rate and storage charges of ₹20 per quintal for two months, what should a two-month futures contract be worth?
Interest for two months is 4,800 × 9% × 2/12 = ₹72. Fair price = 4,800 + 72 + 20 = ₹4,892. ₹4,872 ignores storage cost, and ₹4,820 ignores interest.
As a commodity futures contract approaches expiry, its price should move towards the spot price at the delivery centre. This process is called:
Contango
Rolling
Convergence
Backwardation

Near expiry the carrying period shrinks to zero, so futures and spot prices come together; this is convergence. Contango and backwardation describe the shape of the futures curve, not the expiry process.
A trader buys 3 lots of a commodity future, each of 1,000 units, at ₹215.50. The day's settlement price is ₹212.80. His mark-to-market result is:
Loss of ₹8,100
Profit of ₹8,100
Loss of ₹2,700
Loss of ₹81,000
Change per unit = 212.80 − 215.50 = −₹2.70. For a long position of 3 × 1,000 units, loss = 2.70 × 3,000 = ₹8,100. ₹2,700 would be the loss on a single lot.
Crude oil futures on Indian exchanges are commonly settled in cash rather than by delivery. Their final settlement price is generally linked to:
The average retail price of petrol in the four metro cities
The price fixed by the oil ministry for refiners
The settlement price of a benchmark international crude oil futures contract
The closing price of the near-month Indian contract on the first trading day

Cash-settled energy contracts in India typically settle against a reference price derived from an international benchmark contract, converted to rupees. Retail fuel prices and ministry prices are not used.
Which factor would cause the futures price of a storable commodity to trade BELOW its spot price?
An increase in interest rates
A rise in warehousing charges
An increase in insurance costs on stored goods
A high convenience yield because current stocks are scarce

When inventories are tight, holders value physical stock highly and the convenience yield can outweigh carrying costs, pushing futures below spot (backwardation). Higher interest, storage or insurance raise the futures price.
In a 'both-option' delivery contract, which statement is correct about positions open at expiry?
Every open position must be settled by physical delivery at the delivery centre without any exception
All open positions are closed out at the international reference price
Delivery occurs only where the seller's and buyer's delivery intentions are matched
Only the buyer can choose whether delivery will take place

In both-option contracts, delivery happens when the seller's intention to deliver is matched with a buyer's intention to take delivery; unmatched positions are cash settled. Compulsory delivery contracts require delivery of all open positions.
A spot price of ₹60,000 and a three-month futures price of ₹60,900 imply an annualised cost of carry (simple) of about:
The three-month premium is 900 ÷ 60,000 = 1.5%. Annualised, 1.5% × 4 = 6%. 1.5% is the unannualised figure, a common mistake.
A commodity's contract specification says 'tick size ₹1 per quintal, trading unit 10 MT'. The value of a one-tick move per lot is:
10 MT equals 100 quintals. A ₹1 per quintal move therefore changes the lot value by 100 × ₹1 = ₹100. Using 10 or 1,000 confuses the units.

Commodity Options.overview: This chapter covers options on commodity futures and options on goods as traded in India. Learners should know call and put pay-offs, intrinsic and time value, moneyness, break-even points, the factors affecting option premiums (underlying price, strike, time, volatility and interest rates) and the option Greeks. It also explains Indian contract features such as European-style exercise, devolvement of exercised options on futures into futures positions, and the exercise of in-the-money options at expiry. Practise pay-off calculations and the impact of volatility and time decay on long and short option positions.
questions: A trader buys a put option on a commodity with a strike of ₹900 at a premium of ₹25. The lot is 100 units. If the underlying settles at ₹850 at expiry, his net profit is:
Intrinsic value at expiry = 900 − 850 = ₹50. Net profit per unit = 50 − 25 = ₹25, so for 100 units profit = ₹2,500. ₹5,000 ignores the premium paid.
A gold call option has a strike of ₹71,000 while the underlying futures trade at ₹72,500 and the premium is ₹1,900. The time value of the option is:
Intrinsic value = 72,500 − 71,000 = ₹1,500. Time value = premium − intrinsic value = 1,900 − 1,500 = ₹400.
Other things remaining the same, an increase in the expected volatility of the underlying commodity will:
Increase call premiums but reduce put premiums
Reduce the premiums of both calls and puts
Increase the premiums of both calls and puts
Have no effect, as volatility affects only futures prices
Higher volatility raises the chance of large favourable moves for both calls and puts, so both premiums rise. The holder's loss is limited to the premium, so the extra volatility is valuable to both.
An option writer who has sold a call is most concerned about which Greek increasing sharply as expiry approaches for an at-the-money option?
Gamma
Rho
Vega of a far-month option
Lambda of the futures
Gamma, the rate of change of delta, is highest for at-the-money options near expiry, so the writer's exposure can swing rapidly. Rho measures interest-rate sensitivity and is usually minor.
A put option on crude oil futures has a strike of ₹6,500 and the futures are trading at ₹6,700. The put is:
In the money
Out of the money
At the money
Deep in the money
A put has intrinsic value only when the underlying is below the strike. With futures at ₹6,700 above the ₹6,500 strike, the put is out of the money.
In options on commodity futures in India, a long call that is exercised results in the holder getting:
A long futures position at the strike price
Delivery of the physical commodity at the strike price immediately
A short futures position at the prevailing market price
Cash equal to the premium paid, returned to him by the exchange
Exercised options on futures devolve into futures positions: the call buyer gets a long futures position at the strike price and the writer gets the matching short position.
Time decay (theta) generally works in favour of:
Option buyers
Option writers
Holders of long futures positions
Both option buyers and writers equally
As time passes, the time value of options erodes. Writers have received the premium and gain as time value falls, while buyers lose. Futures positions have no time value.
Using put-call parity for European options on futures, if the call and put on the same strike have equal premiums, the futures price is most likely:
Well above the strike price
Equal to the strike price
Well below the strike price
Equal to zero, as parity has broken down
Put-call parity for options on futures gives C − P = (F − K) discounted. If C equals P, then F equals K, so the futures price is at the strike.

Strategies using Commodity Futures and O.overview: This chapter applies futures and options to real needs: hedging by producers, processors, traders and consumers, speculation, arbitrage and spread trading. Topics include short and long hedges, basis risk, hedge ratios and the number of contracts, calendar and inter-commodity spreads (such as crack and crush spreads), and option strategies like protective puts, covered calls, bull and bear spreads, straddles and strangles. When revising, practise identifying the right hedge for a business exposure, computing effective prices after a hedge and finding the maximum profit, maximum loss and break-even of common option strategies.
questions: A trader buys a ₹6,000 strike call at ₹180 and sells a ₹6,200 strike call at ₹90 on the same commodity and expiry. His maximum profit per unit is:
This bull call spread costs a net ₹90 (180 − 90). The maximum pay-off is the strike difference of ₹200, so maximum profit = 200 − 90 = ₹110. The maximum loss is the ₹90 net premium.
A trader buys a gold call and a gold put, both with strike ₹72,000, paying ₹1,100 and ₹900 respectively. His break-even prices at expiry are:
A long straddle costs 1,100 + 900 = ₹2,000. It breaks even when the price moves ₹2,000 either side of the strike: ₹70,000 and ₹74,000.
A refiner fears that the margin between crude oil prices and product prices will narrow. A position in crude oil futures against offsetting positions in petroleum product futures is known as a:
Crush spread
Calendar spread
Crack spread
Butterfly spread
The crack spread captures the refining margin between crude and its products. The crush spread relates soybeans to meal and oil, while a calendar spread uses different expiries of the same commodity.
A copper importer must buy 50,000 kg in two months. The optimal hedge ratio is 0.8 and one futures lot is 5,000 kg. The number of lots to buy is:
Number of lots = hedge ratio × exposure ÷ lot size = 0.8 × 50,000 ÷ 5,000 = 8. Ten lots would be a one-to-one hedge ignoring the hedge ratio.
A cotton mill buys cotton futures at ₹5,200 to hedge a future purchase. When it buys cotton in the spot market at ₹5,600, it closes the futures at ₹5,550. Its effective purchase cost is:
Futures gain = 5,550 − 5,200 = ₹350. Effective cost = spot price − futures gain = 5,600 − 350 = ₹5,250. The difference from ₹5,200 reflects the change in basis.
A farmer holding a short futures hedge will be better off than expected when the basis (spot minus futures):
Weakens, i.e. becomes more negative
Strengthens, i.e. becomes more positive
Remains exactly unchanged
Becomes equal to the cost of carry
A short hedger is long the physical and short futures, so he gains if spot rises relative to futures, which is a strengthening basis. A weakening basis hurts the short hedger.
A stockist holding chana inventory writes call options on chana futures against it. This strategy, which earns premium but caps upside, is a:
Covered call
Protective put
Long strangle
Bear put spread
Writing calls against an existing long position is a covered call: the premium cushions small falls but gains above the strike are given up. A protective put would buy a put instead.
A trader buys near-month cardamom futures and sells far-month cardamom futures, expecting the price gap to narrow. This is an example of a/an:
Inter-commodity spread
Inter-exchange arbitrage
Outright directional position
Calendar (intra-commodity) spread
Positions in the same commodity across different expiries form a calendar or intra-commodity spread, which profits from changes in the price difference rather than the overall price level.

Trading Mechanism.overview: This chapter explains how commodity derivatives are traded on Indian exchanges. It covers the electronic order-matching system, order types (limit, market, stop-loss, immediate-or-cancel and good-till types), price-time priority, trading sessions for agricultural and non-agricultural contracts, daily price limits, position limits, contract launch calendars and the rules on client registration such as KYC and unique client codes. Revise how orders are matched, what each order type does, why price bands and position limits exist, and the responsibilities of trading members towards clients when accepting and executing orders.
questions: On an electronic commodity exchange, two buy orders are at the same price. Which order is executed first?
The order for the larger quantity
The order placed by a hedger rather than a speculator
The order placed by an institutional client
The order that was entered earlier in time
Exchanges follow price-time priority: at the same price, the order entered first is matched first. Size, client type or purpose of the trade do not change priority.
A trader wants to buy only if the price rises to ₹9,150 so as to limit losses on an existing short position. Which order suits this need?
A sell limit order at ₹9,150
A buy stop-loss order with a trigger price of ₹9,150
A buy limit order at ₹8,800
An immediate-or-cancel sell order at the market price
A stop-loss buy order becomes active only when the trigger price is reached, so it caps losses on a short position. A buy limit order at a lower price would not protect against a rise.
An immediate-or-cancel (IOC) order on a commodity exchange:
Remains in the order book until the end of the trading day
Is executed only at the closing session price
Must be fully executed or else it is converted to a market order
Executes whatever quantity is available at once and cancels the rest
An IOC order is matched immediately to the extent possible and any unexecuted quantity is cancelled. A day order would remain in the book until the session ends.
The unique client code (UCC) used in commodity derivatives trading mainly helps to:
Fix the brokerage rate payable by each client to the member
Decide which accredited warehouse a client must use for any delivery
Exempt small clients from margin requirements
Track each client's trades and positions for surveillance
The UCC links every order to a specific client, allowing exchanges to monitor client-level positions, enforce limits and detect manipulation. It has no role in brokerage or warehouse allocation.
When a commodity futures contract hits its daily price limit, exchanges typically:
Cancel all trades executed during the day and refund all margins collected to the members
Close the contract permanently and settle at the previous day's price
Permit trades only within the band, relaxing it in phases after a cooling-off
Allow unlimited price movement for the rest of the day
Daily price limits restrict trades beyond the band. Exchanges usually provide for a cooling-off period and phased relaxation of the limit, rather than cancelling trades or delisting the contract.
Client-level position limits in an agricultural commodity are usually linked to:
The estimated deliverable supply or production of that commodity
The client's annual income as declared in the KYC form
The broker's net worth only
The number of trading days left in the contract

For agricultural commodities, position limits are generally set with reference to the deliverable supply so that no single participant can corner the market. The client's income is relevant for suitability, not exchange limits.
A client calls his broker to place an order but does not specify the price. The broker places a market order. A market order:
Has execution certainty but no price certainty
Has price certainty but no execution certainty
Is executed only at the previous day's settlement price
Can be modified by the exchange to the best bid of the next day
A market order is executed immediately against the best available counter-orders, so the trade is almost certain but the price is not known in advance. A limit order provides price certainty instead.
Before trading in commodity derivatives, a client receives the 'Risk Disclosure Document'. Its main purpose is to:
Guarantee a minimum return to clients who follow the broker's research advice
Record the client's bank account details for margin payments
Exempt the broker from any liability for errors in execution
Explain the risks of leveraged trading so the client decides knowingly
The risk disclosure document informs clients about leverage, volatility, liquidity and other risks of derivatives trading. It gives no guarantee and does not exempt brokers from their obligations.

Clearing, Settlement and Risk Management.overview: This chapter covers what happens after a trade: novation by the clearing corporation, the margining system (initial or SPAN-type margin, extreme loss margin, mark-to-market, additional and delivery margins), daily settlement, final settlement by cash or delivery, the delivery process through accredited warehouses and vaults, and the Settlement Guarantee Fund. It also explains risk controls such as position limits and capital adequacy of clearing members. Focus on how margins are computed and collected, the sequence of the delivery process, and how the clearing corporation manages defaults to protect the market.
questions: Through novation, the clearing corporation in a commodity futures trade:
Acts only as a record keeper without taking any counterparty role
Transfers the trade to a warehouse for delivery on the same day
Guarantees a profit to both the buyer and the seller
Becomes the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer
Novation substitutes the clearing corporation as counterparty to both sides, which is the basis of its settlement guarantee. It does not guarantee profits and is not merely a record keeper.
A trader buys one gold mini contract of 100 grams at ₹72,000 per 10 grams. If the initial margin is 8%, the initial margin required is:
Contract value = (100 ÷ 10) × 72,000 = ₹7,20,000. Initial margin at 8% = ₹57,600. ₹7,20,000 is the full contract value, not the margin.
The Settlement Guarantee Fund (Core SGF) maintained by a clearing corporation is used to:
Pay daily mark-to-market profits to all clients
Fund the exchange's technology and staff costs
Meet settlement obligations if a clearing member defaults
Compensate traders for losses due to price movements
The core SGF is a default fund that allows the clearing corporation to complete settlement when a member fails. Normal MTM pay-outs come from losing members, and market losses are not compensated.
Mark-to-market settlement in commodity futures means that:
Profits are paid only when the position is finally closed or the contract expires
Margins are fixed once at the start of the contract and are never revised by the exchange afterwards
Only losses are collected while profits are held back until expiry
Open positions are revalued at the daily settlement price and gains or losses settled daily
MTM settles notional gains and losses daily against the settlement price, preventing losses from accumulating. Profits are credited and losses debited each day.
Which margin is designed to cover losses in situations beyond those captured by the normal VaR-based initial margin?
Mark-to-market margin
Pay-in margin
Extreme loss margin
Delivery period margin
The extreme loss margin is an additional buffer for price moves larger than those assumed in the VaR or SPAN-based initial margin. MTM covers realised daily losses, not tail risk.
In a compulsory-delivery agricultural contract, a seller wishing to deliver must ensure that the commodity:
Is transported directly to the buyer's factory by the seller at the seller's own cost and risk
Is sold first in the local mandi and the sale proceeds deposited with the exchange
Is in an accredited warehouse and meets the contract's quality specifications
Is certified only by the seller's own quality inspector
Exchange deliveries take place through accredited warehouses, and the goods must be tested and certified by approved assayers as meeting contract specifications. Self-certification is not accepted.
A clearing member fails to pay MTM losses on time. The clearing corporation is most likely to first:
Cancel the trades of the member's clients from the very start of the contract
Ask the opposite counterparties to accept lower payments for that day's settlement
Block the member's trading and close out positions using its collateral
Suspend trading on the entire exchange for the day

The clearing corporation acts against the defaulting member by blocking trading, closing out positions and using the member's margins and collateral, then other default resources if needed. Counterparties are still paid in full.
A clearing corporation increases margins on a contract when it enters the delivery period mainly because:
Exchanges earn more fees from higher margins
The risk of delivery default and price manipulation rises close to expiry
Delivery contracts are not covered by the Settlement Guarantee Fund
Speculators are legally barred from holding positions in the delivery period
Near expiry, open positions turn into delivery obligations, increasing the risk of default and squeeze. Higher delivery-period margins protect the system. Margins are not a fee income.

Legal and Regulatory Environment.overview: This chapter covers the legal framework for commodity derivatives in India after the merger of the Forward Markets Commission with SEBI. It explains the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act and the inclusion of commodity derivatives as securities, the SEBI Act, regulations on stock brokers and intermediaries, the notification of commodities by the Central Government, the role of exchanges and clearing corporations, and the regulation of warehousing. Revise who regulates what, the powers of SEBI and exchanges, the reasons for position limits and surveillance, and why the old Forward Contracts (Regulation) Act was repealed.
questions: After the FMC–SEBI merger, the Forward Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1952 was:
Retained as the main law with SEBI as its administrator
Repealed, with commodity derivatives brought under the SCRA framework
Amended to apply only to agricultural commodities
Merged into the Warehousing (Development and Regulation) Act
The Finance Act, 2015 repealed the FCRA and brought commodity derivatives within the definition of securities under the SCRA, with SEBI as regulator. The warehousing law is separate.
Which body regulates the warehouses that issue negotiable warehouse receipts in India?
Securities and Exchange Board of India
Warehousing Development and Regulatory Authority
Reserve Bank of India
Food Corporation of India

The WDRA regulates warehouses under the Warehousing (Development and Regulation) Act, 2007, including registration and e-NWRs. SEBI regulates exchanges and intermediaries, while FCI is a procurement agency.
A stock broker wishes to offer commodity derivatives trading to clients. Under current SEBI rules it must:
Obtain a separate licence from the Ministry of Consumer Affairs for each commodity it wishes to offer
Register with the WDRA as a warehouse service provider
Be a SEBI-registered stock broker with membership of the exchange's commodity segment
Only obtain approval from its bank for handling client funds
Commodity derivatives brokers are SEBI-registered stock brokers with membership of the relevant segment of a recognised exchange. No separate ministry or WDRA licence is required for broking.
Why are exchanges required to run surveillance on commodity derivative contracts?
To detect manipulation, abnormal price moves and position concentration
To ensure that prices of agricultural commodities never fall below the minimum support price
To fix daily closing prices for each contract
To approve each client's trading strategy in advance
Surveillance identifies unusual trading, manipulation and excessive concentration so corrective action can be taken. It does not target any particular price level or pre-approve strategies.
SEBI may suspend trading in a particular agricultural commodity derivative. The most likely reason is:
The commodity having too many registered warehouses in the producing states
A fall in trading volumes on the exchange for one day
A request from a single large trader holding a losing position in that contract
Concerns about excessive volatility or its effect on food inflation
Regulators have occasionally suspended trading in sensitive agricultural contracts amid inflation or volatility concerns. A single trader's losses or warehouse numbers are not grounds for suspension.
Recognised commodity derivatives exchanges in India must have a separate clearing corporation mainly to:
Allow the exchange to avoid SEBI regulation of its trading platform
Enable the exchange to own and operate warehouses directly
Separate trading from clearing and strengthen risk management
Provide loans to clients for margin payments when prices move sharply
Separating clearing into a distinct entity improves risk management and governance. Clearing corporations are themselves regulated by SEBI and do not provide margin loans.
Under SEBI's regulations, which entity's rules, bye-laws and regulations govern day-to-day trading conduct of members in commodity derivatives?
The recognised stock exchange on which the member trades
The Commodity Board of the relevant crop
The Central Warehousing Corporation
The state agricultural produce market committee
Members are bound by the rules, bye-laws and regulations of the recognised exchange, approved by SEBI. Commodity boards and APMCs regulate physical markets, not exchange trading.
A person repeatedly places and cancels large orders without the intention of trading, to create a false impression of demand. This practice is:
Legitimate hedging
Spoofing, a prohibited manipulative practice
Permitted arbitrage
Normal market making
Placing orders without intent to execute, to mislead other participants, is spoofing, which is prohibited under SEBI's rules on fraudulent and unfair trade practices.

Accounting and Taxation.overview: This chapter explains how commodity derivative transactions are accounted for and taxed. It covers the accounting treatment of margin deposits, daily mark-to-market settlements, open positions at year-end and hedging under applicable accounting guidance, as well as Commodity Transaction Tax, the treatment of profits as business income, the distinction between speculative and non-speculative transactions, GST implications on physical delivery and the treatment of exchange charges and brokerage. Focus on concepts rather than rates that change frequently, and on how hedging transactions are distinguished from trading for accounting purposes.
questions: Initial margin paid to a broker for commodity futures is generally shown in the trader's books as:
An expense in the profit and loss account
A current asset, as a deposit recoverable on closure of positions
Income received in advance
Part of the cost of the commodity purchased
Initial margin is a deposit, not an expense, so it appears as a current asset until positions are closed. Only realised and MTM gains or losses affect profit.
On which of the following commodity derivative transactions is Commodity Transaction Tax generally NOT payable?
Derivatives on agricultural commodities notified as exempt
Futures on gold traded on a recognised stock exchange in India
Options on crude oil futures
Futures on base metals such as copper
CTT applies to non-agricultural commodity derivatives; derivatives on specified agricultural commodities are exempt. Gold, crude oil and base metal contracts attract CTT.
Why is trading in exchange-traded commodity derivatives, on which CTT is paid, treated as non-speculative for income-tax purposes?
Tax law excludes eligible exchange trades from speculative transactions
Because all commodity contracts on Indian exchanges are settled by compulsory physical delivery
Because commodity profits are fully exempt from tax
Because CTT replaces income tax on such profits

The tax law carves out eligible commodity derivative trades on recognised exchanges from speculative transactions, so they are non-speculative business income. CTT is an additional transaction tax, not a substitute for income tax.
A trader has a non-speculative business loss from commodity futures this year. Under the income-tax rules, this loss can generally be:
Set off only against speculative income of the same year and of later assessment years
Set off against salary income in the same year
Set off against other business income and carried forward, subject to conditions
Neither set off nor carried forward under any circumstances
Non-speculative business losses can be set off against other heads except salary in the same year, and unabsorbed losses carried forward against business income, subject to timely filing of returns.
A manufacturer takes delivery of copper through a commodity exchange contract. On the physical delivery, the manufacturer will typically pay:
Commodity Transaction Tax only, without GST
Goods and Services Tax on the value of the goods delivered
Securities Transaction Tax on the delivery value
No tax, as exchange deliveries are tax exempt
Physical delivery is a supply of goods, so GST applies on its value. CTT relates to the derivative transaction itself, and STT applies only to securities like shares.
An exporter uses commodity futures solely to hedge the price of goods it will sell. For accounting purposes, it should:
Treat the futures as long-term investments carried at historical cost until they mature
Document the hedge relationship and apply hedge accounting if eligible
Ignore the futures until the export sale is completed
Record the full contract value as a liability

Hedge accounting requires documentation of the hedged item, the hedging instrument and effectiveness. Without it, futures are measured at fair value through profit or loss. Contract value is not recorded as a liability.
Brokerage and exchange transaction charges paid by a business trader in commodity derivatives are generally:
Added to Commodity Transaction Tax payable
Not deductible because they relate to derivatives
Deductible only against capital gains
Deductible as business expenses in computing business income
For a trader whose derivatives income is business income, brokerage and exchange charges are ordinary deductible expenses. There is no capital gains head involved in such business income.
At the year-end, a company holds open commodity futures positions that have been marked to market daily. The cumulative MTM losses already paid are:
Recognised in the profit and loss account for the year
Shown as a recoverable deposit until expiry
Ignored until the contracts are closed
Added to the cost of inventory automatically
MTM losses paid daily reflect the fall in fair value of open futures and are recognised in profit or loss, unless hedge accounting rules require deferral. They are not a recoverable deposit.

Codes of Conduct and Investor Protection.overview: This chapter covers the conduct expected of brokers, authorised persons and their employees in commodity derivatives, and the protections available to clients. Topics include the SEBI code of conduct for stock brokers, segregation of client funds and securities, KYC, contract notes and statements of accounts, prohibition of fraudulent and unfair trade practices, investor grievance redressal through SCORES and online dispute resolution, the Investor Protection Fund, and arbitration. Learners should be able to spot mis-selling, unauthorised trading and misuse of client funds, and know the escalation path available to an aggrieved client.
questions: A client discovers trades in his account that he never authorised. His first step should be to:
Complain to the broker at once and escalate to the exchange or SEBI if unresolved
Wait for the year-end statement of accounts before taking any action against the broker
Settle the losses directly with the opposite counterparty
Close his bank account to stop margin payments

Unauthorised trades should be disputed promptly with the broker in writing; unresolved complaints can then be escalated to the exchange, SEBI's SCORES and online dispute resolution. Delay weakens the client's case.
Segregation of client funds by a commodity broker means that:
Each client's trades are executed on different exchanges
Client money is kept separately and cannot be used for the broker's own trading
Clients must keep their funds in a separate bank chosen by the exchange
Clients' profits are held by the broker until the year-end
Client funds must be maintained separately from the broker's own funds and used only for that client's obligations. Using client money for proprietary trading is a serious violation.
A broker's dealer tells a new client that a particular commodity strategy 'can never make a loss'. This is:
Misrepresentation, which the code of conduct prohibits
Acceptable if the client signs the risk disclosure document
Permitted for hedging strategies only
Acceptable marketing as long as no fee is charged

Guaranteeing returns or claiming a derivatives strategy is loss-free is misleading. The code of conduct requires fair and accurate representation of risks, which a signed risk disclosure does not override.
Disputes between a client and a trading member that are not settled through grievance redressal can be referred under SEBI's current framework to:
The local civil court only, as arbitration is not available
Online conciliation and arbitration through the ODR platform
The Warehousing Development and Regulatory Authority
The commodity board for the relevant crop

SEBI's online dispute resolution framework allows unresolved disputes with market intermediaries to go for online conciliation and arbitration. WDRA and commodity boards do not resolve broker disputes.
The Investor Protection Fund of an exchange is primarily used to:
Pay compensation for trading losses due to adverse price moves
Compensate eligible clients when a member is declared a defaulter
Fund the exchange's advertising and marketing
Pay CTT on behalf of small clients
The IPF compensates genuine claims of clients against defaulting members, subject to limits, and supports investor awareness. Market losses from price moves are not compensated.
Which of the following must a trading member provide to clients periodically under the regulatory framework?
A statement of accounts for funds and positions
A guarantee of minimum annual return
A copy of the broker's internal audit report
The names of other clients trading the same commodity
Brokers must send periodic statements of funds and securities or positions, along with contract notes. Guaranteeing returns or sharing other clients' details would be improper.
An authorised person (AP) of a broker collects margin money from a client in cash in his own name. This is:
Permitted if the AP issues a handwritten receipt
Permitted for amounts below the daily margin requirement of that particular client account
Required to speed up margin payments
Not permitted, as client funds must reach the broker through banking channels
Authorised persons cannot accept client funds in their own name; payments must go to the broker's designated client bank account. Cash dealings in an AP's name create risk of misuse.
A dealer uses his knowledge of a client's large pending sell order to sell for his own account first. This is a breach mainly because it:
Breaches only the exchange's dress code for dealers
Puts the dealer's interest ahead of the client's: front running
Is permitted if the dealer later informs the client about the trade and its price
Is acceptable when the market is volatile
Trading ahead of a client's order using knowledge of that order is front running, a breach of the duty to act in the client's interest. Later disclosure does not cure it.

Retirement Planning: An Overview.overview: This chapter sets out why retirement planning matters and the risks a retiree faces: longevity risk, inflation risk, health-cost risk, sequence-of-returns risk and the decline of traditional family support. It contrasts defined-benefit and defined-contribution arrangements, explains the shift in India from government pensions to contributory schemes, and introduces the life-cycle of accumulation, transition and distribution. When revising, focus on identifying each retirement risk from a scenario, understanding why starting early matters, and how inflation erodes the purchasing power of a fixed income over a long retirement.
questions: A retiree's biggest worry is that she may live to 95 and exhaust her savings. This is known as:
Liquidity risk
Reinvestment risk
Longevity risk
Credit risk of the issuer of her bonds
Longevity risk is the risk of outliving one's savings because life turns out longer than planned. Liquidity, reinvestment and credit risks are different investment risks.
Inflation averages 8% a year. Using the Rule of 72, roughly how long will it take for the purchasing power of a fixed pension to halve?
About 12 years
About 6 years
About 9 years
About 18 years
Under the Rule of 72, time to halve purchasing power ≈ 72 ÷ inflation rate = 72 ÷ 8 = 9 years. Twelve years would apply at 6% inflation.
In a defined-benefit pension plan, who mainly bears the investment risk?
The individual member
The employer or plan sponsor
The pension fund's custodian
The member's nominee
In a defined-benefit plan, the pension is fixed by formula, so the sponsor must make good any shortfall in fund returns. In a defined-contribution plan the member bears this risk.
A retiree suffers heavy equity losses in the first two years of retirement while also withdrawing money. Even if markets recover later, his corpus may not. This illustrates:
Interest-rate risk on deposits
Currency risk
Sequence-of-returns risk
Concentration risk in a single stock
Sequence-of-returns risk arises because withdrawals during early losses lock in those losses, leaving a smaller base to benefit from later recovery. The order of returns matters during withdrawal.
Which of the following is the best description of the 'accumulation phase' in retirement planning?
The years after retirement when the corpus is drawn down
The working years in which savings are built up for retirement
The period in which an annuity is paying out to the retiree
The time taken to settle the retiree's estate after death
The accumulation phase covers working years when contributions are made and invested. The distribution or decumulation phase comes after retirement, when savings are drawn down.
Why do many advisers recommend that retirement planning start in a person's twenties?
Tax laws allow retirement savings only for people below 30
Longer compounding periods sharply reduce the monthly saving needed
Pension products are not available to investors above 40
Employers stop contributing to provident funds after 35
The longer money compounds, the smaller the regular contribution needed to reach a target. There is no tax or product rule restricting retirement saving to young people.
A self-employed doctor has no employer pension. Compared with a government employee covered by an old defined-benefit pension, her main additional need is to:
Build her own retirement corpus through voluntary saving
Avoid all equity investments to preserve capital
Rely on gratuity under the Payment of Gratuity Act
Depend on the Employees' Pension Scheme

Self-employed people have no employer pension, gratuity or EPS, so they must create their own corpus through products like NPS, PPF and mutual funds. Avoiding equity entirely would raise inflation risk.
Which statement about the impact of medical inflation on retirement planning is most accurate?
Medical costs fall after retirement because people work less
Government schemes fully cover all private hospital expenses of retirees
Healthcare costs often rise faster than general inflation, so they need a separate provision
Health costs can be ignored if the retiree has a large equity portfolio

Medical inflation in India typically exceeds headline inflation, and health needs rise with age. Planners therefore provide for health insurance and a separate medical reserve rather than assuming general inflation.

Pension Systems & Regulatory Framework (.overview: This chapter covers the structure of the Indian pension system and its regulation. It explains the pillars of pension provision, the statutory schemes for organised-sector workers (EPF, EPS), government pension arrangements, and the role of the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority under the PFRDA Act, 2013 in regulating the National Pension System and other pension schemes. It also introduces intermediaries such as the NPS Trust, central recordkeeping agencies, pension funds, trustee bank, custodian, points of presence, annuity service providers and retirement advisers. Revise each intermediary's role and the powers of PFRDA.
questions: Which entity in the NPS architecture holds the assets of NPS in trust for the benefit of subscribers?
The Central Recordkeeping Agency
The NPS Trust
The Point of Presence
The Annuity Service Provider
The NPS Trust, set up by PFRDA, holds NPS assets for the benefit of subscribers and oversees pension funds. CRAs keep records, POPs onboard subscribers and ASPs pay annuities.
Individuals who wish to act as retirement advisers to NPS subscribers are registered and regulated by:
SEBI
IRDAI
EPFO
PFRDA
Retirement advisers for NPS are registered with PFRDA under its retirement adviser regulations. SEBI regulates investment advisers for securities and IRDAI regulates insurance intermediaries.
Which body administers the Employees' Provident Fund and the Employees' Pension Scheme for the organised private sector?
Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority
National Pension System Trust
Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO)
Life Insurance Corporation of India
EPF and EPS are administered by the EPFO under the EPF and Miscellaneous Provisions framework. PFRDA regulates NPS, not EPF.
A bank appointed in the NPS structure to receive contributions from POPs and nodal offices and transfer them to pension funds is the:
Trustee bank
Custodian
Annuity service provider
Sponsor bank of the pension fund
The trustee bank manages the banking side of NPS: it receives contributions and passes them to pension fund managers and pays out withdrawals as instructed. The custodian holds securities.
In NPS, which intermediary is responsible for the safekeeping of securities bought by pension fund managers?
The trustee bank
The custodian
The Point of Presence
The retirement adviser
The custodian holds and settles the securities in which NPS money is invested. The trustee bank handles fund flows, not securities.
Which of the following is a power of PFRDA under the PFRDA Act, 2013?
Fixing interest rates on PPF and small savings schemes
Deciding EPF interest rates each year
Granting licences to life insurers to sell annuities
Registering and regulating intermediaries and protecting subscriber interests

PFRDA registers and regulates NPS intermediaries and protects subscribers. Small savings rates are set by the government, EPF rates are decided under the EPF framework, and insurers are licensed by IRDAI.
Annuity service providers that pay pensions to NPS subscribers on exit are:
Life insurers empanelled by PFRDA
Pension fund managers of NPS
Scheduled commercial banks acting as POPs
Mutual funds offering monthly income schemes
Only IRDAI-registered life insurers empanelled by PFRDA can act as ASPs for NPS annuities. Pension fund managers manage accumulation, not annuity payment.
Which pension arrangement is designed for workers in the unorganised sector and guarantees a fixed minimum pension backed by the government?
Employees' Pension Scheme
NPS corporate model
Voluntary Provident Fund
Atal Pension Yojana
APY targets unorganised-sector workers and offers a government-backed fixed pension based on contribution level. EPS covers organised-sector employees, and VPF is an EPF add-on.

National Pension System – Architecture.overview: This chapter explains how NPS is organised for different groups of subscribers: the Government sector model for Central and State Government employees, the corporate model, the all-citizen model and NPS Vatsalya for minors. It covers Tier I and Tier II accounts, the PRAN, KYC and onboarding through POPs and eNPS, contribution rules, portability across jobs and locations, and the flow of contributions through the trustee bank to pension funds. Focus on who can join under which model, how Tier I and Tier II differ in withdrawal and tax treatment, and the role of each intermediary in the contribution cycle.
questions: A subscriber changes jobs from a private company to a different city. What happens to his NPS account?
He must close the account and open a new one with a fresh PRAN
His corpus is transferred compulsorily to EPF
The account is frozen until he reaches 60
The same PRAN continues; only the employer or POP mapping changes
NPS is portable: the PRAN stays the same across jobs and locations, and only the associated employer or POP changes. No closure or transfer to EPF is required.
Which statement about the NPS Tier II account is correct?
It is a voluntary account with flexible withdrawals and no lock-in
It has the same withdrawal restrictions as Tier I
It can be opened without holding a Tier I account
Its corpus must be used to buy an annuity at 60
Tier II is a voluntary savings facility with free withdrawals. It requires an active Tier I account and has no annuity requirement. Tier I is the restricted pension account.
Rahul, a salaried employee, wants to open NPS online without visiting any branch. Which channel can he use?
Only a post office savings bank counter
eNPS, using Aadhaar or PAN-based online KYC
Only through his employer's HR department
A registered mutual fund distributor's offline form
eNPS allows individuals to open and fund NPS accounts online using Aadhaar or PAN-based verification. Post offices and employers are other channels but not the only ones.
NPS Vatsalya accounts are opened for:
Senior citizens above 70 who cannot join regular NPS
Minors, with contributions made by a parent or guardian
Non-resident Indians only
Government employees covered by the Unified Pension Scheme
NPS Vatsalya allows parents or guardians to save for a minor's pension. It is operated by the guardian until the child reaches majority.
Under the corporate model of NPS, which of the following is true?
Employer contributions can be made in addition to the employee's own contributions
Only the employer can contribute; employees cannot add anything
The employer chooses the pension fund and employees can never change it
Employees lose their PRAN on leaving the company
In the corporate model, both the employer and the employee may contribute. Subscribers retain their PRAN when they leave, and choices of fund and allocation can be offered to employees.
Under the all-citizen model, an NPS subscriber's contribution passes through which sequence?
Pension fund → POP → trustee bank
Custodian → CRA → POP
POP → trustee bank → pension fund
Annuity service provider → trustee bank → POP
The subscriber contributes through a POP, which remits money to the trustee bank; after reconciliation with the CRA's records, funds go to the chosen pension fund for investment.
Which of the following is a function of the Central Recordkeeping Agency for an NPS subscriber?
Selecting stocks for the subscriber's equity scheme
Issuing the PRAN and maintaining records of contributions and units
Paying the monthly annuity after exit
Holding the securities bought by pension funds and settling their trades with exchanges
The CRA issues PRANs, maintains records of contributions, switches and units, and provides statements. Stock selection is done by pension funds, annuities by ASPs and custody by the custodian.
Which individual is NOT eligible to open an NPS account under the all-citizen model?
A citizen aged 75 seeking to open a new account
A citizen aged 19 with a savings bank account
An NRI who is a citizen of India, subject to applicable rules
A self-employed citizen aged 45
The all-citizen model is open to Indian citizens within the prescribed entry age band, which is far below 75. NRIs who are citizens may join subject to FEMA and NPS rules.

NPS – Investment Options & Fund Manageme.overview: This chapter covers how NPS money is invested. It explains the asset classes (equity, corporate debt and government securities, with limited alternative assets), Active Choice and Auto Choice with life-cycle funds, default schemes for government subscribers, the selection and change of pension fund managers, and investment guidelines prescribed by PFRDA. Learners should understand how life-cycle funds reduce equity with age, how active choice allocations are capped, the trade-off between return and volatility across asset classes, and how often a subscriber can revise choices. Use concepts rather than memorising limits that PFRDA revises from time to time.
questions: If a subscriber in the all-citizen model does not indicate any investment choice, his contributions are invested under:
Active Choice with 100% government securities
Auto Choice using the aggressive life-cycle fund
Active Choice with an equal split across all asset classes
Auto Choice using the moderate life-cycle fund
Where no choice is made, NPS defaults to Auto Choice with the moderate life-cycle fund (LC50). Aggressive or conservative options must be selected actively by the subscriber.
Which type of securities forms the main holding of the NPS 'C' asset class?
Corporate bonds and other fixed-income instruments of companies
Commodities such as gold and silver
Central government securities only, including treasury bills and state development loans
Cash held with the trustee bank
Asset class C is the corporate debt class, covering bonds and debt instruments of companies and similar entities. Government securities form asset class G.
Ankit, 50, chooses Active Choice and wants to allocate the maximum permitted to equity. Which statement is correct?
There is no upper limit on equity allocation under Active Choice for any subscriber
PFRDA caps equity under Active Choice and tapers the cap as the subscriber ages
Active Choice permits equity only for subscribers under 35
Equity is compulsory at 75% under Active Choice for everyone
Active Choice lets subscribers decide allocation within limits; PFRDA sets a ceiling on equity which reduces with age in later years. There is no compulsory equity allocation.
A subscriber is dissatisfied with her pension fund's performance. What can she do?
Withdraw her entire Tier I corpus immediately without restriction
Ask the CRA to manage the money directly
Transfer the corpus to a mutual fund of her choice
Switch to another pension fund manager as permitted by PFRDA

NPS allows subscribers to change their pension fund manager periodically within PFRDA rules. Tier I money cannot be freely withdrawn or moved into mutual funds, and the CRA does not manage investments.
Compared with the aggressive life-cycle fund, the conservative life-cycle fund under Auto Choice:
Keeps equity constant throughout the subscriber's life
Invests only in corporate bonds
Is available only to Government sector subscribers
Starts with a lower maximum equity allocation

The conservative life-cycle fund starts with a lower equity cap than the moderate and aggressive funds, and all reduce equity with age. It is available to non-government subscribers choosing Auto Choice.
Why does a life-cycle fund reduce equity exposure as the subscriber approaches retirement?
Because equities always underperform debt over long periods
Because PFRDA does not permit equity after the age of 45
To lower the risk of a large loss just before the corpus is needed
To maximise returns in the final years of saving when the corpus is at its largest
As retirement nears, there is less time to recover from a market fall, so de-risking protects the corpus. Equities usually outperform over long periods, which is why they dominate early on.
Government sector NPS subscribers who do not exercise a choice have their contributions invested in:
Only the equity scheme of a single pension fund
The Tier II account by default
Atal Pension Yojana
A default scheme split across pension funds in proportions set by the government and PFRDA
For government employees, default contributions go to a default scheme managed by specified pension funds in prescribed proportions. Many government subscribers now also have the option to choose.
Which factor is LEAST relevant when a 28-year-old chooses between Auto and Active Choice?
The name of the CRA that issued her PRAN
Her risk appetite and investment knowledge
Her willingness to review allocations regularly
Her time horizon to retirement
Choice of investment option should depend on risk appetite, time horizon and ability to manage allocations. The CRA only maintains records and has no bearing on investment outcomes.

NPS – Exit, Withdrawal & Annuity.overview: This chapter covers how money leaves NPS: normal exit at superannuation or the prescribed age, premature exit before that age, exit on death, partial withdrawals from Tier I for specified purposes, deferment of lump sum and annuity, systematic lump-sum withdrawal options and the requirement to use part of the corpus to buy an annuity. It also explains the choice of annuity service provider and annuity type. Since PFRDA has revised exit limits over time, focus on the structure — the annuity requirement, the small-corpus exception, the stricter treatment of premature exit and the documents and process for claims.
questions: Compared with normal exit at the retirement age, premature exit from NPS before that age generally requires:
No annuity purchase at all
The full corpus to be paid as lump sum
A penalty equal to all employer contributions made since the account was opened
A larger share of the corpus to be used for buying an annuity
NPS discourages early exit by requiring a larger proportion to be annuitised on premature exit than on normal exit, except where the corpus is below the small-corpus threshold.
An NPS subscriber at exit has a very small accumulated corpus, below the threshold specified by PFRDA. Typically, she can:
Only buy an annuity with the entire corpus
Not exit until the corpus crosses the threshold
Withdraw the entire corpus as a lump sum without buying an annuity
Transfer the corpus to her EPF account
PFRDA allows full lump-sum withdrawal where the corpus is below a prescribed small-amount threshold, because an annuity on a tiny amount would be uneconomic.
Partial withdrawal from NPS Tier I is allowed for specified purposes. Which is a permitted purpose?
Treatment of a specified critical illness of the subscriber or family
Repayment of an outstanding credit card bill or personal loan of the subscriber
Purchase of shares in an IPO
Foreign holiday travel

Partial withdrawals are allowed only for listed purposes such as children's education or marriage, house purchase or construction and treatment of specified illnesses. Consumption or investment needs do not qualify.
Partial withdrawals from NPS Tier I are calculated with reference to:
The subscriber's own contributions, not the employer's
The entire corpus including employer contributions and returns
Only the returns earned in the last financial year
The annuity value expected at retirement
Partial withdrawal limits are a percentage of the subscriber's own contributions (excluding employer contributions), subject to minimum holding period and number of withdrawals.
A subscriber at 60 wants to receive the lump-sum portion in instalments rather than at once. NPS permits this through:
Conversion of Tier I into a fixed deposit with the trustee bank
Transferring the lump sum to Tier II only
Systematic withdrawal of the lump sum over a chosen period
A loan against the NPS corpus
NPS offers systematic lump-sum withdrawal, letting the subscriber draw the lump-sum portion periodically while the balance stays invested. NPS does not provide loans against the corpus.
A subscriber wants the highest possible annuity income now but also wants his wife to continue receiving pension after his death. Which option balances these needs?
Joint-life annuity without return of purchase price
Single-life annuity with return of purchase price
Single-life annuity without return of purchase price
Annuity certain for five years only
A joint-life annuity continues to the spouse; choosing it without return of purchase price keeps the payout higher than a return-of-purchase-price variant. A single-life annuity stops at his death.
Which document is essential for the nominee to claim NPS benefits after the subscriber's death?
The subscriber's latest income-tax return only
The nominee's EPF passbook
A no-objection certificate from the subscriber's employer in all cases
The subscriber's death certificate along with the claim form and KYC
Death claims require a death certificate, the withdrawal form and the nominee's KYC and bank details. Income-tax returns and EPF passbooks are not required.
A subscriber may defer buying the annuity at exit. The main advantage of deferment is that:
The corpus becomes exempt from all market risk during the whole period of deferment
The corpus remains invested and the annuity can be bought later, possibly at better rates
It allows him to withdraw 100% in cash later
Annuity rates are guaranteed to rise each year of deferment

Deferring the annuity keeps money invested and lets the subscriber choose a later time, perhaps when he needs income or rates are better. The corpus still carries market risk and rates are not guaranteed.

Other Retirement Products (EPF, PPF, SCS.overview: This chapter covers retirement products other than NPS: Employees' Provident Fund and Employees' Pension Scheme, Voluntary Provident Fund, Public Provident Fund, Senior Citizens' Savings Scheme, Atal Pension Yojana, post office schemes, and mutual fund options such as retirement funds, balanced advantage funds and systematic withdrawal plans. Learners should know each product's eligibility, tenure, liquidity, risk and tax treatment, and match products to client needs. Interest rates on small savings are revised quarterly, so focus on features and suitability rather than current rates.
questions: The monthly pension under the Employees' Pension Scheme is calculated as pensionable salary × pensionable service ÷ 70. For pensionable salary of ₹15,000 and 35 years of service, the pension is:
Pension = 15,000 × 35 ÷ 70 = ₹7,500 per month. ₹5,250 would result from dividing by 100 instead of 70.
Which of the following can a PPF subscriber do after the account completes its initial tenure?
Convert it into an NPS Tier I account
Transfer it to the employer for EPF credit
Withdraw only the interest and leave the principal locked forever
Extend it in blocks, with or without further contributions
On maturity, a PPF account can be extended in blocks with or without fresh contributions, or closed. It cannot be converted to NPS or EPF.
Who among the following is eligible to open a Senior Citizens' Savings Scheme account before 60, subject to conditions?
Any salaried employee aged 45 or above
Any NRI aged 55 or above
A minor whose parent is a senior citizen
A person who retired under a voluntary retirement scheme and meets the age and timing conditions

SCSS is primarily for resident individuals aged 60 or more, but certain retirees, such as those on VRS or superannuation within the specified age band, may join earlier if they invest within the prescribed time of receiving benefits. NRIs cannot open SCSS.
Interest on a Senior Citizens' Savings Scheme account is paid:
Only at maturity
Monthly
Half-yearly in arrears after the third year
Quarterly
SCSS pays interest every quarter, making it suitable for regular income. It is not cumulative and does not pay monthly.
Which person is NOT eligible to join Atal Pension Yojana under the current rules?
A 25-year-old domestic worker with a savings bank account
An income-tax payer aged 30
A 35-year-old farm labourer
A 19-year-old street vendor
Since October 2022, income-tax payers are not eligible to join APY. Other citizens within the entry age band can join through a bank or post office savings account.
A retiree invests in a mutual fund and sets up a systematic withdrawal plan. Compared with a bank fixed deposit giving monthly interest, the SWP:
Guarantees a fixed return like a deposit
Is fully exempt from tax in all cases, irrespective of holding period or the fund type
Requires a lock-in of five years
Can be more tax-efficient but its value fluctuates with the market
SWP withdrawals are partly capital redemption, so only gains are taxed, making them potentially tax-efficient. However, the underlying units carry market risk, unlike a fixed deposit.
Why might a retiree prefer SCSS to an ordinary bank fixed deposit for part of his corpus?
It has no upper limit on investment
It allows withdrawals at any time without any deduction or penalty on the interest
It is government-backed and usually offers a higher rate than regular deposits
Its interest is exempt from income tax
SCSS carries sovereign backing and its rate is typically higher than standard bank deposit rates. It has an investment ceiling, premature closure attracts a deduction, and interest is taxable.
An employee voluntarily contributes more than the mandatory 12% to EPF. This additional contribution is called:
Employees' Deposit Linked Insurance
Employer's matching contribution
Pension Fund Tier II
Voluntary Provident Fund
Contributions above the mandatory rate go to the Voluntary Provident Fund, which earns the EPF rate. EDLI is a life insurance scheme, and the employer is not required to match VPF.

Retirement Planning Process & Corpus Est.overview: This chapter covers the step-by-step retirement planning process and the calculations behind it. Steps include gathering client data, estimating current and future expenses, projecting them with inflation to the retirement date, choosing assumptions for return, inflation and life expectancy, computing the corpus needed using present-value-of-annuity methods, valuing existing assets, identifying the shortfall and determining the saving required. Revise time-value-of-money calculations — future value, present value, annuities and growing annuities — and the effect of real rates of return. Always state assumptions and review the plan periodically.
questions: A client's current monthly household expenses are ₹50,000. If inflation is 7% a year, what will these expenses be in 18 years (approximately)?
₹1.13 lakh
₹1.28 lakh
₹2.10 lakh
₹1.69 lakh
Future expense = 50,000 × 1.07^18 ≈ 50,000 × 3.38 ≈ ₹1.69 lakh a month. ₹1.13 lakh would result from simple rather than compound inflation.
A client wants ₹1 crore in 20 years and expects 10% a year compounded monthly. How much must he invest at the end of each month (approximately)?
Using the future value of an annuity formula with r = 10%/12 and n = 240, the monthly SIP ≈ ₹13,169. ₹41,667 simply divides ₹1 crore by 240, ignoring returns.
A client has ₹25 lakh in retirement savings that will grow at 7% a year for 10 years until he retires. What will this amount to at retirement (approximately)?
₹42.5 lakh
₹35.0 lakh
₹49.2 lakh
₹57.6 lakh
A retiree needs ₹6 lakh a year in today's terms for 25 years, withdrawn at the start of each year. If the real rate of return (after inflation) is 1.5%, the corpus needed is about:
₹1.50 crore
₹96 lakh
₹1.26 crore
₹1.08 crore
PV of an annuity due of ₹6 lakh for 25 years at 1.5% ≈ ₹126.2 lakh, i.e. about ₹1.26 crore. ₹1.50 crore ignores returns entirely (6 × 25).
A client needs ₹2 crore in 15 years. What amount must be saved at the end of each year if investments earn 10% a year (approximately)?
₹13.33 lakh
₹4.80 lakh
₹8.10 lakh
₹6.29 lakh
Annual saving = 2 crore × 0.10 ÷ (1.10^15 − 1) ≈ ₹6.29 lakh. ₹13.33 lakh divides the target by 15 years and ignores compounding.
Why is the real rate of return used when computing the corpus for an inflation-indexed retirement income?
It allows payments in today's terms to be discounted while allowing for rising expenses
It always gives a higher corpus than nominal calculations do
It removes the need to estimate life expectancy, since real returns adjust for longevity
Because inflation does not affect expenses after retirement
Using the real rate converts a growing stream into constant real payments, simplifying the calculation of a corpus that must fund inflation-linked withdrawals. Life expectancy is still needed.
A plan was prepared five years ago assuming 6% inflation. Actual inflation has averaged 8%. The adviser should:
Keep the plan unchanged because it was prepared by a professional
Review the assumptions and revise the corpus and saving targets
Reduce the client's equity allocation to zero
Advise the client to stop contributing until inflation falls

Retirement plans need periodic review. Higher actual inflation increases future expenses, so assumptions and saving targets should be revised. Abandoning equity or stopping savings would worsen the gap.
Which assumption, if overestimated, will most likely cause a retirement corpus to fall short?
The expected rate of return on investments
The client's life expectancy
The rate of inflation
The amount of expenses in retirement
An overly optimistic return assumption means too little is saved. Overestimating life expectancy, inflation or expenses would instead make the plan more conservative.

Investment & Asset Allocation for Retire.overview: This chapter explains how to build and manage portfolios for retirement. It covers the risk and return characteristics of equity, debt, gold and real estate, strategic and tactical asset allocation, age-based and glide-path approaches, rebalancing, diversification, the bucket strategy, and the need to beat inflation over a long retirement. It also discusses real returns, the effect of costs and taxes, and the trade-off between growth and stability. When revising, focus on matching allocation to the client's horizon, risk capacity and income needs, and on why some equity is still needed after retirement.
questions: A retiree earns 8% on his investments while inflation is 6%. His real rate of return (exact) is:
Real return = (1.08 ÷ 1.06) − 1 ≈ 1.89%. Simple subtraction gives 2%, which is only an approximation.
A 'bucket strategy' for retirement income typically involves:
Investing the entire corpus in a single balanced fund and withdrawing a fixed sum every month
Holding only gold and real estate after retirement
Spending the equity portion first and keeping cash for later years
Keeping near-term needs in safe assets and longer-term money in growth assets
The bucket approach holds a few years of expenses in liquid, safe assets and invests money for later years in growth assets, reducing the need to sell equities in a downturn.
A client's target allocation is 40% equity and 60% debt. After a strong year, equity has risen to 52% of the portfolio. Rebalancing means:
Selling some equity and buying debt to restore 40:60
Buying more equity to ride the momentum
Switching entirely to debt to lock in gains
Doing nothing until equity falls back
Rebalancing returns the portfolio to its target risk level by selling the asset that has grown above its weight and buying the one below. It is a discipline, not a market call.
Why do most planners keep some equity exposure even for retirees in their sixties?
Equity returns are guaranteed over a five-year period
Retirement may last decades, and equity helps the corpus keep pace with inflation
Retirees are exempt from tax on equity gains once they cross the age of sixty
Debt instruments are not available to senior citizens
A retirement of 25 to 30 years needs growth to offset inflation. Equity provides that potential but is not guaranteed, and there is no special tax exemption for retirees on equity gains.
Which client is likely to have the highest capacity to take equity risk in retirement savings?
A 63-year-old retiree with no pension and modest savings
A 35-year-old with stable income and 25 years to retirement
A 58-year-old planning to retire in two years with large EMIs
A 70-year-old who depends fully on his corpus for expenses
Risk capacity depends on time horizon, income stability and dependence on the portfolio. A young earner with a long horizon can absorb volatility far better than retirees who depend on the corpus.
Strategic asset allocation differs from tactical asset allocation in that strategic allocation:
Sets long-term target weights based on goals and risk profile
Shifts weights frequently to exploit short-term market views
Is applied only to equity mutual funds
Ignores the client's time horizon
Strategic allocation is the long-term policy mix tied to goals and risk tolerance. Tactical allocation involves short-term deviations from it to exploit market opportunities.
A retiree's portfolio includes 70% in a single private-sector company's shares, where he worked for 30 years. The main risk the adviser should highlight is:
Inflation risk on fixed deposits
Concentration risk
Currency risk
Reinvestment risk on annuities
Holding most wealth in one stock exposes the client to company-specific losses. Diversification across issuers and asset classes reduces this risk.
A retiree compares two debt funds with similar risk. Fund A has an expense ratio of 0.3% and Fund B 1.2%. Over 20 years, the higher cost will most likely:
Have no effect because both funds hold similar bonds
Increase returns, because higher fees usually mean better and more active management
Matter only in the first year
Reduce the final corpus noticeably due to compounding of the cost difference
Costs compound over time, so an extra 0.9% a year significantly lowers final value. Higher fees do not guarantee better performance in similar-risk debt funds.

Distribution Phase & Annuities.overview: This chapter deals with converting a corpus into retirement income. It covers annuity types (immediate and deferred, life annuity, with or without return of purchase price, joint-life, increasing and guaranteed-period annuities), annuity pricing and the factors that affect annuity rates, withdrawal strategies such as fixed-percentage rules and systematic withdrawals, annuity laddering, and managing longevity and sequence risk while drawing down.
