Revise how to choose between annuity options for a given client situation and how to compute simple payouts and sustainable withdrawal amounts.
questions: A retiree buys an annuity with ₹60 lakh at a rate of 6.8% a year payable monthly. The approximate monthly annuity before tax is:
Annual annuity = 60 lakh × 6.8% = ₹4,08,000. Monthly ≈ 4,08,000 ÷ 12 = ₹34,000. ₹40,800 confuses the annual figure's decimal place.
A retiree has a corpus of ₹1.2 crore and withdraws ₹4.8 lakh in the first year. His initial withdrawal rate is:
Withdrawal rate = 4.8 lakh ÷ 120 lakh = 4%. 4.8% would treat ₹4.8 lakh as a percentage directly.
Which factor generally leads to a HIGHER annuity payout for the same purchase price?
Choosing the return-of-purchase-price option
Adding a spouse under a joint-life option
Choosing an annuity that increases every year
Buying the annuity at an older age
Older buyers have a shorter expected payout period, so insurers offer a higher rate. Return of purchase price, joint-life and increasing features all reduce the starting payout.
Annuity laddering means:
Buying an annuity whose payout increases each year
Investing the monthly annuity income in equity funds to build a second corpus
Buying several annuities at different times instead of one at retirement
Switching annuity providers every year
Laddering spreads annuity purchases over time, reducing the risk of locking the whole corpus at low rates and allowing higher rates at older ages.
A key disadvantage of a life annuity without return of purchase price is that:
Its payout is lower than all other annuity options
It stops paying after a fixed term even if the annuitant is alive
Its payouts change with stock market levels
Nothing is left for heirs if the annuitant dies early
This option gives the highest payout, but on death the purchase price is not returned, so heirs receive nothing. Payments continue for life and do not depend on markets.
A retiree wants protection against inflation in her annuity income. Which annuity feature addresses this?
A life annuity with return of purchase price
An increasing annuity whose payout rises at a fixed rate each year
An annuity certain for ten years
A joint-life annuity with 50% to the spouse
An increasing annuity raises payments periodically, offsetting part of inflation. The other options address legacy, guaranteed term or spouse protection, not inflation.
Why might a retiree combine an annuity with a mutual fund SWP rather than putting the entire corpus into an annuity?
Because annuities cannot be bought for more than ₹10 lakh
Because SWPs guarantee a higher income than annuities for the rest of the retiree's life
To get guaranteed lifelong income while keeping some growth and liquidity
To avoid paying any tax on retirement income
An annuity covers essential expenses for life, while an SWP portion offers growth potential and access to capital. Neither eliminates tax, and SWP income is not guaranteed.
A deferred annuity is most suitable for a client who:
Needs income starting next month
Wants to withdraw the entire amount in cash at any time
Is still working and wants pension income to start some years later
Has no need for any regular income
A deferred annuity accumulates during a deferment period and starts payouts later, suiting people who are still working. Immediate annuities begin almost at once.

Taxation of Retirement Benefits.overview: This chapter covers the tax treatment of retirement savings and benefits. It explains deductions for contributions to NPS and other schemes (including the employer's NPS contribution), the treatment of EPF and PPF, the taxability of pension, commuted pension, gratuity, leave encashment, annuity income and NPS withdrawals, and the choice between the old and new tax regimes. Since tax law and section numbers have changed with the new Income-tax Act, focus on concepts — which benefits are deductible, exempt or taxable, and under what conditions — rather than memorising rates and limits that may change.
questions: Which NPS-related deduction remains available to a salaried employee even under the new (default) tax regime?
Deduction for the employee's own additional NPS contribution of up to ₹50,000
Deduction for contributions to NPS Tier II
Deduction for contributions to Atal Pension Yojana
Deduction for the employer's contribution to the employee's NPS account

Under the new regime, most deductions are unavailable, but the employer's contribution to NPS remains deductible within the prescribed percentage of salary. The additional ₹50,000 deduction for own contribution is an old-regime benefit.
Gratuity under the Payment of Gratuity Act is computed as 15/26 × last drawn salary × completed years of service. For a last drawn salary of ₹52,000 and 20 years of service, gratuity is:
For a non-government employee who also receives gratuity, how much of the commuted pension is exempt from tax?
One-third of the full value of the pension commuted
One-half of the commuted amount
The entire commuted amount
None of it
For non-government employees receiving gratuity, one-third of the commuted value of full pension is exempt; without gratuity, one-half is exempt. Government employees get full exemption.
A private-sector employee withdraws his EPF balance after three years of continuous service to start a business. The withdrawal is generally:
Fully exempt in all cases
Taxable, because continuous service is less than five years
Exempt only if he invests in NPS
Taxable only on the employer's contribution and never on interest
EPF withdrawals before five years of continuous service are generally taxable unless termination is due to reasons beyond the employee's control. After five years, withdrawals are exempt.
Uncommuted (monthly) pension received by a retired employee from a former employer is taxed as:
Income from other sources
Capital gains
Salary income
Exempt income
Pension received from a former employer is treated as salary, so the standard deduction applies. Pension received by a family member after the employee's death is treated differently.
Leave encashment received by a private-sector employee at retirement is:
Exempt up to a statutory ceiling, with the excess taxable
Fully taxable as salary without any exemption, whatever the employee's length of service
Fully exempt regardless of the amount
Taxed as long-term capital gains

Leave encashment at retirement for non-government employees is exempt up to the statutory limit and computation rules; amounts above that are taxable as salary. Government employees enjoy full exemption.
Employer contributions to an employee's EPF, NPS and superannuation fund together exceed the aggregate limit specified in tax law. The excess is:
Taxed as a perquisite in the employee's hands
Exempt because retirement savings are never taxed
Taxed in the employer's hands
Refunded to the employer
Tax law caps the aggregate employer contribution to these funds; the excess, along with related accretions, is taxable as a perquisite to the employee.
Interest earned on a Senior Citizens' Savings Scheme account is:
Fully exempt like PPF interest
Taxable only on maturity
Taxable as income, though senior citizens may claim specified deductions
Taxed at a flat 1%
SCSS interest is taxable at slab rates and attracts TDS above thresholds. Under the old regime, senior citizens may claim a deduction for interest income within limits, but it is not exempt like PPF.

Health, Insurance & Estate Aspects in Re.overview: This chapter covers non-investment risks in retirement: health costs, insurance needs and estate planning. Topics include individual and senior-citizen health policies, top-up and super top-up covers, waiting periods for pre-existing diseases, government health schemes, the declining need for life cover after retirement, long-term care, reverse mortgage, nominations versus wills, succession laws, probate and trusts. When revising, focus on matching health cover to the retiree's situation, understanding how nominees and legal heirs differ, and the steps a retiree should take to ensure a smooth transfer of assets.
questions: A retiree has a base health policy of ₹5 lakh. A super top-up policy will:
Replace the base policy entirely
Pay a fixed daily cash amount regardless of bills
Pay hospital bills above a deductible once the aggregate claims in a year exceed it
Cover only outpatient consultations
A super top-up pays when total claims in a policy year cross the deductible, making it a cost-effective way to raise cover above the base policy. Hospital cash plans pay fixed daily amounts.
Under a will, a person's mutual fund units are left to his daughter, but his son is the registered nominee. Generally, the nominee:
Becomes the absolute owner, overriding the will
Cannot receive the units until the will is challenged
Receives the units from the fund but holds them for the legal heirs as per the will
Must sell the units and pay the proceeds to the government
In most financial assets, the nominee is a custodian who receives the asset for the benefit of the legal heirs or beneficiaries under the will. Nomination does not override succession.
Why does a retiree's need for life insurance usually decline after retirement?
Dependants are fewer and liabilities such as home loans are usually paid off
Life insurance is not available after 60
Pension income is fully exempt from tax
Health insurance replaces life insurance automatically once a person turns sixty
Life insurance replaces income for dependants. In retirement, children are typically independent and loans repaid, reducing the need. Some cover may still be useful for a spouse or estate purposes.
A reverse mortgage is most suitable for which retiree?
A tenant looking for a cheaper rental
A homeowner with low income who wishes to stay in the house
A retiree wanting to buy a second home
A young professional saving for a down payment
A reverse mortgage lets senior homeowners convert home equity into income while continuing to live in the house. It needs a self-owned residential property.
Which step most reduces disputes over a retiree's estate among his children?
Holding all assets in cash at home
Avoiding nominations to prevent confusion
Making a clear, properly witnessed will and keeping it accessible
Transferring everything to one child informally and asking him to share it fairly
A clear and valid will, executed with witnesses and known to the executor, minimises disputes. Informal transfers or missing nominations tend to create conflict and delays.
A retiree buying a new health policy at 62 should pay special attention to:
The insurer's share price
Whether premiums are deductible under the new tax regime
Waiting periods for pre-existing diseases and co-payment clauses
The policy's maturity benefit
Senior citizen policies often have waiting periods, co-payment and sub-limits that affect claims. Health policies do not pay maturity benefits, and premium deduction is an old-regime benefit.
A retired couple wants to ensure that if one becomes mentally incapacitated, the other can manage bank accounts and investments. A useful legal tool is:
A durable power of attorney
A gift deed
A nomination form
A rent agreement
A power of attorney authorises another person to act on one's behalf. A nomination works only after death, while a gift deed transfers ownership outright.
Why might a retiree with a disabled child consider setting up a private trust?
To avoid all income tax permanently on the family's assets and on the child's income
Because wills are not valid for parents of disabled children
To manage assets for the child's lifetime through a trustee after the parents' death
To transfer assets without any documentation
A trust lets a trustee manage and use assets for the child's benefit over the long term. It does not remove all taxes, and wills remain valid; a trust simply provides ongoing management.

Ethics, Code of Conduct & Grievance Redr.overview: This chapter covers the conduct expected of retirement advisers and NPS intermediaries. Topics include fiduciary duty, suitability and know-your-client, disclosure of conflicts and remuneration, confidentiality, avoiding mis-selling and misleading claims, record keeping, and the code of conduct under PFRDA's regulations. It also covers grievance redressal for NPS subscribers — the Central Grievance Management System, escalation to the NPS Trust and PFRDA, and the ombudsman mechanism. Revise how to handle ethical dilemmas in scenario questions and the order in which a subscriber can escalate a complaint.
questions: An adviser recommends a product mainly because it pays her a higher commission, though a cheaper suitable product exists. This violates the principle of:
Acting in the client's best interest
Maintaining confidentiality
Record keeping
Continuing professional education
Advisers must put the client's interest first. Choosing a product for higher commission when a more suitable option exists breaches this duty, even if the product is not wholly unsuitable.
An NPS subscriber's grievance has not been resolved satisfactorily by the intermediary within the specified time. A further escalation option available under PFRDA's framework is:
Filing a complaint with the EPFO
Approaching the NPS Trust and then the ombudsman appointed under PFRDA regulations
Approaching the Insurance Ombudsman for all NPS matters, including those involving POPs
Escalating to the SEBI SCORES portal
NPS grievances are lodged through CGMS; unresolved complaints can be escalated to the NPS Trust and then to the ombudsman under PFRDA regulations. EPFO and SEBI do not handle NPS grievances.
Before recommending an asset allocation, the adviser must first:
Understand the client's goals, finances and risk profile
Select the products with the best past returns
Ask the client to sign a waiver of liability
Fix the client's retirement age at 60 regardless of preference
Suitability requires understanding the client's needs, circumstances and risk tolerance before recommending. Past returns alone are not a basis for advice.
An adviser tells a 59-year-old client that an equity fund 'will surely give 15% every year'. This is:
Acceptable since equity has historically delivered high returns
Allowed if the client is a senior citizen
A misleading assurance of returns that must be avoided
Permitted if mentioned only verbally
Market-linked returns cannot be guaranteed. Promising assured returns is misleading and breaches the code of conduct regardless of the mode of communication.
Why must a retirement adviser keep records of advice given and the client's risk profile?
To share with other clients as case studies
To demonstrate that recommendations were suitable if questioned later
Because records allow the adviser to justify charging higher fees to long-standing clients
Records are optional if the client trusts the adviser
Records provide evidence of the basis for advice and are required by regulation. They must be kept confidential and are not optional.
A client asks the adviser to backdate a document to qualify for a tax benefit. The adviser should:
Agree if the client is a long-standing customer
Agree if the amount involved is small
Forward the request to the CRA for approval
Refuse, as falsifying documents is unethical and illegal
Falsifying records is fraudulent and breaches the code of conduct and law. No relationship or amount justifies it.
An adviser receives a referral fee from an annuity provider whenever clients buy its annuities. She should:
Keep it confidential to avoid confusing clients
Disclose the arrangement to clients before they decide
Recommend only that provider's annuities to maximise income
Refund the fee to the provider
Material conflicts of interest, including referral fees, must be disclosed so clients can judge the advice. Disclosure does not remove the duty to recommend what is suitable.
Which online system lets an NPS subscriber lodge and track grievances?
SEBI SCORES
IRDAI Bima Bharosa
The Central Grievance Management System of the CRAs
RBI Integrated Ombudsman portal for complaints against banks acting as POPs
NPS grievances are registered and tracked through CGMS hosted by the CRAs. SCORES, Bima Bharosa and RBI's portal cover securities, insurance and banking complaints respectively.

Overview of Alternative Investments.overview: This chapter introduces alternative investments and how they differ from traditional listed equity, bonds and cash. It covers private equity, venture capital, private credit, real estate, infrastructure, hedge-fund strategies and commodities, along with their common features: illiquidity, long horizons, higher minimum investments, complex fees, limited transparency and appraisal-based pricing. Learners should understand why investors use alternatives — diversification, access to the illiquidity premium and specialist skill — and the risks, including valuation uncertainty and manager dispersion. Focus on comparing alternatives with traditional assets and identifying which investors they suit.
questions: Which characteristic is most typical of alternative investments compared with listed large-cap shares?
Higher minimum ticket sizes
Daily pricing on a recognised stock exchange with continuous liquidity
Lower fees because managers are passive
Full transparency of holdings every day
Alternatives usually require large minimum investments, are illiquid and charge higher, more complex fees. Daily exchange pricing and full transparency are features of listed securities.
The extra return investors expect for locking up capital in long-dated private funds is known as the:
Illiquidity premium
Equity risk premium on large-cap listed shares
Term premium on government bonds
Currency premium
Investors demand compensation for being unable to sell easily; this is the illiquidity premium. The equity risk premium relates to listed equity versus risk-free assets.
Why is the dispersion of returns between top and bottom managers usually wider in private equity than in large-cap equity mutual funds?
Private equity managers are not allowed to diversify across companies at all
All private equity funds track the same index
Outcomes depend heavily on manager skill in sourcing and value creation
Regulators fix the returns of private equity funds

Private equity returns depend on deal sourcing, negotiation and active value creation, so manager selection matters greatly. Listed large-cap funds hold similar stocks and their returns cluster more closely.
Which of the following is a real asset rather than a financial claim?
A corporate bond issued by a toll road company
A toll road owned by an infrastructure fund
A listed share of an infrastructure company
Units of a liquid mutual fund that holds treasury bills
A toll road is a tangible, real asset. Bonds, shares and fund units are financial claims, even if they relate to infrastructure companies.
An investor sees that a private equity fund's quarterly reported returns have a very low standard deviation. A key caution is that:
Smoothed, appraisal-based valuations can understate true volatility
Low volatility proves the fund carries no market risk at all and can replace debt holdings
Private equity is always less risky than government bonds
Reported volatility of private funds is audited daily
Private fund valuations are periodic and judgement-based, which smooths returns and understates risk. Low reported volatility does not mean the absence of market risk.
Private credit funds typically earn returns by:
Buying listed shares and holding them for dividends
Investing only in gold and silver
Lending to companies and earning interest and fees
Holding cash in bank deposits
Private credit funds lend directly to companies, earning interest, fees and sometimes equity kickers. They are a form of debt investment, not listed equity or commodities.
For which investor is a meaningful allocation to alternative investments most suitable?
A wealthy family with long horizon and surplus liquidity
A retiree who needs monthly income from a small corpus and may need cash for medical bills
A young saver building an emergency fund
A trader who needs daily access to all funds
Alternatives suit investors with long horizons, large wealth and no need for near-term liquidity. Those needing regular income or liquidity are poorly matched to locked-in products.
Venture capital differs from buyout private equity mainly because venture capital:
Acquires controlling stakes in mature companies using significant debt financing
Invests only in listed companies
Backs early-stage firms with minority stakes
Avoids technology businesses
Venture capital funds early-stage, often loss-making companies and usually takes minority stakes. Buyouts acquire control of mature businesses, typically with leverage.

Alternative Investment Funds in India.overview: This chapter explains the AIF framework in India under the SEBI (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012. It covers the definition of an AIF, what is excluded from it, and the three categories: Category I (venture capital including angel funds, SME, social impact, infrastructure and special situation funds), Category II (private equity, private debt and funds of funds without leverage) and Category III (hedge-fund style funds using complex strategies and leverage). It also reviews the growth of the AIF industry. Focus on classifying a fund by its strategy and on the key differences among the three categories.
questions: A fund that invests in units of other Category I and II AIFs, without leverage, would normally be registered as:
Category II AIF (fund of funds)
Category I AIF as a social impact fund
Category III AIF
A mutual fund under SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations
Funds of AIFs are generally registered as Category II AIFs. Category III is for funds using complex strategies and leverage, and mutual funds have a separate framework.
Which fund is NOT covered by the SEBI AIF Regulations?
A private equity fund pooling money from HNIs
A venture debt fund raising ₹200 crore privately
A mutual fund registered under SEBI's mutual fund regulations
A long-short fund for sophisticated investors
Mutual funds, collective investment schemes and certain other regulated vehicles are excluded from the AIF definition. Privately pooled PE, debt and hedge-style funds fall within it.
Angel funds in India are a sub-category of:
Category II AIF private equity funds investing in late-stage companies
Category III AIF
Category I AIF (venture capital funds)
Portfolio management services
Angel funds are a sub-category of venture capital funds under Category I, pooling money from angel investors for start-ups. They are not PMS or Category III.
A fund that invests in listed and unlisted securities of stressed companies, including through acquisition of stressed loans, falls in which sub-category?
Special situation fund under Category I
Infrastructure fund under Category I
Hedge fund under Category III
Fund of funds under Category II
Special situation funds invest in special situation assets such as stressed loans and securities of stressed companies and are a Category I sub-category.
Which feature is allowed for Category III AIFs but not for Category I and II AIFs?
Investment in unlisted companies of any kind, including early-stage start-ups
Charging a management fee
Leverage for investment purposes
Raising money from accredited investors
Category III AIFs can use leverage, within SEBI limits, to make investments. Category I and II AIFs may borrow only temporarily for operational needs, and all categories can charge fees.
A debt fund that lends to unlisted mid-sized companies without leverage would typically register as:
Category I AIF as an SME fund
Category III AIF
Category II AIF
A non-banking financial company
A private debt fund without leverage or special incentives is a Category II AIF. Category III is for complex trading strategies, and NBFCs are regulated by the RBI under a different framework.
Category I AIFs are distinguished mainly because they invest in sectors that:
Have the highest expected returns
Are listed on recognised stock exchanges
Government or regulators view as socially or economically desirable
Require leverage to generate returns
Category I covers funds investing in start-ups, SMEs, social ventures, infrastructure and special situations, which policymakers consider desirable and may support with incentives.
The rapid growth of commitments raised by AIFs in India over the last decade is best explained by:
A legal requirement for banks to invest a fixed share of deposits in AIFs
Rising HNI wealth and demand for private-market access
AIFs guaranteeing higher returns than fixed deposits
Mutual funds being banned from equity investing
AIF growth reflects growing wealth, demand for private-market exposure and institutional interest. AIFs do not guarantee returns, and there is no deposit-investment mandate for banks.

Concepts in the AIF Industry.overview: This chapter introduces core private fund concepts. It covers commitments and drawdowns, first and final close, investment period and fund tenure, the J-curve, vintage year, management fee and carried interest, hurdle rate, catch-up, waterfall structures, sponsor commitment, co-investment and the difference between gross and net returns. When revising, practise numerical questions on uncalled commitment, hurdle amounts and simple carry calculations, and be able to explain how these terms affect an investor's cash flows and returns over the life of a close-ended fund.
questions: An investor committed ₹5 crore to a Category II AIF and 35% has been drawn down so far. The uncalled commitment is:
₹1.75 crore
₹3.25 crore
₹5.00 crore
₹3.50 crore
Drawn amount = 35% × 5 crore = ₹1.75 crore. Uncalled = 5 − 1.75 = ₹3.25 crore. ₹1.75 crore is the amount already called.
The 'vintage year' of a private equity fund usually refers to:
The year the fund manager was incorporated as a company
The year the fund made its first investment or capital call
The year the fund is expected to wind up
The year the fund's last investment is exited
Vintage year marks the start of a fund's investing activity and is used to compare funds that faced similar market conditions. It is not the manager's founding or the fund's end.
A fund's investors must receive their capital plus an 8% annual compounded return before carry is paid. On ₹100 crore held for three years, the amount investors must receive first is about:
₹124.00 crore
₹108.00 crore
₹133.10 crore
₹125.97 crore
With compounding, 100 × 1.08³ ≈ ₹125.97 crore. ₹124 crore uses simple interest, and ₹133.10 crore uses 10% instead of 8%.
The 'investment period' of a close-ended AIF is the period during which:
Investors can redeem their units at NAV on demand
Only exits are allowed and no new investments are made
The manager can make new portfolio investments
The fund raises capital from new investors every month without a final close
During the investment period the manager deploys commitments into new deals. After it ends, the fund mainly manages and exits existing investments.
A fund generates proceeds of ₹160 crore on ₹100 crore of capital. The hurdle amount is ₹30 crore and carry is 20% of profits above the hurdle with no catch-up. The manager's carry is:
₹12 crore
₹8 crore
₹30 crore
₹6 crore
Profit = ₹60 crore. Profit above hurdle = 60 − 30 = ₹30 crore. Carry = 20% × 30 = ₹6 crore. ₹12 crore applies 20% to the whole profit, as a full catch-up would.
'Gross IRR' and 'net IRR' of an AIF differ mainly because net IRR:
Includes only realised investments and ignores unrealised holdings
Deducts fees, expenses and carried interest
Is calculated before management fees
Uses the hurdle rate instead of actual cash flows
Net IRR reflects the investor's actual experience after fees, fund expenses and carry. Gross IRR measures portfolio performance before these costs.
A co-investment opportunity in a private fund context means:
The fund invests in another AIF of the same manager
Two managers jointly manage a single scheme
An investor transfers its commitment to another investor at a discount
Investors invest directly alongside the fund in a specific deal
Co-investment lets fund investors take an additional direct stake in a particular portfolio company alongside the AIF, often at lower or no fees. Transferring a commitment is a secondary sale.
A 'first close' in fundraising means that:
The fund has stopped accepting all new investors permanently
The fund has accepted initial commitments and can begin operating
All capital has been drawn down
The fund's first investment has been exited
At first close, the fund admits its initial investors and can start investing, while it may continue raising money until the final close.

AIF Regulatory Framework.overview: This chapter covers the main requirements of the SEBI AIF Regulations and circulars. Topics include registration, minimum corpus and minimum investment, the limit on number of investors, sponsor or manager continuing interest, accredited investors and large value funds, tenure and its extension, investment conditions and concentration limits for each category, leverage rules, the PPM and its filing through a merchant banker, the direct plan option, investor charter and grievance redressal, and reporting. Revise the key thresholds and the reasons behind them; where limits are frequently revised, understand the principle.
questions: A Category I AIF has a corpus of ₹80 crore. The minimum continuing interest required from the sponsor or manager is:
₹5 crore
₹4 crore
₹80 lakh
₹2 crore
For Category I and II AIFs, continuing interest is the lower of 2.5% of corpus or ₹5 crore. 2.5% of 80 crore = ₹2 crore, which is lower than ₹5 crore.
A Category II AIF has investable funds of ₹240 crore. Under the general concentration limit, the maximum it can invest in one investee company is:
₹24 crore
₹60 crore
₹48 crore
₹120 crore
Category I and II AIFs may invest up to 25% of investable funds in a single investee company (large value funds have a higher limit). 25% × 240 = ₹60 crore.
Which statement about accredited investors in AIFs is correct?
They can redeem units of close-ended Category II AIFs on demand at NAV
They may invest below the ₹1 crore minimum
They must invest at least ₹10 crore in every scheme
They are exempt from KYC requirements
Accredited investors are exempt from the ₹1 crore minimum investment requirement and can access accredited-investor-only schemes. They are still subject to KYC and fund lock-ins.
The minimum tenure of a Category I or II AIF is:
Three years
One year
Five years
Ten years
Category I and II AIFs must be close-ended with a minimum tenure of three years from the final close. Category III may be open-ended or close-ended.
A new AIF scheme must file its placement memorandum with SEBI through:
The fund's statutory auditor
A SEBI-registered merchant banker
A stock exchange
The custodian of the AIF
SEBI requires the PPM of a new scheme to be filed through a SEBI-registered merchant banker, who carries out due diligence on the disclosures.
Which grievance redressal route is available to an investor with an unresolved complaint against an AIF manager?
The Insurance Ombudsman
The NPS Central Grievance Management System
SEBI SCORES, followed by online dispute resolution if needed
The Banking Ombudsman of RBI for all investment complaints
AIF investors can lodge complaints on SEBI's SCORES and, if unresolved, use the online dispute resolution mechanism for securities market disputes.
Category I and II AIFs may borrow only for temporary funding needs. Which condition is part of this framework?
Borrowing is capped as a share of investable funds and for a short period
Borrowing is unlimited if investors approve
Borrowing is permitted only to buy listed shares
Borrowings must be at least 50% of the corpus
SEBI permits such AIFs to borrow only to meet temporary shortfalls, within limits on amount, duration and frequency. Leverage for investment is not allowed for these categories.
SEBI requires every AIF scheme to offer a 'direct plan'. Its main feature is:
A guaranteed minimum return
Shorter lock-in than the regular plan
A lower minimum investment of ₹10 lakh
No distribution or placement fee is charged
A direct plan is for investors coming directly or through SEBI-registered investment advisers or PMS and carries no distribution fee. It has the same lock-in and minimums.

Alternative Investment Fund Structuring.overview: This chapter covers how AIFs are legally organised. It explains the choice between trust, company, limited liability partnership and body corporate structures, and why most Indian AIFs are trusts. It describes the documents that create and govern the fund — trust deed, contribution agreement, investment management agreement and PPM — and the roles of sponsor, trustee, manager, custodian and other parties. It also covers structures for foreign investors, such as offshore feeders and unified structures, and the FEMA treatment of downstream investment. Focus on who does what in each structure and the reasons for choosing a structure.
questions: Which document appoints the investment manager of a trust-based AIF and sets out its duties and fees?
The trust deed alone without any separate agreement with the manager
The contribution agreement
The custodian's agreement
The investment management agreement
The trustee appoints the manager through an investment management agreement, which specifies powers, duties and fees. The contribution agreement governs investors' commitments.
A key reason most Indian AIFs are structured as trusts is that trusts:
Are the only structure permitted by SEBI for AIFs
Pay no tax under any circumstances
Are flexible to set up and wind up
Allow unlimited leverage
Trusts are flexible to establish and dissolve and fit the statutory pass-through regime for Category I and II AIFs. Companies and LLPs are also permitted, and trusts are not tax-free in all cases.
In a trust-based AIF, who is the 'settlor'?
The person who creates the trust with an initial settlement
The investor with the largest commitment
The custodian holding the assets
The merchant banker filing the PPM
The settlor creates the trust by settling an initial sum and executing the trust deed, usually the sponsor. Investors become contributors or beneficiaries through contribution agreements.
Why might an AIF choose an LLP structure instead of a trust?
LLPs need no registration with SEBI to operate as AIFs
Partners' liability is limited
LLPs are exempt from FEMA rules
LLPs are the only structure for Category III funds
An LLP gives partners limited liability and a contractual framework familiar to global investors. It must still register with SEBI as an AIF and follow FEMA.
If an Indian AIF's sponsor and manager are owned and controlled by resident Indian citizens, its downstream investment is treated under FEMA as:
Foreign direct investment in all cases
Foreign portfolio investment
Domestic investment, even if some investors are foreign
Not permitted at all

Under FEMA, downstream investments by an AIF are treated as foreign investment only if the sponsor or manager is not owned and controlled by resident Indian citizens. Foreign LP money alone does not change this.
In a unified structure, foreign investors invest:
Only through an offshore fund that invests via the FPI route
Only in listed Indian shares through a mutual fund
Through an Indian bank fixed deposit
Directly into the Indian AIF alongside domestic investors

In a unified structure, offshore and domestic investors invest directly into the same Indian AIF, sometimes using an offshore pooling vehicle. In contrast, a pure offshore structure uses FPI or FDI routes.
Which party in a trust-based AIF is primarily responsible for ensuring that the manager acts in accordance with the trust deed and PPM?
The trustee
The placement agent
The investee company
The tax consultant
The trustee oversees the fund on behalf of beneficiaries and ensures the manager follows the trust deed and PPM. Placement agents only help raise capital.
An AIF offers two classes of units: Class A for investors and Class B for the manager team, which carries entitlement to carried interest. Class B units are used mainly to:
Channel carried interest to the manager team
Give the manager team voting control over all investor decisions
Avoid the minimum investment requirement for investors
Allow the manager to redeem units at any time
Separate unit classes allow carried interest and different fee terms to be allocated to the manager team, as disclosed in the PPM. They do not give overriding control or waive investor requirements.

Risk and Return – Fund and Investor Pers.overview: This chapter covers how risk and return are measured for private funds and from an investor's viewpoint. It explains IRR and its limitations, multiples such as TVPI, DPI and RVPI, the public market equivalent approach, the J-curve, and the main risks: illiquidity, valuation, leverage within portfolio companies, concentration, manager and key-person risk, currency and regulatory risk. Revise the calculation and meaning of the multiples, why IRR can be flattered by early exits or subscription lines, and how investors diversify across vintages, managers and strategies.
questions: A fund has paid-in capital of ₹80 crore, distributions of ₹60 crore and residual NAV of ₹52 crore. Its TVPI is:
TVPI = (distributions + NAV) ÷ paid-in = (60 + 52) ÷ 80 = 1.40x. 0.75x is the DPI (60 ÷ 80) and 0.65x is the RVPI (52 ÷ 80).
Using the same fund (paid-in ₹80 crore, distributions ₹60 crore, NAV ₹52 crore), the RVPI is:
RVPI = residual value ÷ paid-in = 52 ÷ 80 = 0.65x. It shows how much value remains unrealised in the portfolio.
Why can IRR alone be misleading when comparing private funds?
IRR ignores the timing of cash flows and so is unaffected by early exits
IRR cannot be calculated for close-ended funds
A quick exit with small gains can show a high IRR
IRR is always lower than the money multiple
IRR is sensitive to timing: a quick exit with modest gains can produce a high IRR but little absolute wealth. Investors therefore look at multiples alongside IRR.
An investor commits to private equity funds of five different vintage years. The main benefit is:
Reducing exposure to one year's entry valuations
Avoiding management fees in later years
Guaranteeing a positive IRR in each fund
Shortening the lock-in of each fund
Vintage diversification spreads capital across different market and valuation conditions, reducing the risk of investing all at a market peak.
A fund uses a subscription credit line to fund deals before calling capital from investors. This tends to:
Reduce the fund's total profits automatically
Raise reported IRR by delaying capital calls
Lower the reported IRR
Eliminate the J-curve and all fees
Delaying capital calls shortens the period investor money is at work, boosting IRR, though interest costs may reduce the absolute multiple. Investors should look at both measures.
The public market equivalent (PME) method helps an investor answer:
What the fund's management fee should be
Whether the fund is legally registered
Whether the fund beat a comparable public index
How many investors the fund has
PME compares a private fund's cash flows with a hypothetical investment in a public index made at the same times, showing relative outperformance.
Which risk is most significant for an Indian investor in an AIF that invests in a few large unlisted companies?
Interest-rate risk on government bonds held as cash management
Inflation-indexation risk
Exchange-rate risk on rupee-denominated holdings
Concentration risk
A small number of large holdings makes outcomes depend on a few companies. Rupee-denominated holdings carry no exchange-rate risk for a domestic investor.
The J-curve suggests that an investor reviewing a fund in year two should:
Immediately sell the interest in the secondary market at any price
Expect the highest returns in the first year
Ignore fees because they do not affect early returns
Not conclude that early negative returns mean failure
Early returns are depressed by fees and costs before investments mature, so negative early IRRs are normal. Fees are a key driver of the J-curve's dip.

Investment Process and Governance of Fun.overview: This chapter covers how AIFs source, evaluate, approve, monitor and exit investments, and the governance that controls these activities. It explains deal sourcing, screening, due diligence, valuation and term negotiation, the role of the investment committee, conflict-of-interest policies, investor approvals for related-party transactions, investment restrictions and concentration limits, monitoring of portfolio companies and the responsibilities of the manager, trustee and compliance officer. Focus on the sequence of the process, who approves what, and governance practices that protect investors.
questions: In the investment process of a PE fund, 'screening' refers to:
The detailed legal review of the share purchase agreement
An initial filter of deals against the fund's strategy
The final exit of a portfolio company
Valuation of the fund's units for investors
Screening is a quick initial assessment of many opportunities against the strategy, size and sector criteria before detailed due diligence on the few that pass.
A member of an AIF's investment committee has a personal stake in a target company. Good governance requires that member to:
Vote in favour to support the company
Keep the interest confidential to avoid delays
Disclose the interest and recuse from the decision
Resign from the manager immediately in every case
Conflicted members should disclose their interest and abstain from deliberation and voting. Resignation is not normally required, but secrecy breaches governance norms.
Which entity in a trust-based AIF is responsible for monitoring the manager's compliance with the PPM and regulations?
The trustee, supported by the compliance officer
The investee companies
The placement agent
The largest investor alone
The trustee oversees the manager, and the manager's compliance officer monitors adherence to regulations and the PPM. Investee companies and agents have no oversight role.
A Category II AIF wants to buy shares from another scheme of the same manager. This is generally:
Prohibited outright without exception
A conflict needing approval as per regulations
Permitted freely as both schemes are managed by the same entity
Allowed only if the shares are listed
Transactions between schemes of the same manager raise conflicts; SEBI requires disclosure and investor consent as prescribed, plus fair valuation. They are not automatically prohibited.
After investing, a PE fund typically monitors portfolio companies by:
Board seats, regular MIS and covenant tracking
Selling the shares within three months of purchase
Relying only on annual audited accounts
Leaving management entirely unsupervised
Active monitoring through board representation, periodic reports and covenant checks lets the fund protect value and intervene early. Annual accounts alone are too infrequent.
Which document defines the fund's investment strategy, which the investment process must follow?
The custodian agreement
The KYC form of the investor
The private placement memorandum
The investee company's articles of association
The PPM sets out the strategy, restrictions and terms; investments must conform to it. Material deviations require investor consent.
An AIF manager allocates a hot deal only to a fund where it earns higher carry, ignoring another fund with the same mandate. This breaches:
The duty of fair allocation among funds
Concentration limits only
Reporting timelines
Stewardship code voting rules
Managers must allocate opportunities fairly as per a disclosed allocation policy, not based on their own economics. Concentration limits and voting rules are separate matters.
Which practice best supports good governance in a fund's investment decisions?
Approvals given orally by the chief investment officer alone, without any written record
Rotating approval rights among junior analysts
Allowing investee companies to vote on fund decisions
Documented IC minutes with reasons for approval
Written records of IC deliberations and reasons create accountability and an audit trail. Oral approvals by one person weaken governance.

Fund Due Diligence – Investor Perspectiv.overview: This chapter explains how investors evaluate an AIF before committing. It covers investment due diligence (strategy, team, track record, attribution, pipeline, portfolio construction), operational due diligence (back office, valuation, custody, compliance, cyber security, service providers), alignment of interest (sponsor commitment, fee terms, carry structure), and assessment of terms and legal documents. It also covers red flags and the use of due diligence questionnaires and reference checks. Focus on what evidence an investor should seek, how to verify track record and how to spot weaknesses.
questions: Which question best tests whether a manager's track record is attributable to the current team?
What were the overall market returns in those years?
How many offices does the manager have?
Which current team members led the past deals?
What is the manager's brand recognition among retail investors?
Attribution analysis checks whether the people who generated past returns are still with the firm. Market returns and branding do not show who created value.
A manager refuses to share the names of the independent valuer and the fund's auditor during due diligence. This is:
A red flag warranting further enquiry
Normal practice to protect business secrets of the fund manager from competitors
Irrelevant to operational risk
Required by SEBI confidentiality rules
Transparency about key service providers is basic; refusal to disclose them raises concerns about valuation and controls. No regulation requires hiding them from investors.
Reference checks with founders of companies previously backed by the manager help an investor assess:
The manager's behaviour as a partner
The fund's tax status
The legal validity of the trust deed
The SEBI registration number
Speaking with founders and co-investors reveals how the manager behaves, adds value and handles difficulties — information that documents cannot provide.
A due diligence questionnaire (DDQ) is mainly used to:
Replace the PPM as the legal offer document
Calculate the fund's NAV
Collect standard information about the manager
Register the investor as an accredited investor
A DDQ gathers consistent information on strategy, team, operations, compliance and terms, making comparison across managers easier. It does not replace the PPM.
An investor learns that the fund manager's chief financial officer also acts as the fund's sole valuation decision-maker without independent review. The main concern is:
Excessive diversification of portfolio holdings
Lack of independence in valuation
Too many service providers
High distribution fees
Valuations drive reported performance and fees. Concentrating valuation decisions in management without independent review creates conflicts and the risk of inflated values.
Which of these best indicates alignment of interest between a manager and investors?
High management fees charged on committed capital throughout the fund's entire life
A guaranteed minimum carry for the manager
Meaningful team investment and carry paid after capital is returned
Carry paid deal by deal with no clawback
Personal capital at risk and a whole-of-fund waterfall tie the manager's rewards to investors' outcomes. High fees and guaranteed carry weaken alignment.
Why do investors look at a manager's portfolio construction plan during due diligence?
To calculate the investor's own tax liability
To verify the custodian's net worth
To set the investor's KYC risk category
To check if diversification and sizing fit the strategy
The plan shows how many companies the fund will hold, typical ticket sizes and reserves for follow-ons, which determine risk and consistency with the stated strategy.
A first-time fund is led by professionals who spun out of a large established PE firm. The investor's key diligence focus should be:
Whether the old firm's brand is mentioned in the PPM and on the new manager's website
The size of the new office
The number of LinkedIn followers of the partners
Whether they can operate their own firm
Spin-out teams may have good deal records but must show they can run a firm — operations, compliance, fundraising and team stability. Branding and office size are not meaningful.

Legal Documentation and Negotiation – In.overview: This chapter covers the main legal documents of an AIF and the terms investors negotiate. Documents include the PPM, trust deed, contribution agreement, investment management agreement and side letters. Key terms include commitment and drawdown mechanics, default provisions, fees and expenses, the waterfall, clawback, key-person and removal clauses, the investor advisory committee, transfer restrictions, MFN rights and confidentiality, along with SEBI's rules on pro-rata rights and differential rights. Focus on the purpose of each clause and how it protects investors or the manager.
questions: An investor fails to fund a drawdown notice. The contribution agreement typically allows the manager to:
Raise the commitments of all other investors without consent
Cancel the fund automatically
Waive the default without any consequences in all cases
Apply default penalties to the defaulting investor
Default clauses permit penalties such as interest, forfeiture of a portion of the interest or forced transfer, protecting non-defaulting investors from funding gaps.
A 'for-cause removal' clause allows investors to:
Remove the manager for events like fraud or breach
Redeem their units at NAV whenever they wish
Appoint a new auditor without any reason
Veto every individual investment
For-cause removal lets investors replace the manager following defined events such as fraud, gross negligence or material breach, usually by a specified majority.
Which clause limits an investor's ability to sell its fund interest to a third party?
Most favoured nation clause
Key-person clause
Hurdle rate clause
Transfer restrictions requiring manager consent
Transfer restriction clauses require the manager's consent before an investor sells its interest, protecting the fund from unsuitable investors.
Under SEBI's framework on investor rights in AIFs, differential rights granted to select investors must:
Be kept secret from other investors
Not harm the rights of other investors
Always include higher returns guaranteed by the sponsor
Be approved by the stock exchange
SEBI requires pro-rata rights generally, permitting differential rights only within its framework and without affecting other investors adversely. Guaranteed returns are not permitted.
Which expense is most likely to be negotiated as borne by the manager rather than the fund?
Fund audit fees
Custodian charges
Legal costs of closing portfolio deals
Manager's own office rent and salaries
Overheads such as the manager's office and staff are usually paid out of the management fee. Fund-level expenses like audit, custody and deal costs are commonly charged to the fund.
An investor advisory committee (IAC) of an AIF commonly:
Makes all investment decisions instead of the manager
Sets the investors' tax rates
Appoints the SEBI inspection team
Reviews conflicts and valuation issues
The IAC, made up of investor representatives, advises on conflicts of interest, valuation questions and certain consents. Investment decisions remain with the manager.
A 'GP giveback' provision allows the manager to:
Return carried interest to investors each year
Recall distributions to meet fund indemnities
Give back unused commitments after the first close
Refund management fees on demand
A giveback lets the fund recall part of past distributions from investors to meet indemnity obligations or liabilities. It differs from a clawback, which recovers excess carry from the manager.
Why do investors often negotiate a cap on organisational (set-up) expenses?
To prevent the fund from being registered with SEBI
To limit fund costs borne by investors
To ensure the fund invests only in listed shares
To avoid paying any management fee at all during the fund's life
Set-up costs such as legal and registration fees are charged to the fund; a cap prevents excessive costs eroding investor returns.

Fund Monitoring, Reporting and Exit.overview: This chapter covers what happens after investors commit. It explains periodic reporting to investors (capital account statements, valuation reports, portfolio updates), reporting to SEBI and the trustee, PPM compliance audits, monitoring of the manager, and exit routes for both the fund's portfolio investments and the investors themselves: IPO, strategic sale, secondary sale, buyback, in-specie distribution, secondaries and continuation funds. It also covers the end of a fund's tenure, extension and dissolution or liquidation options. Focus on which exits suit which situations and how investors keep track of a fund's progress.
questions: Which document shows an individual investor's contributions, distributions and share of NAV in an AIF?
Capital account statement
Private placement memorandum
Trust deed
Investment management agreement
A capital account statement tracks each investor's commitment, amounts called, distributions and current value. The PPM and trust deed are constitutional documents.
A PE fund sells its stake in a portfolio company to another PE fund. This exit route is called a:
Initial public offering
Buyback by the promoter
Secondary sale
Write-off
Selling to another financial investor is a secondary sale. An IPO lists the shares, and a buyback involves the company or promoters repurchasing them.
A close-ended AIF's tenure has ended but some unlisted holdings remain unsold. One option within SEBI's framework is to:
Convert the scheme into an open-ended mutual fund
Extend the tenure indefinitely without investor approval
Distribute the holdings in specie to investors who agree
Sell the holdings to the sponsor at book value without consent
SEBI permits in-specie distribution of unliquidated investments with investor approval, or use of the dissolution route. Indefinite extension or forced sales to the sponsor are not allowed.
Why is an IPO often an attractive exit for a PE fund?
It guarantees the fund can sell its entire stake on listing day
It eliminates lock-in requirements on pre-IPO shareholders
It may achieve a high valuation and liquidity
It avoids SEBI disclosure rules
Listing can deliver a strong valuation and a liquid market, but pre-IPO shareholders face lock-ins and full sale is rarely immediate.
An investor in a 10-year AIF needs liquidity in year five. A realistic option is to:
Redeem units from the fund at NAV on request
Ask SEBI to cancel its commitment
Stop paying capital calls without consequences
Sell its interest on the secondary market
Close-ended AIFs do not offer redemption; investors needing liquidity can sell their interests to secondary buyers, typically at a discount and with manager consent.
An AIF must report periodically to SEBI. A key purpose of such reporting is to allow SEBI to:
Approve each individual investment in advance
Calculate investors' income tax
Set the fund's management fee
Monitor the industry's investments and risks
Periodic reporting enables SEBI to oversee activity, leverage, concentration and compliance across AIFs. SEBI does not pre-approve investments or set fees.
A GP-led continuation vehicle typically gives existing investors:
A compulsory transfer of all their units to the new vehicle
A choice to sell or roll over into the new vehicle
A guaranteed premium over NAV
The right to manage the continuation vehicle
In a continuation fund, selected assets move to a new vehicle; existing investors can usually sell for cash or roll their interest. Fairness requires an independent price process.
The annual audit of compliance with the terms of the PPM is meant to:
Verify the scheme's adherence to its PPM
Replace the statutory audit of accounts
Value each portfolio company
Calculate carried interest
The PPM audit checks whether the scheme has followed its stated terms and disclosures. It complements, but does not replace, the statutory financial audit or valuations.

Valuation.overview: This chapter covers how AIFs value their portfolio investments. It introduces fair value and the main approaches — market (comparable companies and transactions), income (discounted cash flow) and cost-based approaches such as the price of a recent investment — along with adjustments for control, marketability and liquidation preferences. It covers SEBI's requirements on independent valuers, valuation frequency and the use of IPEV or industry-endorsed guidelines, and the importance of a consistent valuation policy. Focus on choosing the right method for a company's stage and on the risks of stale or biased valuations.
questions: A company has EBITDA of ₹30 crore and comparable companies trade at 8x EV/EBITDA. If net debt is ₹60 crore, the equity value is:
₹240 crore
₹180 crore
₹300 crore
₹210 crore
Enterprise value = 30 × 8 = ₹240 crore. Equity value = EV − net debt = 240 − 60 = ₹180 crore. ₹240 crore is the enterprise value, not equity.
Which valuation approach is most suitable for an infrastructure asset with long, predictable contracted cash flows?
Price of the most recent funding round
Discounted cash flow
Liquidation value
Book value of share capital
Predictable long-term cash flows suit DCF valuation. Recent round prices fit early-stage companies, and liquidation value suits distressed situations.
Under SEBI's framework, the valuation of AIF investments must be done by an independent valuer. 'Independent' mainly means the valuer:
Is a large investor in the fund
Is the fund's own investment committee
Is appointed by the investee company
Is not an associate of the manager or sponsor
Independence requires the valuer to be free from relationships with the manager, sponsor and trustee that could bias valuations. Investors or investees cannot provide unbiased values.
A PE fund holds preference shares with a 1x liquidation preference in a company that may be sold at a modest valuation. The valuation should:
Reflect the preference's effect on proceeds
Ignore the preference and value all shares equally
Assume the preference will never be used
Use only the par value of preference shares
Liquidation preferences change how sale proceeds are distributed, especially at lower exit values, so they must be reflected in fair value.
Why might an AIF apply a discount for lack of control to a minority stake?
A minority holder cannot direct company decisions
Minority stakes are always worth more than controlling stakes
SEBI requires a fixed 50% discount on all minority stakes
Minority stakes cannot be valued at all
Without control, the investor cannot set strategy, dividends or a sale, which can reduce the value per share compared with a controlling stake. There is no fixed regulatory discount.
A fund continues to value a start-up at its last round price two years after investment, though the company has missed every milestone. This is a concern because:
Last-round price is never allowed in any valuation
The valuer is required to use book value
Missed milestones always increase value
Stale values overstate NAV and performance
Valuations must be updated for developments; keeping an outdated round price after poor performance overstates value and can mislead investors.
The 'comparable transactions' method values a company using:
Book value of the company's fixed assets
Prices paid in recent acquisitions of similar firms
The company's share capital
The fund's original cost
Precedent transaction multiples reflect what buyers have paid for similar businesses, often including a control premium, unlike trading multiples of listed peers.
A company is expected to produce free cash flow of ₹12 crore next year, growing at 4% forever. At a 14% discount rate, its enterprise value is:
₹85.7 crore
₹120 crore
₹300 crore
₹66.7 crore
Using the growing perpetuity formula, EV = 12 ÷ (0.14 − 0.04) = ₹120 crore. ₹85.7 crore ignores growth (12 ÷ 0.14).

Taxation – India Specific.overview: This chapter covers the Indian tax treatment of AIFs and their investors. It explains the statutory pass-through regime for Category I and II AIFs, under which non-business income is taxed in investors' hands with the same character, while business income is taxed at fund level; TDS on income distributed to investors; the treatment of losses; the taxation of Category III AIFs at fund level; the position of non-resident investors and treaty benefits; and GST on management fees. Since tax provisions are being renumbered under the new Income-tax Act, focus on principles rather than section numbers.
questions: Capital gains earned by a Category II AIF on selling unlisted shares are taxed in investors' hands as:
Business income in all cases
Income from other sources
Capital gains, with the same character
Exempt income
Under the pass-through regime, income other than business income keeps its character in investors' hands, so capital gains remain capital gains.
When a Category I or II AIF distributes income (other than business income) to a resident investor, the fund generally:
Pays no attention to tax because income is exempt
Pays the final tax on behalf of all investors at the maximum marginal rate
Deducts GST from the distribution
Deducts tax at source as prescribed
The AIF deducts TDS on income credited or paid to investors, as prescribed by law; investors then pay tax on their share, claiming credit for TDS. GST does not apply to distributions.
A Category II AIF incurs a capital loss on an investment. The loss is generally:
Retained at fund level forever
Passed through to investors who meet holding conditions
Converted into business loss
Ignored for tax purposes
Losses other than business losses are passed to investors, provided they have held units for the prescribed minimum period. Business losses stay at fund level.
Business income earned by a Category I AIF trust is taxed:
At the fund level
Only in investors' hands as exempt income
As capital gains in investors' hands
At a concessional rate of 1%
Business income is excluded from pass-through and is taxed at the fund level; distributions of that income to investors are then exempt in their hands.
A non-resident investor in a Category II AIF wants to claim lower tax under a tax treaty. She typically needs to provide:
Only her passport copy
A tax residency certificate and documents
Nothing, since non-residents are exempt
Her Indian bank fixed deposit receipts
Treaty benefits require a tax residency certificate and related documentation; the AIF may then apply the treaty rate on income allocable to her.
Management fees charged by an AIF manager attract:
Goods and Services Tax
Securities Transaction Tax
Commodity Transaction Tax
No indirect tax
Management fees are a supply of services and attract GST, which increases the cost borne by the fund. STT and CTT apply to securities and commodity transactions.
Why do Category I and II AIFs issue investors an annual statement of income allocated, by nature of income?
Because investors cannot see the fund's NAV otherwise
So investors can report each income type
To claim GST credits
Because SEBI fixes investors' tax rates
With pass-through, investors are taxed on their share of each income type — capital gains, interest, dividends — so the AIF must report the breakdown for correct filing.
Unlike Category I and II AIFs, a Category III AIF set up as a trust is generally taxed:
Only in investors' hands with full pass-through for all types of income
At zero rate because it invests in listed securities
Only on unrealised gains
At the fund level, as no statutory pass-through applies
Category III AIFs do not enjoy statutory pass-through, so income is generally taxed at the trust level under trust-taxation rules.

Good Practices.overview: This chapter covers ethical and regulatory standards for AIF distributors. It explains SEBI's rules on distribution — NISM certification, the direct plan option, disclosure and payment of distribution fees (with limits on upfront commission for Category I and II), suitability and appropriateness assessment, KYC and AML obligations — and good conduct such as fair disclosure of risks, fees and lock-ins, avoiding mis-selling and conflicts, and maintaining records. Learners should be able to judge whether a recommendation is suitable, identify mis-selling and know what must be disclosed to an investor before they commit.
questions: Before recommending a Category II AIF, a distributor should explain to the client that:
The client can redeem at NAV any time
Returns are assured by the sponsor
The money will be locked in for years
The fund is regulated as a mutual fund
Category II AIFs are close-ended and illiquid; investors must understand the lock-in and drawdown commitments. Returns are not assured and AIFs are not mutual funds.
A distributor tells a client that an AIF is 'SEBI-approved, so it cannot lose money'. This is:
Misleading, as registration is not a guarantee
Accurate, as SEBI guarantees AIF returns
Acceptable if the client is an HNI
Accurate for Category I funds only
SEBI registration means the fund is regulated, not that its returns are protected. Claiming otherwise is mis-selling.
Which of the following must a distributor disclose to the investor?
Personal details of other clients
The distribution fee earned from the AIF
The manager's internal deal pipeline
The SEBI inspection reports of other distributors
Distributors must disclose commissions and fees they receive from the AIF so the investor understands potential conflicts. Other clients' information must remain confidential.
An AIF distributor's KYC and AML obligations include:
Accepting cash in large amounts to speed onboarding
Ignoring politically exposed persons
Skipping KYC for accredited investors
Verifying identity and source of funds
AML rules require verifying identity, beneficial ownership and source of funds, with enhanced checks for higher-risk clients like PEPs. Accredited investors still need KYC.
A client wants to invest in an AIF through the direct plan after receiving advice from a SEBI-registered investment adviser. The distributor should:
Insist that the client invests through the regular plan
Charge the full distribution fee anyway
Refuse to process the client's KYC
Not claim distribution fee on that investment
Direct plans carry no distribution fee; investors advised by registered investment advisers may use them. Pushing a regular plan for a fee would be improper.
Which situation suggests possible mis-selling of an AIF?
A family office with large surplus invests 5% of its portfolio
An accredited investor invests after reading the PPM
A client nearing retirement invests most of her savings in one illiquid fund
A business owner commits after independent advice
Putting most of a near-retiree's savings into one illiquid fund ignores liquidity needs and diversification, suggesting unsuitable advice.
Why does SEBI restrict upfront distribution commissions for Category I and II AIFs?
To increase the distributor's total income
To guarantee higher returns to investors
To reduce incentives for churning and mis-selling
To allow early redemption
Spreading commission as trail over the fund's life aligns the distributor's income with the investor's holding and reduces incentives to push products for upfront fees.
A distributor keeps records of risk-profiling and suitability assessments for each AIF client. This mainly helps to:
Avoid paying GST on distribution fees
Increase the fund's IRR
Bypass the minimum investment
Show the advice was appropriate
Records demonstrate that the distributor assessed suitability before recommending and are required for compliance and dispute resolution.

Overview of Alternative Investments.overview: This chapter introduces alternative investments with an emphasis on hedge-fund style strategies, which Category III AIFs resemble. It contrasts traditional long-only investing with absolute-return approaches using short selling, derivatives, arbitrage and leverage, and outlines the broader universe of alternatives — private equity, private credit, real estate and commodities. Learners should understand the objectives of alternatives (diversification, absolute returns, downside management), their distinctive risks (leverage, liquidity, model and counterparty risk) and why reported statistics can mislead. Focus on matching strategy descriptions to their likely risk and return behaviour.
questions: A 'long-short equity' strategy typically aims to:
Profit from both rising and falling stocks
Hold only cash during market downturns
Track a market index as closely as possible
Invest only in government bonds
Long-short managers buy stocks expected to outperform and short those expected to underperform, so they can earn from stock selection in both directions. Index tracking is a passive approach.
Which risk is specifically introduced when a fund uses leverage?
Magnified losses and margin calls
Lower expected returns in all market conditions
Elimination of market risk
Removal of counterparty risk
Leverage enlarges both gains and losses and can force selling when margins are called. It does not remove market or counterparty risk.
A global macro strategy primarily takes positions based on:
Detailed analysis of a single small-cap company
Views on economies, rates and currencies
Merger announcements only
Pairs of closely related stocks
Global macro funds trade interest rates, currencies, commodities and indices based on macroeconomic views. Merger arbitrage and pair trades are different strategies.
Why might the historical correlation of a hedge-fund strategy with equities rise during a market crisis?
Liquidity stress makes many assets fall together
Hedge funds are required by law to buy equities in a crisis
Short positions automatically become long positions
Correlations are fixed and cannot change
In crises, deleveraging and liquidity shortages lead to simultaneous selling, raising correlations precisely when diversification is most needed.
Compared with traditional investments, alternative investments usually have:
Lower fees and daily holdings disclosure
Higher fees and less transparency
No minimum investment
Guaranteed liquidity
Alternatives generally carry management and performance fees, limited disclosure and higher minimums. Liquidity is often restricted.
An investor says a fund with high average returns and low volatility is 'obviously safe'. What should an adviser point out?
Low volatility always means low risk, so the fund can replace fixed deposits
Strategies selling options can hide rare large losses
Average returns guarantee future returns
Hedge funds cannot have losses above 10%
Strategies that sell insurance-like options can earn steady returns until a rare event causes large losses. Volatility does not capture such tail risk.
A 'relative value' strategy seeks to profit from:
An overall rise in the stock market
Long-term holding of real estate
Mispricing between related securities
Interest on bank deposits
Relative value strategies buy the cheaper and sell the dearer of related instruments, aiming to profit as prices converge, with limited directional exposure.
Which statement about 'absolute return' funds is correct?
They guarantee positive returns every year
They aim for positive returns but do not guarantee them
They must always outperform the Nifty 50 index in every calendar year
They are prohibited from using derivatives
An absolute-return objective targets positive returns regardless of the market, but it is an aim, not a guarantee. Such funds commonly use derivatives.

Growth of AIFs in India and Suitability.overview: This chapter traces the growth of the AIF industry in India and the position of Category III AIFs within it. It covers drivers of growth such as rising HNI and family-office wealth, the search for differentiated strategies and the regulatory framework introduced in 2012. It then explains how to judge whether a Category III fund suits an investor: risk profile, investable surplus, liquidity needs, understanding of complex strategies, time horizon and portfolio concentration. It also compares Category III AIFs with PMS and mutual funds. Focus on suitability scenarios and product comparisons.
questions: A client wants a liquid, low-cost diversified equity product with no minimum ticket. Compared with a Category III AIF, the more suitable choice is:
A leveraged long-short Category III AIF
A Category II private equity AIF
An angel fund
An equity mutual fund
Mutual funds offer liquidity, low minimums and diversification. Category III AIFs require ₹1 crore (except accredited investors) and use complex strategies.
Which factor is MOST important in assessing a client's suitability for a Category III AIF?
The client's preferred bank branch
Understanding of complex strategies and ability to bear losses
Whether the client already holds a credit card issued by the sponsor's bank
The client's city of residence
Category III AIFs may use leverage, derivatives and short selling; investors must understand these and be able to absorb losses. Banking preferences are irrelevant.
Compared with a PMS, a key difference of a Category III AIF is that:
Investors hold units of a pooled fund
Investors hold securities directly in their own demat accounts
There is no minimum investment
It cannot use derivatives
In an AIF, investors own units of a pooled vehicle, while in a PMS the securities are held in the client's own name. Category III AIFs can use derivatives.
An investor's total investable portfolio is ₹20 crore and she has a high risk appetite. Investing ₹2 crore in a Category III AIF would most likely be viewed as:
Unsuitable, because she exceeds the minimum ticket
Prohibited, as AIF investments must exceed 50% of wealth
Unsuitable, since high-risk investors cannot invest in AIFs
A reasonable satellite allocation
A 10% allocation for an experienced, high-risk investor with ample wealth is a reasonable satellite position. There is no rule requiring a minimum share of wealth.
Which development has supported the growth of Category III AIFs in India?
A ban on equity mutual funds for HNIs
More HNIs seeking differentiated strategies
Guaranteed returns offered by Category III funds
Exemption of Category III AIFs from SEBI regulation
Growing wealth and demand for strategies beyond long-only funds have driven growth. Category III AIFs are SEBI-regulated and do not guarantee returns.
A client needs to withdraw her money at short notice for a property purchase next month. A close-ended Category III AIF is:
Unsuitable, as money may be locked in
Ideal, as Category III funds offer daily redemption by law
Suitable only if the fund is long-only
Suitable because AIFs guarantee capital
Close-ended funds do not allow early redemption, and even open-ended ones may have notice periods. Short-term liquidity needs are best met elsewhere.
Accredited investors may invest in Category III AIFs below the usual minimum. Accreditation primarily reflects the investor's:
Years of experience with the same bank
Age above 60
Income or net worth meeting SEBI's criteria
Possession of a NISM certificate
Accreditation is based on income, net worth or financial assets as set by SEBI, verified by an accreditation agency. Age and certifications are not criteria.
A client invests in a Category III fund because last year it returned 45%. The distributor should highlight that:
Past returns may not repeat and risks matter
A 45% return guarantees similar results next year
SEBI caps losses of Category III funds
High returns mean the fund is risk-free
Past performance is not indicative of future results, especially for leveraged or concentrated strategies. The investor should consider risk, strategy and drawdowns.

Introduction to Category III AIF Ecosyst.overview: This chapter describes the participants in the Category III AIF ecosystem and their roles: sponsor, investment manager, trustee, custodian, prime broker, fund accountant or administrator, registrar and transfer agent, auditor, valuer, legal and tax advisers, distributors and investors. It also covers how money and securities flow among them, the importance of independent service providers for investor protection, and the responsibilities of each party under SEBI's framework. Revise who does what, and which roles must be independent of the manager, using scenario questions about errors or conflicts.
questions: Which party in a Category III AIF is responsible for independently auditing the fund's financial statements?
Statutory auditor
Prime broker
Investment manager
Distributor
The statutory auditor gives an independent opinion on the fund's accounts. The prime broker provides financing and trading services, and the manager runs the portfolio.
The registrar and transfer agent of a Category III AIF mainly handles:
Trading decisions and risk limits
Securities lending to the fund and financing of its leveraged positions
Selection of stocks
Investor records and unit transactions
The RTA maintains investor records, processes subscriptions and redemptions and services investors. Trading decisions rest with the manager.
Why should the custodian of a Category III AIF be independent of the manager?
To allow the manager to trade without records
To protect assets from misuse by the manager
Because the custodian decides investments
Because custodians earn performance fees
An independent custodian holds assets separately and reconciles positions, reducing the risk of misappropriation. It does not take investment decisions.
A Category III fund relies on its prime broker for leverage and stock borrowing. A key risk for investors is:
Counterparty risk if the prime broker fails
Inflation risk on the government bonds the fund holds for margin purposes
Currency risk on rupee holdings
Absence of any market risk
Heavy reliance on a prime broker exposes the fund to that broker's credit and operational risk; collateral may be at risk if it fails.
Which of these is a function of the fund administrator?
Marketing the fund to new investors
Deciding the fund's strategy
Granting accreditation to investors
Independent NAV calculation and accounting
Administrators calculate NAV, maintain books and reconcile positions independently. Marketing is done by distributors, and accreditation by recognised agencies.
The sponsor of a Category III AIF differs from the investment manager in that the sponsor:
Makes the daily trading decisions and sets position limits for the portfolio
Holds custody of securities
Audits the fund's accounts
Sets up the AIF and keeps continuing interest
The sponsor establishes the fund and maintains the required continuing interest; the manager takes investment decisions. The sponsor and manager may sometimes be the same entity.
A distributor of a Category III AIF should:
Promise investors a minimum return
Manage the fund's portfolio
Act as the custodian of investor units
Hold the required NISM certification
AIF distributors must hold the relevant NISM certification and assess suitability. They cannot promise returns or perform the manager's or custodian's functions.
Which service provider would most likely detect a mismatch between the manager's reported positions and actual holdings?
The fund's marketing agency
The investor relations team of the manager, while preparing quarterly letters
The distributor
The administrator reconciling with custodian records
