Independent administrators reconcile manager records with custodian and broker statements, flagging discrepancies. Marketing and distribution functions do not do this.

Category III AIF: Fund Structures and Se.overview: This chapter covers how Category III AIFs are legally set up and the service providers that support them. It explains trust, company and LLP structures, the trust deed, investment management agreement and PPM, open-ended versus close-ended structures, master-feeder and side-by-side structures for foreign investors, unit classes, and the roles of custodian, prime broker, administrator, valuer and auditor. It also covers dematerialisation of units and the importance of operational infrastructure for trading-intensive strategies. Focus on structural choices and the work each provider performs.
questions: An open-ended Category III AIF differs from a close-ended one in that it:
Allows periodic subscriptions and redemptions
Can never use leverage
Has a fixed maturity date of three years that cannot be extended by investors
Is exempt from SEBI regulation
Open-ended funds accept subscriptions and allow redemptions at specified intervals, often with notice periods. Category III funds of either type may use leverage within limits.
In a master-feeder structure, the feeder fund:
Trades securities directly while the master only collects fees
Acts as the custodian of the master fund
Pools investors and invests into the master
Calculates NAV for the regulator
Feeders collect money from particular investor groups, such as offshore investors, and invest in a master fund that holds the portfolio. Trading happens at master level.
Why is a trust structure common for Category III AIFs in India?
Trusts pay no tax on any income they earn, whatever its nature or source
It is flexible and familiar to Indian investors
Only trusts can use derivatives
Trusts are not regulated by SEBI
Trusts are simple to establish and wind up and are widely used. They are taxed under trust-taxation rules, can be used for any category, and remain SEBI-regulated.
A Category III fund issues a separate unit class with a lower management fee for investors committing more than ₹25 crore. This is permissible if:
It is disclosed and within SEBI's rules
It is kept confidential from smaller investors
The sponsor guarantees returns to that class
The class is not reported to SEBI
Differential fee classes are allowed when disclosed and consistent with SEBI's framework on investor rights. Secrecy or guarantees are not permitted.
Units of AIF schemes are required to be held in dematerialised form mainly to:
Allow units to be traded on stock exchanges daily
Improve transparency and record keeping
Remove the minimum investment requirement
Avoid KYC
Demat holding improves record keeping, transferability and regulatory oversight. It does not make units exchange-traded or waive KYC and minimums.
A side-by-side structure means that:
The AIF has two managers making separate decisions
Two Indian AIFs merge into one
An offshore fund invests alongside the Indian AIF in the same deals
The fund invests side by side with a mutual fund
In a side-by-side structure, a parallel offshore fund invests alongside the domestic AIF, typically in the same proportions, under common management.
Which service provider is most critical for executing a high-frequency quantitative strategy?
A real estate valuer
A legal adviser on property titles
An insurance surveyor
A broker with robust execution technology
Quantitative strategies depend on reliable, low-latency execution and connectivity from brokers. Property-related service providers are irrelevant.
The valuer of a Category III AIF is most important for:
Actively traded large-cap shares
Cash balances
Illiquid or thinly traded positions
Exchange-traded futures with daily settlement prices
Liquid securities have observable prices; valuers add most value where prices are not readily available and judgement is required.

Regulatory Framework.overview: This chapter covers SEBI's rules for Category III AIFs. Key topics are registration and the PPM, minimum corpus and minimum investment, accredited investors, number of investors, continuing interest of the sponsor or manager, leverage limits and the method for computing exposure, concentration limits, permitted investments including derivatives and commodity derivatives, disclosure and reporting, NAV computation and disclosure, risk management, the direct plan and distribution fee rules, investor charter, grievance redressal and penalties. Focus on the numerical thresholds that are stable and the principles behind limits that SEBI revises from time to time.
questions: A Category III AIF has a corpus of ₹300 crore. The minimum continuing interest of the sponsor or manager is:
₹15 crore
₹7.5 crore
₹5 crore
₹10 crore
For Category III, continuing interest is the lower of 5% of corpus or ₹10 crore. 5% of ₹300 crore is ₹15 crore, so the requirement is ₹10 crore.
A Category III AIF has NAV of ₹80 crore. Under SEBI's leverage cap, its maximum gross exposure is:
₹80 crore
₹240 crore
₹120 crore
₹160 crore
Gross exposure of a Category III AIF cannot exceed two times its NAV. 2 × ₹80 crore = ₹160 crore.
While computing leverage for a Category III AIF, positions taken purely for hedging that meet SEBI's conditions:
Must be doubled in exposure computation
May be offset in computing exposure
Are always prohibited
Are ignored only for open-ended funds
SEBI's methodology allows offsetting of eligible hedging and portfolio-rebalancing positions when calculating exposure, so genuine hedges do not consume the leverage limit.
Category III AIFs may participate in exchange-traded commodity derivatives. This is permitted:
Without any limits
Subject to SEBI's conditions and limits
Only for agricultural commodities notified by the government
Only if the fund is close-ended
SEBI allows Category III AIFs to trade commodity derivatives within prescribed conditions, including concentration limits per commodity. It is not unlimited.
Which body issues accreditation certificates to individuals wishing to be accredited investors?
Accreditation agencies recognised by SEBI
The AIF manager itself
The Reserve Bank of India
Any practising chartered accountant who certifies net worth
Accreditation is granted by SEBI-recognised accreditation agencies, typically subsidiaries of depositories or exchanges. Managers and CAs cannot accredit investors.
The minimum corpus requirement for each scheme of a Category III AIF is:
₹10 crore
₹100 crore
₹20 crore
₹1 crore
Each AIF scheme, including Category III, must have a minimum corpus of ₹20 crore. ₹1 crore is the minimum per-investor investment.
A Category III AIF wants to make a material change to its PPM, such as a change in strategy. Investors who disagree should generally be:
Bound by the change without recourse
Charged an exit penalty
Given an exit option before the change
Required to double their investment
SEBI requires material changes to be communicated with an exit option for dissenting investors, protecting them from unwanted changes.
Which is an obligation of a Category III AIF manager under SEBI's framework?
Disclosing NAV to investors at prescribed frequency
Guaranteeing a minimum return to investors
Distributing all realised profits to investors every month as dividends
Listing the units on a stock exchange
Managers must compute and disclose NAV periodically as prescribed. Guaranteeing returns or monthly payouts is not required, and listing is not mandatory.

Fees Structure, Fund Performance and Ben.overview: This chapter covers how Category III AIFs charge fees and how their performance is measured and compared. It explains management fees, performance fees, high-water marks, hurdle rates (hard and soft), crystallisation, and the impact of fees on net returns. It covers performance measures such as absolute and annualised returns, standard deviation, Sharpe, Sortino, Treynor and information ratios, maximum drawdown, alpha and beta, and SEBI's performance benchmarking framework. Practise numerical questions carefully and understand why benchmarks must reflect a fund's strategy and net exposure.
questions: A fund returned 16% with standard deviation of 12%; the risk-free rate is 7%. Its Sharpe ratio is:
Sharpe = (16 − 7) ÷ 12 = 0.75. 1.33 divides the return by volatility without subtracting the risk-free rate.
A fund returned 14% with downside deviation of 10%; the risk-free rate is 6%. Its Sortino ratio is:
Sortino = (14 − 6) ÷ 10 = 0.80. Unlike Sharpe, it penalises only downside volatility.
A unit's NAV is ₹125 at the year-end. The high-water mark is ₹115. With a 20% performance fee and no hurdle, the fee per unit is:
Fee applies only to gains above the high-water mark: (125 − 115) × 20% = ₹2. ₹5 would apply the fee to gains from ₹100.
NAV rises from ₹100 to ₹125 in a year. There is a 10% hard hurdle and a 20% performance fee. The fee per unit is:
With a hard hurdle, the fee is only on returns above ₹110: (125 − 110) × 20% = ₹3. With a soft hurdle and full catch-up, the fee would be ₹5.
A fund's gross return is 18%. It charges a 2% management fee and then 20% of the remaining gain as performance fee. The approximate net return is:
After management fee, return = 16%. Performance fee = 20% × 16% = 3.2%. Net = 16 − 3.2 = 12.8%.
A fund's active return over its benchmark is 4% and its tracking error is 5%. Its information ratio is:
Information ratio = active return ÷ tracking error = 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8. It measures consistency of outperformance per unit of active risk.
Over the last two years, a hedge-style fund's unit value slid from its high of ₹200 to a low of ₹150 and then recovered. What maximum drawdown should be reported?
Drawdown = (200 − 150) ÷ 200 = 25%. 33.3% divides the fall by the trough instead of the peak.
Why should an investor care about how often a Category III fund crystallises its performance fee?
It decides the leverage limit SEBI allows the fund to use in a given year
More frequent crystallisation can raise total fees
It sets the minimum investment
It has no effect on investor returns
If fees crystallise often, managers may earn fees on interim gains that later reverse, raising total fees in volatile periods. Annual crystallisation is generally more investor-friendly.

Category III AIF Investment Strategies a.overview: This chapter covers the main strategies used by Category III AIFs and how investors evaluate them. Strategies include long-only concentrated equity, long-short equity, market-neutral, arbitrage (cash-futures, merger, statistical), event-driven, quantitative and systematic, volatility and options-based, multi-strategy and global macro. Due diligence covers investment process, risk management, liquidity terms, leverage, style drift, operational controls, valuation, service providers and team. Revise how each strategy makes money, its typical risks, and the questions an investor or distributor should ask in due diligence.
questions: A fund holds long positions of ₹120 crore and short positions of ₹80 crore with NAV of ₹100 crore. Its gross and net exposures are:
Gross 40%, net 200% long
Gross 120%, net 80% long
Gross 200%, net 40% long
Gross 200%, net 80% short
Gross exposure = 120 + 80 = 200 crore (200% of NAV). Net = 120 − 80 = 40 crore long (40% of NAV).
In merger arbitrage, the main risk is that:
Interest rates on bank deposits fall
The acquirer pays a dividend
The deal fails and the spread widens
Index futures expire
Merger arbitrage profits from the spread between the target's price and the deal value; if the deal fails, the target's price usually falls sharply.
A fund holds long stocks of ₹100 crore with beta 1.2 and short index futures of ₹80 crore (beta 1.0). Its beta-adjusted net exposure is about:
₹20 crore long
₹40 crore long
₹180 crore long
₹40 crore short
Beta-adjusted long = 100 × 1.2 = 120; short = 80 × 1.0 = 80. Net = 120 − 80 = ₹40 crore long.
A statistical arbitrage strategy typically:
Takes large concentrated bets on single companies
Invests in real estate projects
Holds stocks for many years without trading
Trades many small pricing anomalies using models
Statistical arbitrage uses quantitative models to exploit short-term mispricings across many securities, relying on diversification and execution efficiency.
Which due diligence finding most indicates style drift?
A long-only fund holding mostly equities
An arbitrage fund holding cash-futures positions
A quant fund using models
A 'market-neutral' fund running large net long exposure
A market-neutral fund should have little net exposure; persistent large net long positions show it has drifted from its stated strategy.
Why should investors check redemption terms such as notice periods and gates in an open-ended Category III fund?
They decide the fund's tax rate
They are irrelevant for liquid strategies because such funds never restrict exits
They determine how quickly money can be withdrawn
They determine the fund's benchmark
Notice periods, lock-ins and gates limit redemptions, especially in stress. Investors need to match these with their liquidity needs.
An options-selling volatility strategy shows steady small gains for years. The main due diligence concern is:
Too much diversification
Lack of any premium income
Exposure to rare but severe losses
High dividend payouts
Selling options earns premiums regularly but can produce large losses during sharp market moves. Due diligence should test stress scenarios and risk limits.
Which question is most relevant when assessing a manager's risk management framework?
Who sets and monitors risk limits independently?
How many branches does the manager have?
What is the manager's advertising budget?
Does the manager sponsor sports events?
Independent setting and monitoring of position, leverage and loss limits is central to risk management. Marketing activities do not indicate risk discipline.

Valuation.overview: This chapter covers how Category III AIFs value their holdings and compute NAV. It explains the valuation of listed equities, derivatives, debt instruments, unlisted or thinly traded securities and suspended stocks, the use of independent valuers and fair value principles, NAV computation (assets less liabilities including accrued fees and expenses, divided by units), frequency of NAV disclosure for open and close-ended funds, and the consequences of mispricing for fees and investor fairness. Practise NAV calculations and understand the treatment of accrued expenses and illiquid holdings.
questions: A Category III fund has total assets of ₹212 crore, liabilities of ₹12 crore and 1.6 crore units. Its NAV per unit is:
A stock held by the fund is suspended from trading. Its valuation should be:
The last traded price before suspension, indefinitely and without review
Zero in all cases
Fair value determined by an approved policy
The price at which the fund bought it
Suspended securities should be valued at fair value in line with the valuation policy, considering all available information. Mechanically using old prices or zero may misstate NAV.
Exchange-traded futures held by a Category III AIF are usually valued at:
The exchange's daily settlement price
The price at which the contract was opened
The underlying stock's 52-week high
The strike price of related options
Futures are marked to the exchange settlement price each day, which reflects current market value.
Accrued but unpaid management fees should be treated in NAV computation as:
An asset that increases NAV
Ignored until paid
Part of investors' capital
A liability that reduces NAV
Accrued fees are obligations of the fund and must be deducted as liabilities to present the true NAV.
Overvaluing illiquid holdings in an open-ended fund harms:
Remaining investors, as redeemers exit at inflated NAV
Only the manager, as its fees fall whenever the portfolio is overvalued
No one, as values eventually adjust
Only new investors who buy at low NAV
Redeeming investors are paid more than the true value, leaving remaining investors with the shortfall. Overvaluation also inflates fees.
A thinly traded corporate bond with no recent trades is best valued by:
Its face value
The coupon rate
The issuer's share price
Using yields of similar bonds with spreads
Without trades, fair value can be estimated from yields on comparable bonds adjusted for credit and liquidity differences.
Why should NAV be computed by an independent administrator rather than the manager alone?
Because managers are not allowed to see NAV
Because independent NAV is always higher
To avoid all audit requirements
To reduce the risk of manipulating NAV
Independent computation provides a check on the manager, whose fees depend on NAV. It does not remove audit requirements.
Options held by a fund that are deep out of the money and illiquid should be valued:
At the premium originally paid
At zero always
At their strike price
Using a model consistent with market inputs
Illiquid options are valued using recognised pricing models with current inputs like volatility. Original premium or strike values do not reflect fair value.

Taxation.overview: This chapter covers the taxation of Category III AIFs and their investors in India. It explains that Category III funds lack statutory pass-through, the taxation of trusts (determinate and indeterminate) at fund level, characterisation of income as capital gains or business income, tax on derivatives trading, treatment of distributions in investors' hands, GST on fees, and the tax position of non-resident investors. It also compares the tax outcome of Category III AIFs with PMS and mutual funds. As tax law has been restructured, concentrate on principles rather than section numbers or rates.
questions: A Category III AIF trust where each beneficiary's share is clearly determinable is generally taxed:
At zero rate
Only when investors redeem their units, at the rate applicable to each investor
Only on dividends received
As a representative assessee on beneficiaries' shares
A determinate trust is taxed in a representative capacity, in the same manner as the beneficiaries would be on their shares. Indeterminate trusts may face higher rates.
A Category III fund frequently trades listed shares within days. Its gains are likely to be characterised as:
Long-term capital gains
Exempt income
Income from house property
Business income
High-frequency trading indicates a trading business, so gains may be treated as business income. Long-term capital gains need longer holding periods.
When a Category III AIF distributes income on which it has already paid tax, investors are generally:
Taxed again at slab rates
Taxed at 30% flat
Not taxed again on it
Liable for GST on it
Since tax is paid at fund level, distributions are generally not taxed again in investors' hands, avoiding double taxation.
Compared with a PMS, a Category III AIF investor typically:
Is not taxed on each underlying trade directly
Must report every trade in her own return
Pays no tax at any stage
Must pay STT separately on each trade
In a PMS, the client is taxed on each transaction in her account. In a Category III AIF, tax is mostly paid at the fund level.
GST on management and performance fees in a Category III AIF is:
Paid by SEBI
Not applicable to fund managers because AIFs are regulated by SEBI
Charged to the fund and reduces net returns
Payable only by the distributor
Fees are a taxable service, and GST on them is a cost borne by the fund, reducing net returns.
Why might a Category III fund's high tax rate at the trust level matter to a low-income investor?
She gets a refund of all tax paid by the fund
She cannot use her lower slab on fund income
Her income becomes exempt
She pays tax twice on every rupee
Because tax is paid at fund level, often at the maximum marginal rate, a low-bracket investor cannot benefit from her lower personal rate.
A Category III fund earns income from derivatives traded on recognised exchanges. Such income is generally treated as:
Speculative income
Non-speculative business income
Exempt income
Capital gains in all cases
Eligible derivative transactions on recognised exchanges are excluded from speculative transactions, so income is generally non-speculative business income.
Securities Transaction Tax on the fund's trades in listed shares is:
Paid directly by each investor
Refunded by the exchange at year-end
Borne by the fund as a cost
Not applicable to AIFs
STT applies to trades on recognised exchanges, and the fund pays it as a transaction cost, reducing returns.

Good Practices.overview: This chapter covers the conduct expected of Category III AIF distributors. It explains SEBI's rules on distribution — NISM certification, direct plans, payment of distribution commission only on an equal-trail basis, disclosure of commissions — and good practices including suitability and appropriateness assessment, clear explanation of strategy, leverage, liquidity and fee terms, avoiding misleading claims about hedging or returns, KYC and AML compliance, handling complaints and maintaining records. Learners should be able to recognise mis-selling and conflicts and know what information must be given to investors before they invest.
questions: How may a Category III AIF pay commission to the distributors who place its units with investors?
Fully upfront at the time of investment
Only as a one-time fee on exit
Only on an equal-trail basis
As a share of the manager's performance fee
SEBI requires Category III distribution fees to be paid only as equal trail, with no upfront payment, to discourage churning.
While pitching a leveraged Category III fund, a distributor shows the client only its best annual returns and does not mention its past drawdowns. This conduct is:
Acceptable marketing practice
Required by SEBI
Incomplete disclosure amounting to mis-selling
Only a minor lapse if returns are high
Investors must be told about risks, including leverage and drawdowns. Highlighting only returns is misleading.
A client's risk profile shows low risk tolerance, but he insists on a high-risk Category III AIF. A good distributor should:
Document the mismatch and explain the risks
Hide the risk profile result
Change the risk profile to match the product
Promise to cover losses
The distributor should explain the mismatch, record the client's informed decision and not alter the profile. Promising to cover losses is prohibited.
A distributor receives complaints from a client about delayed redemption. The distributor should:
Ignore it, as it concerns the manager
Ignore it, as redemption issues concern only the manager and not the distributor
Withdraw the client's units personally
Help escalate it to the manager and SEBI channels
Distributors should help clients raise grievances with the manager and, if needed, through SEBI's SCORES and ODR mechanisms.
Which statement to a client is appropriate for a long-short fund?
The fund cannot lose money because all its positions are fully hedged
SEBI guarantees the fund's capital
Returns are fixed at 12% a year
Hedging reduces some risk but losses are possible
Hedged funds can still lose money from stock selection, leverage or basis risk. No return or capital is guaranteed.
Why should a distributor assess a client's entire portfolio before recommending a Category III AIF?
To compute the fund's NAV
To avoid over-concentration in risky products
To decide the fund's leverage
To decide the leverage the fund will use for that particular client's units
Looking at the full portfolio shows whether the new investment leads to excessive concentration or illiquidity.
A distributor recommends switching a client from one Category III fund to another every year without clear reasons. This may indicate:
Normal portfolio rebalancing
Churning for commissions
Mandatory regulatory action
Tax-loss harvesting required by law
Frequent unexplained switching benefits the distributor more than the client and may be churning. Recommendations must be in the client's interest.
A distributor must keep client information confidential. Sharing it is permitted:
With any other fund manager
With friends who are prospective clients
With client consent or as required by law
Whenever the distributor wishes
Client data may be shared only with consent or as legally required, such as to regulators. Casual sharing breaches confidentiality.

Investments Landscape.overview: This chapter sets the context for AIF management by surveying the investment landscape: real versus financial assets, the main asset classes, the role of financial intermediaries, the savings–investment link, nominal and real returns, and the range of investors from retail savers to institutions and family offices. It also introduces the growth of private markets alongside public markets. When revising, focus on classifying assets, computing real returns with the Fisher relationship, and understanding why different investors — with different horizons, liabilities and liquidity needs — choose different mixes of traditional and alternative assets.
questions: A fund earns a nominal return of 12% when inflation is 5%. Using the exact Fisher relationship, the real return is about:
Real return = 1.12 ÷ 1.05 − 1 ≈ 6.67%. Subtracting inflation directly gives the 7% approximation.
Which investor is typically best suited to commit capital to a 10-year closed-end fund?
An endowment with perpetual horizon
A household saving for a car to be bought next year
A corporate treasury managing its weekly payroll cash
A retiree drawing monthly living expenses
Endowments and similar long-horizon institutions can tolerate long lock-ups. Short-term or income-dependent investors need liquidity.
Financial intermediaries such as banks and funds mainly help the economy by:
Fixing the prices of all listed securities on the exchange every day
Eliminating all investment risk for savers
Replacing the need for capital markets
Channelling savings to productive uses
Intermediaries pool savings and allocate them to borrowers and businesses, transforming maturity, size and risk. They cannot remove risk entirely.
An AIF holds the following. Which one is a financial asset (a claim on another party) and not a real asset?
A warehouse used for storing grain
Farmland leased to tenants
A debenture of a listed company
A toll road operated by a concessionaire
A debenture is a claim on the issuer's cash flows, making it a financial asset. Warehouses, farmland and roads are real assets.
Private markets have grown relative to public markets partly because:
Stock exchanges have stopped approving new listings of small and mid-sized companies
Companies stay private longer, funded by private capital
Private investments are guaranteed by SEBI
Public markets are closed to institutions
Abundant private capital lets companies scale before listing, shifting value creation into private markets. Private investments carry no regulatory guarantee.
A family office wants to preserve wealth across generations. Compared with a young salaried saver, it can usually:
Hold only cash and deposits because its size makes market investing unnecessary
Avoid all diversification
Take more illiquidity risk for higher returns
Ignore inflation completely
With a long horizon and large asset base, a family office can lock up part of its capital to earn the illiquidity premium. It still needs diversification and inflation protection.
The main difference between primary and secondary markets is that in primary markets:
Existing securities change hands between investors
Only derivatives are traded
Prices are fixed by the regulator
Issuers raise fresh capital from investors
Primary markets involve new issues where money goes to the issuer. Secondary markets provide trading among investors.
An investor's required return on a private fund should be higher than on a comparable listed fund mainly because of:
Lower fees in private funds
Illiquidity and higher uncertainty
Daily liquidity in private funds
Government guarantees on private funds
Private funds are illiquid, opaque and costly, so investors demand a premium over comparable public investments.

Types of Investments.overview: This chapter describes the instruments and asset types that AIF managers use: equity and preference shares, convertible instruments, debt and structured credit, mezzanine and venture debt, real estate and infrastructure, commodities and derivatives. It explains the capital structure of a company and how claims rank, the features of convertible and hybrid instruments, and how instrument design affects risk and return. Focus on where each instrument sits in the capital structure, how conversion and liquidation rights work, and which instruments suit different strategies such as venture, buyout, credit and special situations.
questions: In a liquidation, which claim is paid first among these?
Equity shares
Senior secured debt
Preference shares
Mezzanine debt that is subordinated to senior lenders
Senior secured lenders rank ahead of subordinated debt, preference and equity holders, which is why their returns are lower.
A compulsorily convertible preference share (CCPS) is popular with Indian PE investors mainly because it:
Offers preference rights and later converts to equity
Pays a fixed coupon that must be paid in cash even in years when the company makes losses
Can never be converted into equity shares
Carries no rights in a liquidation
CCPS offers preferential rights, such as liquidation preference, and converts into equity, which is often favoured under FEMA for foreign investors.
Venture debt is typically provided to:
Mature companies with strong cash flows only
Governments for infrastructure
Retail investors for personal loans
VC-backed start-ups to extend runway
Venture debt supplements equity in VC-funded companies, often with warrants, helping them extend runway without immediate dilution.
Which instrument gives its holder the right but not the obligation to buy shares at a fixed price in future?
A warrant
A non-convertible debenture
A commercial paper
A fixed deposit
A warrant is an option to buy shares at a set price. NCDs, CP and deposits are plain debt instruments.
Infrastructure investments are attractive to long-term investors mainly because they often offer:
Very short holding periods with quick exits through the stock market
Daily liquidity on stock exchanges
Stable, long-dated, sometimes inflation-linked cash flows
No exposure to regulatory risk
Infrastructure assets such as roads and power often have long concessions and contracted revenues, sometimes indexed to inflation. They carry regulatory and construction risk.
A 'payment-in-kind' (PIK) feature in a mezzanine loan means that:
Interest is paid in commodities
The loan is repaid in shares at once
Interest is added to principal instead of paid in cash
No interest is ever charged, since the lender is repaid only through equity warrants
PIK interest accrues to the principal, conserving the borrower's cash but increasing the lender's risk and final payoff.
Which investment type is most associated with special situation funds?
Seed-stage start-ups that are still developing their first product
Listed large-cap blue chips
Government treasury bills
Stressed and distressed assets
Special situation funds invest in stressed loans and securities of companies under distress or restructuring.
A real estate debt fund lending to developers faces which key risk?
Project delays and developer default
Exchange-rate risk on rupee loans made to Indian developers
Dividend cut by listed companies
Index rebalancing risk
Real estate lenders depend on project completion and sales; delays, approvals and developer default are the key risks.

Concept of Informational Efficiency.overview: This chapter covers the efficient market hypothesis and its forms — weak, semi-strong and strong — and what each implies for technical analysis, fundamental analysis and insider information. It discusses market anomalies, behavioural biases, limits to arbitrage, and why private and less-researched markets may be less efficient, giving skilled managers room to add value. When revising, focus on matching evidence or strategies to the form of efficiency they test, and on why informational inefficiency is a core argument for active management in alternative assets.
questions: If a market is weak-form efficient, which strategy should NOT consistently earn excess returns?
Using inside information illegally
Analysing unpublished field research
Trading on past price patterns
Investing in private companies
Weak-form efficiency means prices reflect all past trading data, so technical analysis cannot consistently beat the market. Other information may still add value.
Strong-form efficiency implies that:
Only past prices and trading volumes are reflected in current prices
Fundamental analysis always works
Even private information cannot earn excess returns
Markets are always mispriced
Under strong-form efficiency, prices reflect all public and private information. Evidence of insider profits suggests real markets are not strong-form efficient.
Which is a behavioural bias that may cause prices to deviate from fundamentals?
Perfect information disclosure
Herding by investors
Zero transaction costs
Rational expectations by all investors
Herding — following the crowd — can push prices away from fair value. The other options describe idealised efficient conditions.
'Limits to arbitrage' explain why mispricing can persist because:
Arbitrage is always riskless and free
Regulators ban all arbitrage
Arbitrage can be costly and risky
Prices cannot move once set
Short-selling constraints, funding costs and the risk that mispricing widens can deter arbitrageurs, so anomalies may persist.
Why are small unlisted companies often considered less informationally efficient?
They are required to publish daily accounts
Their share prices are fixed by SEBI
Few analysts cover them and information is scarce
They are traded on stock exchanges continuously with many market makers
Limited disclosure and coverage mean prices may not reflect all information, giving diligent investors an edge.
A share price rises sharply on the day of a positive earnings announcement and then drifts upward for weeks. The drift is evidence against:
Weak-form efficiency only
Strong-form inefficiency
The existence of stock markets
Semi-strong form efficiency
Prices in a semi-strong efficient market adjust quickly to public news. A slow drift after announcements is a known anomaly.
For an AIF manager, the main practical implication of market inefficiency in private markets is that:
Passive indexing is the only possible approach
All managers will earn the same returns
Due diligence is unnecessary
Skill in sourcing and diligence can add value
Inefficiency rewards skill in finding and analysing deals, which is why manager selection matters greatly in private markets.
An investor consistently earns excess returns using only published financial statements. This would contradict:
Weak-form efficiency only
Semi-strong form efficiency
The random walk of past prices only
No form of efficiency
Published statements are public information; persistent excess returns from analysing them contradict semi-strong efficiency.

Introduction to Modern Portfolio Theory.overview: This chapter introduces Markowitz's modern portfolio theory. It covers expected return and risk of a portfolio, variance and standard deviation, covariance and correlation, the benefit of diversification, the efficient frontier, and how investor preferences determine the optimal portfolio. It also discusses the limits of MPT for alternative assets, such as smoothed returns and non-normal distributions. Practise computing portfolio return and standard deviation for two assets, and understand how correlation changes diversification benefits.
questions: A portfolio has 60% in an asset with expected return 14% and 40% in one with 8%. The expected portfolio return is:
Expected return = 0.6 × 14 + 0.4 × 8 = 8.4 + 3.2 = 11.6%. 11% is a simple average ignoring weights.
Using the same weights (60:40), if the assets' standard deviations are 20% and 10% and correlation is zero, the portfolio standard deviation is about:
σ = √(0.6²×0.2² + 0.4²×0.1²) = √(0.0144 + 0.0016) ≈ 12.6%. 16% is the weighted average, which applies only when correlation is +1.
Two assets with standard deviations of 20% and 10% have correlation of −1. A 50:50 portfolio has standard deviation of:
With perfect negative correlation, σ = |0.5×20 − 0.5×10| = 5%. A different weighting (1/3 : 2/3) could reduce it to zero.
Diversification is most effective when assets have:
Perfect positive correlation
Identical returns at all times
Low or negative correlation
The same issuer
Lower correlation means assets do not move together, so combining them reduces portfolio risk.
Which risk can be reduced by diversification?
Systematic market risk
Risk from economy-wide recessions
Unsystematic (company-specific) risk
Changes in the general level of interest rates
Company-specific risk can be diversified away. Market-wide risks affect all assets and remain.
A portfolio lies below the efficient frontier. This means:
It is the optimal portfolio for all investors, whatever their risk tolerance
Another portfolio offers more return for the same risk
It has zero risk
It cannot be improved
Portfolios below the frontier are inefficient; one with higher return at the same risk exists.
A key limitation of MPT when applied to private equity is that:
Private equity returns are reported daily
Private equity has no correlation data at all, so no optimisation is possible
MPT works only for bonds
Reported returns are smoothed, understating risk
Appraisal-based valuations smooth returns, lowering measured volatility and correlation, so optimisers may over-allocate to private assets.
The optimal portfolio for an investor on the efficient frontier depends on:
The number of stocks listed on the exchange
The custodian of the portfolio
The fund's legal structure
Her risk preference
The investor's risk tolerance determines which efficient portfolio she chooses — the tangency with her indifference curve.

Introduction to Capital Market Theory.overview: This chapter builds on portfolio theory to cover capital market theory: the risk-free asset, the capital market line, the market portfolio, the security market line and the Capital Asset Pricing Model. It explains beta as a measure of systematic risk, required return, and performance measures derived from these ideas — Sharpe, Treynor and Jensen's alpha — together with multi-factor models. Practise CAPM and performance-measure calculations, and understand when each measure is appropriate, for example Treynor for diversified portfolios and Sharpe for total-risk comparison.
questions: Risk-free rate is 7%, expected market return is 13% and a portfolio's beta is 0.8. Its CAPM required return is:
A fund returned 15% with beta 1.5 when the risk-free rate was 6%. Its Treynor ratio is:
Treynor = (15 − 6) ÷ 1.5 = 6.0. It measures excess return per unit of systematic risk.
A fund returned 16% with beta 1.2. The risk-free rate was 6% and the market returned 12%. Its Jensen's alpha is:
CAPM return = 6 + 1.2 × 6 = 13.2%. Alpha = 16 − 13.2 = +2.8%. +4% compares with the market return without adjusting for beta.
The capital market line (CML) plots:
Individual securities' expected returns plotted against their betas
Bond yields against maturity
Company earnings over time
Efficient portfolios of the risk-free and market portfolio
The CML shows combinations of the risk-free asset and the market portfolio, with total risk on the x-axis. The SML uses beta.
A stock plots above the security market line. This suggests it is:
Overvalued, since it offers less than its required return
Undervalued, offering more than its required return
Risk-free
Perfectly priced
A security above the SML offers a higher expected return than CAPM requires for its beta, implying undervaluation.
Beta of a portfolio with 50% in a stock of beta 1.2 and 50% in a stock of beta 0.8 is:
Portfolio beta is the weighted average: 0.5 × 1.2 + 0.5 × 0.8 = 1.0.
Multi-factor models extend CAPM by:
Removing the risk-free rate
Using several risk factors such as size and value
Assuming that all assets have exactly the same beta as the market
Ignoring market risk
Factor models explain returns with several systematic factors beyond the market, such as size, value and momentum.
Which measure is most appropriate to compare a fund that is an investor's entire portfolio?
Treynor ratio
Sharpe ratio
Beta alone
Dividend yield
When a fund is the whole portfolio, total risk matters, so the Sharpe ratio (using standard deviation) is appropriate. Treynor suits well-diversified holdings within a larger portfolio.

AIFs in India and Its Suitability.overview: This chapter explains the AIF categories under SEBI's regulations and how a manager or adviser judges suitability. It covers Category I sub-categories (venture capital and angel funds, SME, social impact, infrastructure, special situation funds), Category II (private equity, private debt, funds of funds) and Category III (hedge-fund style, PIPE and long-short), along with the characteristics that make AIFs suitable only for sophisticated investors with surplus wealth and long horizons. Focus on classifying a proposed fund correctly and on recognising when an AIF is unsuitable for an investor.
questions: A fund that invests in listed shares through preferential allotments and uses derivatives and short positions would most likely be a:
Category III AIF
Category I SME fund
Category II fund of funds
Category I social impact fund
Strategies involving listed securities with derivatives and shorting fall under Category III.
An AIF set up to invest in unlisted small and medium enterprises would register as:
Category III hedge fund
Category I SME fund
Category II debt fund
A mutual fund
SME funds are a Category I sub-category, reflecting policy support for smaller businesses.
Which investor is LEAST suitable for a Category II PE fund?
One needing the money within two years
An HNI with long horizon and surplus wealth
A pension fund with long-term liabilities
A family office seeking diversification
PE funds lock in capital for many years. An investor needing funds soon cannot accommodate the illiquidity.
A fund focusing on companies creating measurable social benefits, such as affordable healthcare, would be a:
Category III long-short fund
Social impact fund under Category I
Category II real estate fund investing in completed office buildings
Portfolio management service
Social impact funds, part of Category I, invest in entities with social objectives and may raise money through the social stock exchange route.
Why are Category I and II AIFs required to be close-ended?
SEBI wants them to trade on stock exchanges like closed-end funds
Their illiquid assets cannot meet redemptions
They hold only cash
Investors prefer daily NAV
Unlisted holdings cannot be sold quickly, so allowing redemptions would harm remaining investors.
A fund of funds investing in multiple Category II AIFs offers an investor:
Lower total fees than investing directly in the underlying funds
Diversification across managers, with an extra fee layer
Daily liquidity
A guaranteed return
FoFs diversify across managers and vintages but add a second layer of fees.
An angel fund primarily pools money from:
Retail investors through SIPs
Banks for infrastructure lending
Mutual funds seeking exposure to listed shares of large companies
Angel investors backing early-stage start-ups
Angel funds, a Category I VCF sub-category, pool capital from angel investors to fund early-stage start-ups.
Which question is most important when judging whether an AIF suits a client?
Can she lock in money and bear a total loss?
Does she prefer to bank with the sponsor's group bank for convenience?
How many credit cards does she hold?
What is her favourite sector?
Suitability depends on ability to tolerate illiquidity and losses, plus understanding of the product.

AIF Ecosystem.overview: This chapter describes the parties involved in an AIF and their responsibilities: sponsor, manager, trustee or board, investment committee, custodian, registrar, fund administrator, valuer, auditor, merchant banker, legal and tax advisers, placement agents and distributors, and investors. It covers SEBI's requirements for key management personnel and their certification, the compliance officer, and the obligations of each party. Focus on who is responsible for which function, which roles must be independent of the manager, and how the ecosystem protects investors.
questions: Which party must file the PPM of a new AIF scheme with SEBI?
A SEBI-registered merchant banker
The investee company
The custodian
The investor with the largest commitment in the scheme
SEBI requires the PPM to be filed through a merchant banker who conducts due diligence on disclosures.
The compliance officer of an AIF manager is responsible for:
Monitoring compliance with regulations and reporting breaches
Selecting investee companies for the fund's portfolio and negotiating terms
Raising capital from investors
Valuing the portfolio
The compliance officer monitors adherence to SEBI rules and circulars and reports non-compliance.
A placement agent's main role is to:
Manage the portfolio and take investment and exit decisions
Audit the accounts
Introduce the fund to potential investors
Hold the securities
Placement agents help raise capital by connecting the fund with investors, for which they receive a fee.
Why does SEBI require AIF managers' key personnel to hold NISM certification?
To give them tax benefits on carried interest they earn
To ensure minimum competence
To exempt them from audits
To guarantee fund returns
Certification ensures key investment team members meet a baseline of knowledge of AIF regulations and practices.
The investment committee of an AIF approves:
Investors' KYC
The fund's audit report
Investment and exit decisions
Fees payable to the custodian and fund administrator
The IC decides on investments and exits in line with the PPM. KYC, audit and custody are other functions.
A custodian is mandatory for an AIF mainly to:
Safekeep assets separately from the manager
Generate investment ideas for the investment committee
Distribute units
Prepare the PPM
Independent custody protects investor assets and provides a check on the manager.
Which party in an AIF provides independent assurance on the financial statements?
The statutory auditor
The placement agent
The investment committee
The sponsor
The statutory auditor independently audits the accounts and reports on their fairness.
An AIF manager outsources fund administration. Responsibility for compliance with SEBI rules remains with:
The manager
The administrator only
The investors
The stock exchange
Outsourcing a function does not transfer regulatory responsibility; the manager remains accountable to SEBI and investors for compliance.

AIF Structuring.overview: This chapter covers the legal and commercial structuring of AIFs. It explains trust, company and LLP forms, documents such as the trust deed, contribution agreement and investment management agreement, unit classes and differential rights, onshore and offshore structures, feeder and co-investment vehicles, FEMA treatment of downstream investment, and the tax and regulatory considerations that drive structuring decisions. Focus on why a particular structure is chosen, how foreign capital is brought in, and how unit classes or co-investment vehicles must be disclosed and kept within SEBI's framework.
questions: An AIF wants to admit foreign investors while keeping its downstream investments classified as domestic under FEMA. The key requirement is that:
Foreign investors together hold less than 10% of the scheme's units
It invests only in listed securities
Its sponsor and manager are Indian-owned and controlled
It registers as an FPI
Downstream investment is treated as domestic when the sponsor and manager are owned and controlled by resident Indian citizens, regardless of foreign LP share.
A co-investment vehicle allows investors to:
Avoid all fund fees permanently on their main fund commitment
Manage the fund
Redeem units early
Invest more in specific deals alongside the fund
Co-investment vehicles let selected investors take extra exposure in particular investee companies, under terms set within SEBI's framework.
Why might a fund choose a company structure despite trusts being more common?
Companies pay no tax
Companies need no SEBI registration
Companies can raise from retail investors freely
Some investors prefer corporate governance
Some investors prefer board governance and familiarity of corporate forms, though tax treatment and flexibility differ.
The contribution agreement in a trust-based AIF mainly governs:
The custodian's fees
The investor's commitment and drawdowns
The SEBI registration process
The investee company's shareholding pattern after each investment
It records each investor's commitment, drawdown mechanics, default consequences and other terms.
Differential rights for certain investors in an AIF are allowed when:
They follow SEBI's framework and do not harm others
They are kept secret from SEBI
They guarantee returns to those investors
They are approved only by the manager
SEBI permits differential rights within its framework, with disclosure, provided other investors' rights are not adversely affected.
An offshore feeder fund investing into an Indian AIF helps foreign investors mainly by:
Avoiding Indian KYC norms
Pooling them in a familiar vehicle
Guaranteeing a currency hedge on all rupee-denominated investments
Allowing daily redemptions
Feeders pool foreign investors in a jurisdiction and vehicle they are comfortable with, simplifying participation.
In a trust-based AIF, the trust deed is executed between:
The investor and the custodian
The manager and the investee
The settlor and the trustee
SEBI and the sponsor
The trust deed is executed by the settlor and trustee, creating the trust and setting out its objects.
Separate unit classes for the manager team typically exist to:
Avoid reporting the manager team's holdings to SEBI and the trustee
Increase leverage
Allocate carry or fee waivers
Allow early redemption
Team classes usually carry carry entitlements and fee waivers, disclosed in the PPM.

Fee Structure and Fund Performance.overview: This chapter covers how AIF managers are paid and how fund performance is measured. It explains management fees on committed or invested capital, fund expenses, carried interest, hurdle or preferred return, GP catch-up, European (whole-of-fund) and American (deal-by-deal) waterfalls, clawback and escrow, and the effect of fees on net returns. Performance topics include IRR, gross and net returns, TVPI, DPI, RVPI and MOIC. Practise waterfall and multiple calculations step by step, and understand how fee bases shift after the investment period.
questions: Fund capital is ₹200 crore and total proceeds are ₹300 crore. The preferred return is ₹16 crore and carry is 20% with a full (100%) GP catch-up. The manager's total carry is:
₹16.8 crore
₹16 crore
₹60 crore
₹20 crore
Total profit = ₹100 crore. With full catch-up and enough profit, the manager ends up with 20% of all profit: ₹20 crore. Without catch-up it would be 20% × (100 − 16) = ₹16.8 crore.
Using the same fund (capital ₹200 crore, proceeds ₹300 crore, preferred return ₹16 crore, 20% carry) but with no catch-up, the carry is:
₹20 crore
₹16.8 crore
₹3.2 crore
₹13.6 crore
Profit above the hurdle = 100 − 16 = ₹84 crore. Carry = 20% × 84 = ₹16.8 crore.
After the investment period, a fund charges 1.5% a year on invested capital of ₹400 crore. The annual management fee is:
₹4 crore
₹8 crore
₹6 crore
₹60 lakh
Fee = 1.5% × 400 = ₹6 crore. Fee bases often shift from commitments to invested capital after the investment period.
A fund has paid-in capital of ₹150 crore, distributions of ₹90 crore and NAV of ₹120 crore. Its TVPI and DPI are:
0.6x and 1.4x
1.4x and 0.8x
1.4x and 0.6x
2.1x and 0.6x
An investor puts ₹100 crore into a fund and receives ₹144 crore exactly two years later, with no other cash flows. The IRR is:
IRR solves 100 × (1 + r)² = 144, so r = 20%. 22% is the simple annual average of 44%.
Why do investors prefer carry placed in escrow until they have received back their contributed capital?
It reduces the risk of needing a clawback
It raises the manager's carry
It removes the hurdle so that carry is earned from the first rupee
It increases management fees
Holding carry in escrow protects against later losses that would otherwise require the manager to return excess carry.
Under a deal-by-deal (American) waterfall, the manager:
Earns carry only after all capital is returned
Never earns carry
Earns carry only on unrealised gains
Can earn carry on each profitable exit early
American waterfalls pay carry deal by deal, so carry can be paid before all capital is returned; a clawback is therefore important.
Fund expenses such as audit and legal fees charged to the fund mainly affect:
Net returns to investors
Only the manager's income
Gross IRR only
The fund's tax status
Fund expenses are borne by investors and reduce net returns, widening the gap between gross and net IRR.

Indices and Benchmarking.overview: This chapter explains how AIF performance is benchmarked. It covers public market indices and their limits for private funds, peer-group benchmarks by strategy and vintage, quartile rankings, the public market equivalent method, and SEBI's framework under which benchmarking agencies publish industry benchmarks using data reported by AIFs. It also covers hedge-fund style benchmarks and risk-adjusted comparison for Category III. Focus on choosing appropriate benchmarks, comparing funds of the same vintage and strategy, and the pitfalls of comparing IRRs with index returns.
questions: A 2020-vintage PE fund ranks in the top quartile. This means its performance is:
Above the Nifty 50 total return index over the same period
Guaranteed for future funds
In the best 25% of comparable 2020 funds
In the top 25% of all AIFs ever
Quartile rankings compare funds with peers of the same strategy and vintage; top quartile means the best 25% of that peer group.
Why is comparing a PE fund's IRR directly with an index's annual return problematic?
IRR is cash-flow weighted while index returns are time-weighted
Index returns include fees
IRR always equals index return
Indices cannot be measured
IRR reflects the timing and size of fund cash flows, while index returns assume a buy-and-hold investment, so a like-for-like comparison needs methods such as PME.
Under SEBI's framework, performance benchmarks for AIFs are published by:
Benchmarking agencies using data reported by AIFs
Each fund manager for its own fund, using its chosen index
The stock exchanges
The Reserve Bank of India
SEBI's framework uses benchmarking agencies that compile data reported by AIFs to publish industry and vintage benchmarks.
A long-short Category III fund should ideally be benchmarked against:
The Sensex alone, since it is India's oldest equity benchmark
Bank fixed deposit rates only
A benchmark reflecting its net exposure and strategy
A gold price index
A long-short fund carries lower net market exposure, so its benchmark should reflect that, or a blend of market and cash.
Peer-group benchmarks for private funds can suffer from:
Too much daily data
Exchange-traded pricing that makes every fund's NAV observable daily
Survivorship and self-reporting bias
Mandatory government audit
If poorly performing funds stop reporting or disappear, peer data can be biased upward.
The Kaplan–Schoar PME ratio is greater than 1. This indicates that the fund:
Underperformed the public index on a cash-flow-matched basis
Had zero returns
Outperformed the public index
Is a public fund
A PME ratio above 1 means the fund's distributions and value exceeded what the same cash flows would have earned in the index.
Vintage-year benchmarking is important because:
Funds of the same year faced similar conditions
All vintages perform identically
SEBI requires one vintage per manager
It removes fee effects
Market conditions at entry strongly affect returns, so comparing funds of the same vintage is fairer.
Which statistic best measures a Category III fund's consistency of outperformance over its benchmark?
Dividend yield
Information ratio
Distributions to paid-in capital (DPI)
Vintage year
The information ratio divides active return by tracking error, measuring consistency of outperformance.

Investment Strategies, Investment Proces.overview: This chapter covers the strategies AIF managers pursue — venture capital, growth, buyouts, private credit, special situations, real estate, infrastructure and Category III trading strategies — and the investment process from sourcing and screening through due diligence, IC approval, structuring, monitoring and exit. Governance topics include the investment committee, conflict-of-interest policies, related-party approvals, allocation policy, compliance with the PPM, and the responsibilities of the manager, trustee and key personnel. Focus on strategy-specific risks and on governance practices SEBI expects.
questions: A leveraged buyout typically creates value through:
Holding minority stakes passively and relying on the promoter to create value
Investing only in listed shares
Operational improvement, debt paydown and multiple expansion
Avoiding any use of debt
Buyouts acquire control, improve operations, use cash flows to repay acquisition debt and may exit at higher multiples.
Growth equity differs from venture capital in that growth equity usually invests in:
Idea-stage start-ups that are yet to generate any revenue
Distressed companies
Proven, revenue-generating businesses
Government bonds
Growth equity backs established businesses needing capital to expand, typically with lower risk than early-stage VC.
A manager's two funds both want to invest in the same deal. Good governance requires:
Giving it to the fund paying more carry
Letting the deal team decide informally
Splitting it without any documentation
Allocating per a disclosed allocation policy
Detailed due diligence findings are presented to the investment committee for final approval, after which the deal moves to documentation and closing.
Which step usually comes immediately before investment committee final approval?
Exit
Detailed due diligence
Monitoring
Distribution to investors
Detailed due diligence findings are presented to the IC for final approval, followed by closing.
A private credit fund's key risk control is:
Covenants and security on loans
Daily share price tracking of the borrower's listed competitors
Index replication
Investing only in cash
Covenants, collateral and regular monitoring protect a private credit fund's lenders against deterioration in the borrower's business.
What responsibility do members of an AIF's investment committee who are not employees of the manager carry for decisions they approve?
Have no responsibility at all, as they are only advisers to the manager
Must be SEBI employees
Share responsibility for decisions they approve
Cannot vote
SEBI holds IC members, including external ones, responsible for decisions they take, subject to the regulations.
A manager plans to invest in a company where a sponsor affiliate is a promoter. This should be:
Disclosed and approved by investors as required
Done quietly to save time
Prohibited for all AIFs in every case
Approved only by the affiliate
Investments involving the sponsor's associates are related-party transactions requiring disclosure and investor approval under SEBI's rules.
An event-driven strategy in Category III typically profits from:
Corporate actions such as mergers and demergers
Long-term holding of rent-yielding real estate in metro cities
Collecting coupons on government bonds
Index tracking
Event-driven funds seek gains from price effects of corporate events such as mergers, demergers, buybacks and restructurings.

Fund Due Diligence – Investor Perspectiv.overview: This chapter covers how investors assess AIF managers before committing. It explains investment due diligence (team, strategy, track record and attribution, portfolio construction, pipeline), operational due diligence (valuation, custody, compliance, cyber security, service providers), alignment of interest, terms and fees, ESG and stewardship considerations, and reference checks. It highlights red flags such as unexplained team departures, selective track records and weak controls. Focus on the evidence investors should seek and how to interpret gross versus net returns and realised versus unrealised performance.
questions: When reviewing a track record, an investor should prefer evidence from:
Unrealised marks set by the manager
Projected returns in marketing material
Industry averages
Realised exits with cash returned
Realised returns are confirmed by cash, while unrealised marks depend on valuation judgement.
Which finding in operational due diligence is a serious concern?
Use of a reputed auditor
A documented valuation policy
A dedicated compliance officer who reports to the board of the manager
No independent reconciliation of positions
Without independent reconciliation of positions with the custodian and brokers, errors or misappropriation may go undetected.
An investor asks for deal-level attribution of a manager's past funds. The aim is to learn:
The location and size of the manager's offices across cities
The fund's legal form
Which professionals generated the returns
The manager's marketing costs
Attribution shows who led successful deals and whether they remain with the team.
A manager's previous fund shows a high IRR but low DPI after eight years. The investor should:
Assume the fund is top quartile
Ignore DPI as irrelevant
Commit immediately
Probe why little cash has been returned
Low DPI late in a fund's life means value is mostly unrealised, so exit prospects and valuations need scrutiny.
Which is the strongest sign of alignment in a fund?
High management fees charged on total commitments for the fund's full life
A significant GP commitment from personal funds
Guaranteed carry
No clawback provision
Personal capital at risk aligns the manager's outcome with investors'; high fees and guaranteed carry weaken alignment.
ESG due diligence on a manager mainly examines:
How environmental, social and governance risks are handled
The manager's personal tax returns
Daily share prices
The fund's NAV only
ESG diligence checks how the manager identifies and manages ESG risks in portfolio companies.
A manager shows only its three best deals in a pitch. This is a concern about:
Over-diversification across too many sectors in the past funds
High DPI
Low fees
Selective presentation of track record
Cherry-picking deals misrepresents overall performance; investors should ask for the full record.
Why do investors check a manager's key-person and succession plans?
SEBI fixes the salaries of key persons named in the PPM
Results may depend on a few individuals
It affects tax rates
It sets the hurdle rate
Departure of key people can disrupt the fund, so succession planning and key-person clauses are important.

Legal Documentation and Negotiations.overview: This chapter covers the legal documents of an AIF and negotiation of terms between managers and investors, and between funds and investee companies. Fund documents include the PPM, trust deed, contribution agreement, investment management agreement and side letters, with terms such as key-person, removal, clawback, MFN, defaults, transfers and advisory committees. Deal documents include term sheets, share subscription and shareholders' agreements, with protections such as anti-dilution, tag-along, drag-along, ROFR, board seats and information rights. Focus on the purpose of each clause.
questions: A right of first refusal (ROFR) in a shareholders' agreement gives the investor:
The right to match an offer before shares are sold to a third party
The right to force all shareholders to sell
A guaranteed dividend
Automatic board control
ROFR lets an existing holder buy shares on the same terms before they go to an outsider.
Full-ratchet anti-dilution protection means that if new shares are issued at a lower price:
The investor's conversion price drops to the new price
The investor loses its preference rights and becomes an ordinary shareholder
The investor must invest more money
Nothing changes for the investor
Full ratchet resets the conversion price to the lower issue price, strongly protecting the investor; weighted-average methods are milder.
An MFN clause in a side letter entitles an investor to:
Manage the fund
Better terms later given to comparable investors
Exit at NAV at any time, irrespective of the fund's lock-in terms
Waive all fees
MFN lets the investor elect to receive more favourable terms offered to other similar investors.
Information rights in a PE investment allow the fund to:
Vote on all employee hirings
Receive regular financial and operating reports
Sell shares without restriction
Fix product prices
Information rights ensure periodic reporting so the investor can monitor its investment.
A 'key-person event' typically triggers:
An increase in carry
Automatic winding up of the fund without any vote by investors
Suspension of the investment period
Higher management fees
When named key people leave, the investment period is often suspended until investors approve a solution.
A put option negotiated by a PE investor against promoters allows the investor to:
Sell its shares to the promoters on specified terms
Buy more shares at a discount
Force a merger
Avoid all taxes
A put gives an exit by requiring promoters to buy the investor's shares, subject to legal limits on assured returns for foreign investors.
Side letters must be handled so that they:
Are hidden from SEBI
Override the PPM without disclosure
Comply with SEBI's rules on investor rights
Guarantee returns
Side letters must fit SEBI's framework on pro-rata and differential rights and be disclosed as required.
A term sheet is generally:
A fully binding share purchase agreement
A SEBI filing
Non-binding on commercial terms, except clauses like confidentiality
A valuation report
Term sheets summarise key terms before definitive documents; most commercial terms are non-binding except confidentiality and exclusivity.

Valuation.overview: This chapter covers fair valuation of AIF portfolio investments. It explains market approaches (trading comparables and precedent transactions), income approaches (DCF and its terminal value), the price of recent investment, net assets, and adjustments for control, marketability and preference rights. It also covers SEBI's requirements on independent valuers, valuation frequency and the use of IPEV or industry-endorsed guidelines, and the governance of valuation policies. Practise EV-to-equity bridges and perpetuity calculations, and understand when to recalibrate valuations after new information.
questions: A company has EBITDA of ₹25 crore. Peers trade at 12x EV/EBITDA and the company's net debt is ₹50 crore. Its equity value is:
₹300 crore
₹350 crore
₹250 crore
₹200 crore
EV = 25 × 12 = ₹300 crore. Equity = 300 − 50 = ₹250 crore. ₹350 crore wrongly adds net debt.
A company's free cash flow next year is ₹8 crore, growing 5% forever. At a 13% discount rate, the enterprise value is:
₹100 crore
₹61.5 crore
₹160 crore
₹105 crore
EV = 8 ÷ (0.13 − 0.05) = ₹100 crore. ₹61.5 crore ignores growth.
Calibration in private company valuation means:
Using the same value every year
Taking the average of all analyst targets
Using book value only
Aligning model inputs with the entry price, then updating
Calibration checks that the method reproduces the transaction price at entry, and then updates inputs as conditions change.
A valuer applies a discount for lack of marketability to a stake because:
It cannot be sold quickly in an open market
It carries more rights than listed shares and therefore commands a premium
SEBI mandates a fixed 30% discount
It is listed on an exchange
An illiquid holding is worth less than an otherwise identical freely tradable one; the discount is judgement-based, not fixed.
The 'price of recent investment' method is most reliable when:
The round was two years ago
The price was set by insiders only
The company has since failed to meet its milestones and is raising a down round
The round was recent and at arm's length
A recent arm's-length round is good evidence of fair value; older or insider-only rounds are weaker evidence.
SEBI requires AIF valuations to be carried out by an independent valuer mainly to:
Increase reported returns so that the fund can raise its next fund faster
Avoid audits
Set tax rates
Reduce bias in NAV and fee computation
Independence limits the manager's influence on valuations that affect performance and fees.
In a DCF, a higher discount rate, other things equal, will:
Raise the valuation
Have no effect
Double the terminal value
Lower the valuation
A higher discount rate reduces the present value of future cash flows.
Precedent transaction multiples often exceed trading multiples because they include:
Lower growth assumptions
A marketability discount
A control premium
Tax refunds
Acquirers pay a premium for control, so deal multiples are typically higher than minority trading multiples.

Fund Monitoring, Reporting and Exit.overview: This chapter covers ongoing management of an AIF after investment. It explains portfolio monitoring, reporting to investors (capital account statements, quarterly reports, valuations), reporting to SEBI and the trustee, the annual PPM compliance audit, exit routes for portfolio companies (IPO, strategic sale, secondary sale, buyback, recapitalisation) and liquidity options for investors (secondaries, continuation funds), as well as fund wind-up, tenure extension, dissolution and in-specie distribution. Focus on choosing exits and on the investor-protection rules around end-of-life options.
questions: A recapitalisation as an exit route means the portfolio company:
Lists on a stock exchange
Raises debt to pay a dividend to shareholders
Is liquidated
Merges with the fund so that its shares are cancelled
In a dividend recap, the company borrows and distributes the proceeds, allowing a partial exit without selling shares.
Extension of a close-ended Category I or II AIF's tenure beyond its stated life requires:
Only the manager's decision
Approval of two-thirds of unit holders by value, within limits
SEBI's prior approval for any extension
No approval at all
Tenure may be extended by up to two years with approval of two-thirds of investors by value; further options follow SEBI's framework.
An investor in a close-ended AIF wants to exit early. The most realistic route is:
Selling its interest in the secondary market
Redeeming its units at NAV from the fund on giving notice
Asking SEBI to refund
Defaulting on capital calls
Close-ended AIFs do not offer redemptions; secondary sales provide liquidity, usually at a discount.
A buyback exit involves:
The company or promoters repurchasing the fund's shares
An IPO
A strategic merger
A write-off
In a buyback, the investee or promoters buy back the investor's stake, often under negotiated put rights.
Which report helps an investor see its share of fund NAV and cash flows?
Private placement memorandum
Trust deed
Term sheet
Capital account statement
The capital account statement shows contributions, distributions and the investor's share of NAV.
In-specie distribution at the end of a fund's tenure means:
Paying cash only
Distributing unsold investments to investors directly
Converting the fund to a mutual fund
Selling all assets to the sponsor
Investors receive the remaining securities themselves instead of cash, subject to approval.
A strategic sale is often favoured over an IPO because it:
Gives a complete exit at once, often with a premium
Always gives a higher price than an IPO
Needs no negotiations
Avoids taxes
Strategic buyers can acquire the whole stake at once and may pay a synergy premium.
Fund monitoring of portfolio companies typically includes:
Daily trading of their shares to capture short-term price moves
Running their payroll
Board participation and KPI tracking
Setting their tax rates
Funds monitor portfolio companies through board seats, management reporting and tracking of key performance indicators.

Taxation.overview: This chapter covers the tax treatment of AIFs and their investors in India. It explains pass-through status for Category I and II AIFs (except business income), TDS on distributions, treatment of losses, taxation of Category III AIFs at fund level under trust rules, characterisation of income as capital gains or business income, non-resident investors and treaty access, GST on management fees and the tax issues around carried interest. Since the new Income-tax Act has renumbered provisions, focus on principles rather than section numbers or rates.
questions: Dividend income received by a Category II AIF is taxed:
At the fund level only, with investors receiving it tax-free
As capital gains
Exempt in all cases
In investors' hands as dividend income
Under pass-through, dividend income retains its character and is taxed in investors' hands.
Business income of a Category II AIF is taxed at fund level. When that income is later distributed, investors are generally:
Taxed again at slab rates
Taxed at double the fund rate
Required to pay GST
Not taxed again on it
Business income taxed at the fund level is exempt in investors' hands on distribution, avoiding double tax.
Losses of a Category I or II AIF (other than business losses) can be passed to investors only if:
They are non-residents
The fund is open-ended
The loss exceeds ₹1 crore
They have held units for the prescribed minimum period
Loss pass-through requires investors to have held units for at least the prescribed period, preventing loss trading.
Carried interest received by managers is a contested tax issue because:
It is always exempt
It may be treated as capital gains or fee income
It is taxed as agricultural income
It is outside Indian tax law
Characterisation depends on structure and facts; tax authorities may treat it as service income rather than capital gains.
A Category III AIF trust with indeterminate shares may be taxed:
At zero
Only on distributions
At the maximum marginal rate
At each investor's own slab rate on the share distributed
When beneficiaries' shares are not determinable, trust income is generally taxed at the maximum marginal rate.
GST on management fees is a cost to investors because:
SEBI levies it
The fund usually cannot claim input credit
It is refunded to the manager after the fund's annual audit
It applies only to carry
AIFs typically cannot set off GST paid on fees, so it raises fund costs.
A non-resident investor in a Category II AIF benefits from a tax treaty by:
Opening a fixed deposit
Registering as an FPI only
Doing nothing
Providing a tax residency certificate and forms
Treaty rates generally require a tax residency certificate and related forms from the non-resident investor.
The main purpose of TDS on AIF distributions to residents is to:
Replace investors' final tax liability on the income distributed
Collect tax early and track income
Exempt investors from filing
Fund SEBI
TDS secures tax revenue and creates an audit trail; investors still declare income and claim credit.

Regulatory Framework.overview: This chapter covers SEBI's AIF Regulations and circulars from a manager's perspective: registration and eligibility, sponsor and manager obligations, continuing interest, minimum corpus and investment, investor limits, accredited investors and large value funds, investment conditions and concentration limits by category, leverage, PPM filing and changes, valuation, reporting, KMP certification, stewardship, PMLA obligations, direct plans and distribution rules, conflicts and penalties. Focus on the stable thresholds and the principles behind rules that SEBI revises frequently.
questions: A Category II AIF has a corpus of ₹500 crore. The sponsor or manager's minimum continuing interest is:
₹12.5 crore
₹10 crore
₹5 crore
₹25 crore
For Category I and II, it is the lower of 2.5% of corpus or ₹5 crore. 2.5% of 500 = 12.5, so the requirement is ₹5 crore.
A Category II AIF with investable funds of ₹320 crore can invest at most how much in one investee company under the general limit?
₹32 crore
₹64 crore
₹160 crore
₹80 crore
Category I and II AIFs may invest up to 25% of investable funds in one investee: 25% × 320 = ₹80 crore.
The maximum number of investors in an AIF scheme (other than angel funds) is:
No limit
SEBI caps an AIF scheme at 1,000 investors, except angel funds, which keeps AIFs as private pools rather than public offerings.
Which of the following must an AIF manager do under the PMLA framework?
Accept cash freely
Skip KYC for HNIs
Share data publicly
Verify investor identity and report suspicious transactions
AIFs must perform KYC, maintain records and report suspicious transactions as reporting entities under the PMLA framework.
Large value funds for accredited investors enjoy:
Exemption from SEBI registration
Certain relaxations, such as higher concentration limits
Guaranteed returns
Unlimited leverage for Category II schemes investing in unlisted debt
SEBI provides relaxations such as higher concentration limits for large value funds of accredited investors.
A Category II AIF wants to borrow to make investments. This is:
Not allowed, except temporary borrowing within limits
Allowed up to 2x NAV
Allowed without limit
Mandatory
Category I and II AIFs may borrow only temporarily for operational shortfalls, within limits.
Material changes to the PPM generally require:
Investor consent or an exit option for dissenters
Only a notice from the manager, with no exit option for investors
Approval by the investee
Nothing
Material changes require investor approval as prescribed and an exit option for dissenting investors.
The minimum investment per investor (other than accredited investors and certain employees) in an AIF is:
₹1 crore
₹25 lakh
₹50 lakh
₹10 crore
SEBI sets ₹1 crore as the minimum investment per investor, with exemptions for accredited investors and certain employees or directors.

Investments Landscape.overview: This chapter places Category I and II AIFs within the wider investment landscape. It covers asset classes, the difference between public and private markets, the investor universe (HNIs, family offices, pension funds, insurers, endowments, development finance institutions and foreign LPs), and how investors' horizons and liabilities shape their appetite for illiquid assets. It also explains the illiquidity premium and the role of private capital in financing start-ups, growth companies and infrastructure in India. Focus on matching investor types to private-market commitments and on why private markets can offer return premiums.
questions: Which type of investor commonly acts as an anchor in Indian infrastructure and SME funds, often with development objectives?
Retail investors through monthly SIPs in liquid funds
Corporate treasuries parking surplus cash for a week
Day traders seeking intraday gains
Development finance institutions
Development finance institutions and government-backed funds frequently anchor funds that support infrastructure and SMEs. Short-horizon investors cannot commit to illiquid funds.
An insurer considering a private equity allocation must mainly reconcile it with:
The daily NAV movements of the liquid mutual fund units it holds for claims
Its brand advertising budget for the year
Its liability profile and regulatory investment limits
