The number of agents it employs
Insurers invest against long-term liabilities and are subject to IRDAI investment norms, which determine how much illiquid exposure they can take.
Private capital matters for the Indian economy mainly because it:
Replaces the need for any bank lending to small and mid-sized businesses in India
Guarantees jobs in every company it backs
Is available only to government-owned companies
Funds companies that cannot easily raise bank loans or list
Start-ups and growth firms often lack collateral or scale for bank loans or IPOs; private equity and venture capital fill that gap.
Compared with a listed equity fund, a Category II PE fund offers investors:
Daily liquidity and lower fees than an index fund
Potential illiquidity premium with long lock-in
Guaranteed returns because holdings are unlisted
Freedom to redeem at NAV whenever needed
PE funds may earn a premium for illiquidity and active ownership, but capital is locked up for years and fees are higher.
A family office with ₹500 crore and no near-term spending needs wants to add private equity. A reasonable first step is to:
Set a target allocation and commit across vintages
Invest the full amount in one fund in one year
Choose the single fund with the highest past IRR and commit the whole amount to it
Wait until markets are at an all-time high
A planned target allocation, built over several vintages and managers, manages timing and manager risk. Concentrating in one fund or chasing past IRR is risky.
The 'denominator effect' faced by institutional investors refers to:
A fall in the value of private assets caused by higher management fees in a weak market
The rise in the number of funds in the market
Private assets exceeding target weight after public markets fall
The reduction in management fees over time
When listed assets fall sharply, the slower-marked private allocation becomes a larger share of the portfolio, possibly breaching targets and limiting new commitments.
Why are pension funds generally considered natural long-term investors in private markets?
They need daily liquidity for all benefits
They are barred by their regulators from holding any listed equities at all
They pay no attention to risk
Their liabilities stretch decades into the future
Pension liabilities are long-dated and predictable, allowing part of the portfolio to be locked up for higher returns.
Which statement about private markets versus public markets is most accurate?
Private markets publish transaction prices continuously, like stock exchanges
Public markets have no regulation
Private markets are free of all risk
Private markets have less disclosure and price discovery
Private markets rely on negotiated deals with limited disclosure and periodic valuations, unlike continuously priced, highly regulated public markets.

Types of Investments.overview: This chapter covers the instruments and strategies used by Category I and II AIFs: common and preference equity, compulsorily convertible instruments, optionally convertible debentures, mezzanine and structured debt, venture debt, private credit, real estate and infrastructure investments, and special situation assets. It explains seniority in the capital structure, liquidation preferences, conversion terms, warrants and covenants, and how FEMA influences instrument choice for foreign capital. Focus on the risk–return trade-offs of each instrument and on which instruments suit early-stage, growth, buyout and credit strategies.
questions: A start-up issues CCPS to a fund at ₹100 per share with a 1x non-participating liquidation preference. On a sale at a low price, the fund will receive:
The higher of its preference amount or its as-converted share
Only its as-converted share of sale proceeds, even if this is below its investment
Twice its investment in all circumstances
Nothing until all equity holders are paid
A non-participating preference gives the holder either its preference amount or what it would get on conversion, whichever is higher.
An optionally convertible debenture (OCD) differs from a CCPS mainly because the OCD:
May be repaid as debt if not converted
Must always convert into equity on a fixed date
Ranks below equity in a liquidation
Cannot carry any coupon
OCDs give the holder a choice to convert or be repaid, so they behave like debt unless converted. CCPS must convert into equity.
A mezzanine lender often receives an 'equity kicker'. This is:
A higher seniority than senior secured debt
A guarantee from the government
Warrants or conversion rights adding upside
An exemption from interest payments
Equity kickers such as warrants compensate mezzanine lenders for subordination with a share in equity upside.
For a stressed company, a special situation fund may acquire its loans from banks mainly in order to:
Earn the original coupon on the loans without taking any credit or recovery risk
Drive a restructuring or resolution and gain from recovery
Avoid all legal processes
List the loans on a stock exchange
Buying stressed loans at a discount gives the fund influence over restructuring or insolvency resolution and upside from recovery.
Which covenant protects a private credit lender by restricting a borrower's further borrowing?
A tag-along right that lets the lender sell its shares alongside the promoter
A dividend reinvestment plan
A negative covenant limiting additional debt
A right of first offer on shares
Negative covenants restrict actions such as taking more debt or selling assets, protecting the lender's position.
Real estate equity funds generally earn returns from:
Fixed coupons guaranteed by the developers whatever the sales of the project
Interest on government securities
Development profits, rental income and value appreciation
Daily trading of property shares
Real estate equity returns come from project margins, rents and capital gains, with risks of delay and market downturns.
Why do foreign investors in Indian start-ups often prefer CCPS over OCDs?
OCDs cannot be issued by Indian companies
CCPS carry a dividend guaranteed by the company irrespective of its profits
CCPS can be redeemed at any time
FEMA treats CCPS as equity, while OCDs are treated as debt
Under FEMA, instruments that compulsorily convert are equity; optionally convertible instruments are debt, subject to ECB rules.
Venture debt carries more risk than a typical corporate loan mainly because borrowers:
Have long records of stable profits and plenty of fixed assets to pledge
Are government-owned entities
Have no equity investors
Are often loss-making with limited collateral
Venture borrowers depend on future equity funding and usually lack cash flows and hard assets, so lenders rely on investor backing and warrants.

AIFs in India and Its Suitability.overview: This chapter explains Category I and II AIFs under SEBI's regulations — venture capital and angel funds, SME funds, social impact funds, infrastructure funds, special situation funds, private equity, private debt and funds of funds — and their role in India's capital formation. It also discusses suitability: which investors can bear illiquidity, long horizons, capital calls and uncertain outcomes, and how a manager should assess investor sophistication. Focus on classifying funds into the right category and sub-category, and on spotting situations where an AIF is unsuitable.
questions: A fund will invest in road and renewable energy projects and seeks to register under a category viewed as economically desirable. It should register as:
Category III long-short fund
Category II fund of funds
Category I infrastructure fund
A real estate investment trust
Infrastructure funds are a Category I sub-category. REITs and InvITs are listed trusts under separate SEBI regulations.
A fund lending to mid-market companies through structured debt, without leverage, would usually register as:
Category I SME fund
Category III AIF
A non-banking finance company
Category II AIF
Private debt funds without leverage or special incentives fall under Category II.
Which investor is the best fit for a Category I venture capital fund?
A retiree who needs stable monthly income from a modest savings corpus
A saver who wants capital protection
A trader seeking returns within a month
One who can tolerate high failure rates and a long lock-in
VC investing involves many failures and a few big winners over long periods, suiting investors with high risk tolerance and patience.
Why is a capital-call structure important to explain to a new AIF investor?
She can skip drawdowns without any consequence
The fund takes all money upfront and returns it monthly
Capital calls are optional for all investors
She must keep cash ready to meet drawdowns when called
Investors commit an amount drawn over time; failing to meet calls can trigger default penalties, so liquidity planning matters.
A Category II AIF plans to invest mainly in units of other AIFs. It is a:
Special situation fund
Social impact fund
Fund of funds
Angel fund
A fund that invests in other AIFs is a fund of funds, typically registered under Category II.
A client with ₹1.5 crore of total savings wants to put ₹1 crore into a PE fund. A manager should be concerned mainly about:
Her preferred sector for investment and whether the fund matches that sector
Whether she lives in a metro city
The colour of the fund's brochure
Concentration and illiquidity relative to her wealth
Committing two-thirds of total savings to an illiquid fund is risky and likely unsuitable, regardless of the investor's interest.
Special situation funds are permitted to acquire stressed loans, subject to conditions, under:
The mutual fund regulations applicable to credit risk and debt schemes
The insurance regulations
SEBI's framework for special situation funds
The PFRDA regulations
SEBI's special situation fund framework under Category I allows acquisition of stressed loans in line with RBI's directions.
Category I and II AIFs must be close-ended mainly because:
SEBI wants them to be listed on stock exchanges and traded daily like shares
They invest only in government bonds
Investors demand daily NAV
Their unlisted holdings cannot be sold quickly to meet redemptions
Illiquid unlisted investments make open-ended redemptions impractical and unfair to remaining investors.

AIF Ecosystem.overview: This chapter describes the participants in a Category I or II AIF: sponsor, manager, trustee, investment committee, custodian, registrar, administrator, valuer, auditor, merchant banker, legal and tax advisers, placement agents and distributors, and investors including LP advisory committees. It explains each party's duties under SEBI's framework, requirements for key personnel and certification, and the compliance officer's role. Focus on responsibilities and independence: which functions protect investors and who is accountable when something goes wrong.
questions: Which party in a trust-based Category II AIF usually appoints the investment manager?
The trustee
The investee companies
The registrar
The placement agent
The trustee, acting for the trust, appoints the manager through an investment management agreement.
Investors in a fund form an advisory committee mainly to:
Run the day-to-day portfolio of the fund in place of the investment manager
Review conflicts and give certain consents
Audit the fund's financial statements
Act as custodian of fund assets
LP advisory committees advise on conflicts of interest, valuation questions and consents required under the documents.
A legal adviser to the fund primarily helps with:
Selecting the stocks the fund will buy
Calculating the NAV every day
Raising capital from retail investors
Drafting fund and deal documents
Lawyers draft the PPM, trust deed, agreements and deal documents and advise on regulatory compliance.
Who is responsible for ensuring that the AIF's operations comply with SEBI regulations on a daily basis?
The manager, through its compliance officer
The investee companies
The investors
The statutory auditor of the investee companies, through its annual audit
The manager is responsible for compliance and must appoint a compliance officer to monitor it.
A sponsor of an AIF differs from the manager in that the sponsor:
Makes all the investment and exit decisions for the fund's portfolio
Holds custody of assets
Sets up the fund and maintains continuing interest
Prepares the audit report
The sponsor establishes the AIF and keeps the required continuing interest; the manager runs investments.
A fund's administrator typically handles:
Choosing which companies to invest in
Capital calls, distributions and investor accounting
Negotiating deal valuations and investment terms with the founders of investees
Approving SEBI registration
Fund administrators process drawdowns and distributions, maintain investor accounts and support reporting.
Why does SEBI require at least one key investment team member to hold NISM certification?
To exempt the manager from SEBI inspections and periodic regulatory reporting
To guarantee investor returns
To allow leverage
To ensure a minimum standard of competence
Certification ensures the team has baseline knowledge of AIF regulations and practices.
A tax adviser's main role in an AIF is to:
Manage the fund's investments and take decisions on new deals
Advise on fund structure and tax compliance
Hold the fund's securities
Distribute units to investors
Tax advisers help with structuring, pass-through compliance, TDS and investor tax reporting.

AIF Structuring.overview: This chapter covers structuring Category I and II AIFs: the choice of trust, LLP or company; the trust deed, contribution agreement, investment management agreement and PPM; unit classes and differential rights; onshore and offshore pooling; feeder funds and parallel funds; co-investment by investors; accredited-investor-only and large value fund schemes; and FEMA treatment of downstream investment. Focus on why a structure is chosen and how SEBI's rules on investor rights, co-investment and disclosure constrain structuring choices.
questions: A parallel fund structure is used when:
One fund invests all its money into another fund managed by the same manager
Separate vehicles invest side by side for different investor groups
Two managers compete for the same deals
A fund invests in listed shares only
Parallel funds, often onshore and offshore, invest alongside each other in agreed proportions for investors with different needs.
Under SEBI's rules, co-investment by a Category I or II AIF's investors in an investee company must be:
Always at a lower price than the AIF paid, to reward the co-investors
Kept undisclosed to other investors
On terms not more favourable than the AIF's
Made only by the manager's relatives
SEBI requires co-investment terms to be no more favourable than those of the AIF for the same investee, among other conditions.
A manager structures a scheme for accredited investors only. A key benefit is:
Exemption from SEBI registration and from filing a placement memorandum
Certain regulatory relaxations available to such schemes
Guaranteed tax exemption
Permission to accept retail investors
Accredited-investor-only schemes and large value funds receive some relaxations, as such investors are considered better able to assess risk.
A trust deed for an AIF mainly sets out:
The detailed terms of each portfolio company investment the fund will make
The salary of the manager's employees
The trust's objectives and powers of the trustee
Daily NAV of the fund
The trust deed creates the trust and defines its objects, the trustee's powers and the beneficiaries.
Why might a manager offer a separate unit class to an anchor investor with a fee discount?
To hide fees from other investors
To allow the anchor investor to take over management of the fund's portfolio
To reward a large early commitment, as disclosed
To avoid KYC of the anchor
Fee discounts for anchors are common if disclosed and consistent with SEBI's framework on differential rights.
An offshore feeder investing into an Indian AIF would typically be subject to:
No regulation at all
Rules of both its home jurisdiction and Indian law
Only Indian mutual fund rules
Only US securities law
Feeders must follow their own jurisdiction's rules and Indian regulations such as FEMA and SEBI norms.
A Category II AIF set up as an LLP gives its partners:
Limited liability
Unlimited personal liability
Exemption from SEBI rules
Daily redemption rights
LLPs offer limited liability to partners, though they are less common for Indian AIFs than trusts.
Investors of a Category I or II AIF generally have rights that are:
Pro-rata to their commitments, subject to permitted exceptions
Decided by the manager case by case for each investor, without any disclosure
Equal irrespective of commitment
Determined by the investee
SEBI requires pro-rata rights in line with commitments, with limited permitted differential rights.

Fee Structure of AIFs.overview: This chapter covers how Category I and II AIF managers are compensated: management fees on commitments or invested capital, step-downs after the investment period, fund expenses and caps, carried interest, hurdle or preferred return, GP catch-up, whole-of-fund and deal-by-deal waterfalls, clawback and escrow, fee offsets from transaction and monitoring fees, and SEBI's disclosure requirements. Practise waterfall calculations and fee computations, and understand how terms shift value between investors and the manager.
questions: A fund with commitments of ₹600 crore charges 2% a year on commitments during a five-year investment period. Total management fees over that period are:
₹12 crore
₹60 crore
₹30 crore
₹120 crore
Annual fee = 2% × 600 = ₹12 crore. Over five years: 12 × 5 = ₹60 crore.
Fund capital is ₹150 crore, total proceeds ₹240 crore and the preferred return is ₹12 crore. With 20% carry and no catch-up, the carry is:
₹18.0 crore
₹15.6 crore
₹2.4 crore
₹48.0 crore
Profit = ₹90 crore; above hurdle = 90 − 12 = ₹78 crore; carry = 20% × 78 = ₹15.6 crore.
For the same fund (capital ₹150 crore, proceeds ₹240 crore, preferred return ₹12 crore, 20% carry) with a full catch-up, carry is:
₹15.6 crore
₹12 crore
₹18 crore
₹20 crore
With full catch-up and sufficient profits, the manager receives 20% of total profit: 20% × 90 = ₹18 crore.
An 8% hurdle compounded annually on ₹50 crore of contributed capital for two years requires investors to receive first:
₹58.00 crore
₹54.00 crore
₹66.64 crore
₹58.32 crore
With annual compounding, 50 × 1.08² = ₹58.32 crore must go to investors first. ₹58 crore wrongly applies simple interest.
A 'management fee offset' means that:
Investors pay double management fees whenever the fund makes a new investment
The manager pays investors a fee
Carry is reduced to zero
Transaction or monitoring fees reduce the management fee
Fees the manager earns from portfolio companies are partly or fully credited against management fees, so investors are not charged twice.
A fund's management fee steps down after the investment period mainly because:
The manager's workload shifts from investing to managing exits
SEBI prohibits fees after five years
Carry is paid instead of fees
Investors stop paying any expenses
Fees often fall or move to invested capital after the investment period, reflecting reduced deployment work.
Why do investors prefer a whole-of-fund waterfall to a deal-by-deal waterfall?
Carry is paid only after all contributed capital is returned
The manager receives carry earlier, which improves alignment with investors
It removes hurdle rates
It increases management fees
Whole-of-fund waterfalls defer carry until investors recover capital and the hurdle, reducing clawback risk.
A clawback obliges the manager to:
Return excess carry received, after final accounting
Return management fees each year
Pay investors a fixed return
Buy all unsold assets of the fund at book value at the end of its life
If carry received exceeds the manager's entitlement on final reckoning, the clawback requires repayment.

Fund Performance and Benchmarking.overview: This chapter covers performance measurement for Category I and II AIFs: IRR (gross and net), multiples such as MOIC, TVPI, DPI and RVPI, the J-curve, the effect of subscription lines, vintage-year and strategy peer benchmarks, quartile rankings, public market equivalent methods, and SEBI's benchmarking framework through benchmarking agencies. Practise calculating each multiple and interpreting differences between IRR and multiples, and understand why comparisons should use the same vintage and strategy.
questions: A fund invested ₹25 crore in a company and realised ₹90 crore on exit. The MOIC is:
MOIC = 90 ÷ 25 = 3.6x. 2.6x would be the net gain multiple (65 ÷ 25).
A fund has paid-in capital of ₹120 crore, distributions of ₹108 crore and NAV of ₹60 crore. Its DPI is:
DPI = 108 ÷ 120 = 0.9x. TVPI is 1.4x and RVPI is 0.5x.
An investor puts in ₹100 crore and receives ₹133.1 crore exactly three years later. The IRR is:
100 × (1 + r)³ = 133.1 gives r = 10%. 11% is the simple average of 33.1%.
Why should a 2018-vintage fund be compared with 2018-vintage peers?
All vintages always deliver the same returns
SEBI requires every manager to raise exactly one fund in each calendar year
Fees differ only by vintage
Entry valuations and market conditions were similar
Funds of the same vintage faced comparable entry valuations and market conditions, which makes peer comparisons fairer.
A fund's DPI is low but TVPI is high in year eight. This means:
Most of the value is still unrealised
Most value has already been returned
The fund has negative returns
Fees have been waived
A high TVPI with low DPI shows value sits in NAV rather than cash returned, so realisation risk remains.
Net IRR is usually lower than gross IRR because net IRR:
Includes only unrealised investments
Ignores cash flow timing
Deducts fees, expenses and carry
Adds back management fees
Net IRR measures investors' actual returns after management fees, fund expenses and carried interest, so it is below gross IRR.
A public market equivalent analysis shows a fund under-performed the Nifty on a cash-flow-matched basis. This means:
The fund outperformed the index after adjusting for the timing of cash flows
The fund's IRR was negative
The index cannot be compared
Investing the same flows in the index would have earned more
PME compares the fund with a hypothetical index investment using the same cash flows; underperformance means the index route would have done better.
SEBI's performance benchmarking framework for AIFs aims mainly to:
Fix minimum returns for each fund
Give investors industry-wide data for comparing funds
Replace valuation by independent valuers with an index-based valuation
Set management fees
Benchmarking agencies publish industry benchmarks based on AIF data, aiding comparison and transparency.

Legal Documentation and Negotiations.overview: This chapter covers documents and negotiated terms at two levels: between the fund and its investors (PPM, trust deed, contribution agreement, investment management agreement, side letters, key-person, removal, default, transfer, MFN and advisory committee clauses) and between the fund and investee companies (term sheet, share subscription agreement, shareholders' agreement, conditions precedent, representations and warranties, indemnities, board rights, veto rights, anti-dilution, tag-along, drag-along, ROFR and exit rights). Focus on the purpose of each clause and how it allocates risk.
questions: In a share subscription agreement, 'representations and warranties' given by the company and promoters mainly:
Confirm facts on which the investor relies, backed by indemnity
Guarantee a minimum return on the investment for the life of the fund
Fix the exit date of the fund
Set the fund's management fee
Reps and warranties state facts about the business; if untrue, the investor can claim under indemnity provisions.
'Conditions precedent' in a deal document are:
Rights that arise only after the fund has exited the investee company
Clauses about the fund's tax status
Investors' redemption rights
Requirements to be met before the investment is completed
CPs, such as approvals and diligence closures, must be satisfied before the investor funds the deal.
Affirmative or veto rights in a shareholders' agreement allow a minority PE investor to:
Run day-to-day operations of the company
Receive a guaranteed dividend
Block key decisions without its consent
Force the company to list within a year
Veto rights over matters such as new issuances, budgets and related-party deals protect minority investors.
A 'no-fault' removal clause in fund documents lets investors:
Remove the manager only after a court has found it guilty of misconduct
Redeem units at NAV
Remove the manager by supermajority without proving cause
Cancel past investments
No-fault removal gives investors a route to replace the manager by a high vote threshold even without misconduct.
A drag-along right is typically subject to conditions such as:
Unlimited use at any price by any shareholder
Approval by SEBI for every sale
A ban on strategic buyers
Minimum price or timing thresholds
Founders usually negotiate safeguards like minimum valuations or time windows before a drag can be exercised.
Why do investors negotiate a cap on the fund's organisational expenses in the LPA or contribution agreement?
To increase the manager's carry
To limit set-up costs charged to the fund
To allow early redemption
To avoid KYC
Caps on organisational expenses prevent excessive legal and set-up costs from being charged to the fund and reducing investors' returns.
A default by an investor on a capital call may lead to:
The fund being dissolved automatically and its assets distributed to the others
SEBI paying the amount
Penalties such as interest, suspension of rights or forced sale
Higher returns for the defaulter
Default clauses protect the fund and other investors through penalties and possible forfeiture.
Information covenants in a PE deal require the company to:
List within two years
Provide regular financial and operational reports
Pay a fixed dividend
Give the fund majority control
Information covenants give the investor periodic accounts, MIS and notices of material events for monitoring.

Investment Strategies.overview: This chapter covers strategies used by Category I and II AIFs: venture capital (seed to late stage), growth equity, buyouts, PIPEs, private credit and venture debt, real estate, infrastructure, special situations and distressed investing, and funds of funds and secondaries. It also covers deal terms that support each strategy, such as anti-dilution, tag-along, drag-along and liquidation preference, and how valuation and exits differ across strategies. Focus on how each strategy creates value and its characteristic risks.
questions: A secondaries fund in private equity primarily:
Invests only in seed-stage start-ups through convertible notes and SAFEs
Lends to real estate developers
Buys existing fund interests or portfolios from other investors
Trades listed shares daily
Secondaries funds buy LP interests or portfolios, often at a discount, providing liquidity to sellers and shorter J-curves.
A start-up raises ₹50 crore from a fund for a 20% post-money stake. The pre-money valuation is:
₹250 crore
₹50 crore
₹300 crore
₹200 crore
Post-money = 50 ÷ 20% = ₹250 crore; pre-money = 250 − 50 = ₹200 crore.
A founder owns 60% of a company. A new round issues shares equal to 25% of the post-money company. The founder's stake becomes:
The new round dilutes all existing holders by 25%, so the founder holds 60% × 0.75 = 45%. 35% wrongly subtracts 25 points.
A PIPE investment by a Category II AIF means investing in:
A listed company through a private placement
An unlisted start-up's seed round
Government bonds
Real estate projects
PIPE is a private investment in public equity — a negotiated placement in a listed company.
The main risk in an early-stage VC strategy is:
Interest-rate changes on bank deposits
A high failure rate among portfolio companies
Low volatility of start-up valuations
Guaranteed dilution protection
Most early-stage companies fail or return little; returns depend on a few big winners.
A growth equity fund typically takes:
Minority stakes in profitable or scaling companies
Majority control in every deal, using heavy acquisition debt
Only debt instruments
Stakes only in listed blue chips
Growth equity provides expansion capital through minority stakes with lower leverage than buyouts.
An infrastructure fund's long-term returns depend heavily on:
Daily stock market movements
Regulatory and concession terms of the projects
The fund's office location
Retail investor sentiment
Infrastructure cash flows depend on tariffs, concessions and regulation, making these key risks.
A fund of funds investing in Category II AIFs offers access to diverse managers but:
Guarantees top-quartile returns
Adds a second layer of fees
Removes all illiquidity
Allows daily redemptions
FoFs charge their own fees on top of underlying fund fees, reducing net returns.

Investment Process and Governance of Fun.overview: This chapter covers the investment process of Category I and II AIFs — sourcing, screening, preliminary evaluation, term sheet, due diligence (commercial, financial, legal, tax, ESG), IC approval, documentation, closing, monitoring, value creation and exit — and fund governance: the investment committee, conflict-of-interest policy, related-party approvals, allocation policy, compliance with PPM and regulations, stewardship responsibilities, and roles of trustee and compliance officer. Focus on sequencing and on governance actions that protect investors.
questions: Commercial due diligence on a target company mainly assesses:
Only the company's tax filings
Market size, competition and the business model
The fund's own fee structure and how it compares with peer funds
Investors' KYC documents
Commercial diligence evaluates the market, competitive position and sustainability of the business plan.
A term sheet is usually signed:
After the fund exits the investment
Before detailed due diligence and final documents
After closing and funding
Only when the company lists
The term sheet records key commercial terms and often grants exclusivity before detailed diligence.
The 100-day plan after a buyout refers to:
Priority actions for value creation after acquisition
The period before SEBI registration
The time allowed to investors to redeem units after the fund's first close
The fund's marketing campaign
Buyout funds agree early priorities with management, such as operational fixes and governance changes.
Under SEBI's stewardship code, an AIF should:
Avoid any engagement with investee management
Vote only as the promoter wishes
Keep its voting policy secret
Monitor and engage with investee companies and disclose voting policy
The stewardship code requires institutional investors, including AIFs, to have policies on monitoring, engagement and voting.
A manager discovers that an investee's CFO is the manager's partner's relative. The manager should:
Disclose the relationship and follow the conflict policy
Ignore it, since a family relationship has no bearing on the fund's interests
Hide it from the investment committee
Immediately sell the stake at any price
Potential conflicts involving relatives of the manager's team must be disclosed and handled under the fund's conflict-of-interest policy.
Legal due diligence on a target typically reviews:
Market growth forecasts only
Fund investors' tax status
Title, licences, contracts and litigation
The fund's carry calculation
Legal due diligence checks ownership of shares and assets, licences and approvals, material contracts and pending litigation of the target.
Which governance practice reduces the risk of biased investment decisions?
Decisions taken by one senior partner alone, without minutes or written records
Recusal of conflicted members and recorded IC minutes
Allowing founders to vote in the IC
Skipping IC review for small deals
Recusal of conflicted members and recorded minutes make investment committee decisions objective, traceable and accountable to investors.
After investment, value creation in a PE portfolio company often includes:
Strengthening management, governance and operations
Daily trading of its shares
Withdrawing all board involvement
Reducing reporting to investors
Active ownership adds value by strengthening management, systems, strategy and governance of portfolio companies, not by trading their shares.

Valuation.overview: This chapter covers fair valuation of Category I and II AIF portfolios: approaches based on market multiples, comparable transactions, discounted cash flows, net assets and the price of recent investment; adjustments for preferences, control and marketability; valuation of debt and distressed holdings; and SEBI's requirements on independent valuers, frequency, and use of IPEV or industry-endorsed guidelines. Practise EV-to-equity bridges and round-based valuations, and understand when values must be recalibrated.
questions: A company has revenue of ₹60 crore, peers trade at 4x EV/revenue, and the company holds net cash of ₹20 crore. Its equity value is:
₹260 crore
₹240 crore
₹220 crore
₹280 crore
EV = 60 × 4 = ₹240 crore. Net cash adds to equity: 240 + 20 = ₹260 crore.
Revenue multiples are most often used to value:
Mature utilities with steady earnings
Government bonds
Early-stage companies with little or no profit
Cash balances
When earnings are negative or volatile, revenue multiples provide a usable reference.
A loan held by a private credit fund that is performing normally is typically valued with reference to:
The borrower's share price only
Discounted cash flows at a market-based yield
Its original amount regardless of credit change
The fund's carry
Loans are valued by discounting expected cash flows at yields reflecting current credit risk.
A down round at a much lower price than the fund's last mark signals that the fund should:
Reassess and likely lower the carrying value
Keep the earlier value unchanged until the company is finally sold or listed
Raise the value
Stop valuing the investment
New arm's-length pricing is strong evidence of fair value and usually requires a markdown.
Net asset value approach is most suitable for:
Asset-holding companies such as real estate holdcos
High-growth software start-ups
Companies with no assets
Listed blue chips
Where value lies mainly in underlying assets, summing their fair values less liabilities is appropriate.
Why does SEBI require AIF valuations to follow a disclosed methodology?
To guarantee high returns
To ensure consistency and allow investors to understand values
To eliminate all professional judgement from the valuation of unlisted holdings
To reduce taxes
Disclosure and consistency help investors assess NAV reliability and compare over time.
A stressed company's equity is valued close to zero while its secured loans retain value because:
Secured lenders rank ahead in recovery
Equity always has higher seniority
Loans are guaranteed by SEBI
Equity holders get paid first
In distress, recoveries flow first to secured creditors according to priority, while equity absorbs losses and may be worth little.
A valuer adjusts a minority stake's value for lack of marketability because:
The stake cannot be readily sold
It is listed and liquid
Minority stakes are always worth more
SEBI fixes the discount
Illiquid holdings typically warrant a discount reflecting difficulty of sale; the amount is judgement-based.

Fund Monitoring, Reporting and Exit.overview: This chapter covers monitoring and reporting during a Category I or II AIF's life and the exits that end it. Topics include portfolio monitoring through board seats and KPIs, investor reporting (capital account statements, quarterly reports, valuation and ESG reports), reporting to SEBI, the annual PPM audit, exit routes (IPO, strategic sale, secondary sale to financial investors, buyback, recapitalisation), GP-led continuation funds, tenure extension, dissolution and in-specie distribution. Focus on exit selection and the protections around end-of-life decisions.
questions: In a GP-led continuation fund transaction, a key safeguard for existing investors is:
Mandatory rollover of all investors
No disclosure of the transfer price to the existing investors of the fund
Manager setting the price alone
An independent price-discovery process such as a fairness opinion
Because the manager is on both sides, independent pricing and informed investor choice are essential.
Lock-in rules after an IPO affect a PE fund's exit mainly by:
Allowing immediate full sale on listing day
Cancelling the shares
Increasing carry automatically
Delaying the sale of pre-IPO shares
Pre-IPO shareholders may face lock-ins, so funds often exit gradually after listing.
A quarterly investor report of a PE fund typically includes:
Daily stock tips
Other investors' personal details
Portfolio updates, valuations and cash-flow summaries
The manager's personal tax returns
Quarterly reports cover portfolio performance, valuations, capital calls and distributions, and key developments in investee companies.
A strategic buyer may pay more than a financial buyer because it:
Is required by SEBI to pay a premium
Avoids due diligence
Can realise synergies with its existing business
Does not need to finance the deal
Synergies in costs or revenues allow strategic acquirers to justify higher prices.
When a fund reaches the end of its extended tenure with unsold assets, investors may approve:
Conversion to an open-ended mutual fund
A dissolution period or in-specie distribution as per SEBI's framework
Indefinite extension of the fund's life by the manager without investor approval
Forced sale to the sponsor at cost
SEBI provides options such as a dissolution period, liquidation scheme or in-specie distribution, with investor approval.
ESG reporting to investors helps them:
Compute the fund's carry
Avoid tax on distributions
Redeem units early
Track how portfolio companies manage ESG risks
ESG reports show progress on environmental, social and governance issues in the portfolio.
A secondary sale of a portfolio stake to another PE fund is common when:
The company is not ready for IPO but the fund must exit
The company has just listed
The fund is still in the first year of its investment period
SEBI bans IPOs
Sales to other financial investors provide an exit where IPO or strategic sale is unavailable.
The annual PPM compliance audit for an AIF checks:
Only the investees' accounts
Adherence to the terms disclosed in the PPM
Investors' income tax
The stock exchange's operations
It verifies that the scheme has followed its PPM, with findings reported to the trustee, manager and SEBI as required.

Taxation.overview: This chapter covers the tax regime for Category I and II AIFs: statutory pass-through for income other than business income, taxation of business income at fund level, TDS on distributions, loss pass-through conditions, taxation of non-resident investors and treaty access, characterisation of gains on portfolio exits, the tax treatment of carried interest and management fees (including GST), and investor reporting. As provisions have been renumbered under the new Income-tax Act, focus on principles rather than section numbers or rates.
questions: Interest income earned by a Category I AIF from its debt investments is taxed:
At the fund level only
As capital gains
Exempt in all cases
In investors' hands as interest income
Under pass-through, interest income retains its character and is taxed in investors' hands.
Why is the classification of exit gains as capital gains or business income important for a Category II AIF?
Capital gains are always exempt in the hands of AIF investors in India
Business income is taxed at fund level, not passed through
Business income is never taxed
It decides SEBI registration
Pass-through applies to non-business income; business income is taxed in the fund, changing investors' tax outcome.
A Category II AIF must deduct TDS on income credited to non-resident investors at:
Zero in all cases
A fixed 1%
The resident TDS rate only, as treaty rates cannot be applied by AIFs
Rates in force, or treaty rates where eligible
For non-residents, TDS applies at rates in force, and treaty rates may be applied if documentation is provided.
An investor who sells AIF units before the minimum holding period may lose the ability to:
Receive any distributions
Claim TDS credit
Set off losses passed through by the fund
File a return
Loss pass-through is allowed only if units are held for the prescribed period.
Carried interest structured through a separate unit class is often argued to be capital gains because:
It arises from units held as investments
It is always exempt
SEBI classifies it as salary income of the investment team members
It is paid by the government
Managers argue carry is investment return on carry units; authorities may contest this depending on facts.
GST on the management fee of a Category II AIF effectively:
Reduces the manager's income tax
Increases the cost borne by investors
Is paid by the investee companies
Applies only to carry
GST is charged on fees and usually cannot be offset by the fund, raising investor costs.
The annual statement issued by a Category I or II AIF to investors helps them:
Redeem units early
Report each type of allocated income correctly
Avoid KYC
Compute the fund's IRR
Investors need the breakdown of income by nature to file returns under pass-through.
A Category I AIF trust's business income, once taxed at fund level, is in investors' hands generally:
Taxed again at slab rates
Taxed as capital gains
Exempt on distribution
Subject to GST
Business income taxed at fund level is not taxed again when distributed.

Regulatory Framework.overview: This chapter covers SEBI's AIF Regulations and circulars applicable to Category I and II managers: registration, sponsor and manager eligibility, continuing interest, minimum corpus and investment, investor limits, accredited investors and large value funds, tenure and extension, investment conditions and concentration limits, temporary borrowing, PPM filing and changes, valuation, reporting, KMP certification, conflict rules, direct plans and distribution fees, investor charter, grievance redressal and penalties. Focus on the stable thresholds and the purpose of rules that SEBI frequently revises.
questions: A Category I AIF has a corpus of ₹150 crore. The minimum continuing interest is:
₹3.75 crore
₹5 crore
₹7.5 crore
₹1.5 crore
Lower of 2.5% of corpus (₹3.75 crore) or ₹5 crore, so ₹3.75 crore.
A Category I AIF with investable funds of ₹180 crore can invest at most how much in one investee company under the general limit?
₹45 crore
₹18 crore
₹36 crore
₹90 crore
Category I and II AIFs may invest up to 25% of investable funds in a single investee: 25% × 180 = ₹45 crore.
The tenure of a close-ended Category II AIF can be extended by up to:
Ten years at the manager's choice
Two years, with two-thirds investor approval by value
Any period without approval
Six months only, and only with SEBI's prior written approval
Extension of up to two years is allowed with approval of two-thirds of unit holders by value.
Investors with an unresolved complaint against an AIF can approach:
The NPS Trust
IRDAI Bima Bharosa
SEBI SCORES and then the ODR mechanism
The Income Tax Ombudsman
AIF grievances go to SEBI's SCORES, with online dispute resolution available for unresolved disputes.
Which statement on direct plans of AIFs is correct?
They have a longer lock-in
They guarantee returns
They carry no distribution fee
They are for retail investors only
Direct plans are for investors approaching directly or via registered advisers and carry no distribution or placement fee.
For Category I and II AIFs, distribution fee paid upfront is limited because SEBI wants:
Distributors paid only at fund exit
Most commission paid as equal trail over the fund's life
No distribution fees at all for any plan, whether direct or regular
Higher upfront fees for large investors
SEBI limits upfront payment to a portion of total distribution fee, with the rest on equal trail, aligning incentives.
Before launching a scheme, an AIF must file its PPM with SEBI through:
Its statutory auditor
A stock exchange
A SEBI-registered merchant banker
The trustee alone
PPMs must be filed through a merchant banker who conducts due diligence.
Which of these is an obligation of the AIF manager under SEBI's framework?
Ensure investments follow the PPM and regulations
Guarantee investors a minimum return each year on their contributed capital
List units on an exchange
Distribute profits every month
Managers must invest per the PPM, maintain records and comply with regulations; they cannot guarantee returns.
